title: The Fathers on Zechariah
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The word of God came to the prophet to show God's anger at the fathers, and it comes to a person who shares in it, as virtue comes to the diligent.
comments.comment:
In the second year of the reign of Darius the Persian king, in the eighth month of the second year of the beginning of the one ruling, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Zechariah, declaring how a great wrath has come upon the fathers of those being reproved, with God being indignant against those being accused. …

The word of God becomes toward someone when he participates in it, just as virtue and knowledge become in a diligent and knowledgeable man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's great anger is fitted to great sin, his very threat shows his goodness, and he only seems to turn away from his people when they turn from him.
comments.comment:
'These,' he says, 'says the Lord of hosts: The Lord was angry with your fathers, a great anger' (Zechariah 1:2). …

A great anger comes upon those sinning greatly and being impious; for God, giving judgment 'to each according to his works' (Romans 2:6) and according to the practice of the one transgressing the divine laws, does not threaten the same punishment to all, but one proportionate and corresponding to those who have sinned. And the threat breathes much goodness; for if God were to punish defensively those cast into this, he would not foretell, but would bring the punishment upon them without delay. …

The possessor of the divine word stands as a protector to urge the captured toward repentance, saying: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn to me,' keeping my commandments and coming to know my truth; for thus you will find me having turned to you. For I, being unmoved and unchangeable, always being the same and likewise, seem to turn away from you and to distance myself from you when you endure this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God threatens before punishing and what it means to turn to him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In great mercy God calls those who have drifted from him to draw near and gain eternal life, and the distance and nearness are of disposition and not of place.
comments.comment: Standing by, he who says these things says that the Almighty will do such things; for with great mercy and boundless kindness, he calls those who distance themselves from God and from virtue to return and draw near, so that by drawing near to him, they may receive eternal life, according to what is written: 'Draw near to the Lord and he will draw near to you' (James 4:8). These said retreats and proximities occur in relation and disposition, but not in place.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The people are told not to be like their wicked fathers, who would not hear the prophets' call to leave evil ways and perished, but to walk the divine ways.
comments.comment: You do not become like those who begot you according to wickedness, whom the prophets called before the present time, so that you might not suffer the same things as them. And what did they call to them? Or to turn away from faulty customs and evil ways? But not having heard and not having attended to them, they perished along with those deceived by false prophets … Since therefore neither the prophets nor the deceived are present, you, to whom I bring the word of God, walk the divine ways and do not pursue the evil ones.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the warning not to be like the fathers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophets had the Spirit of truth and gave profitable instruction, and because the fathers would not heed it, what the Lord had set out to do came upon them.
comments.comment: For divine and profitable instructions are announced to us in our Spirit—this is the Holy—by my servants the prophets who have it; for these, having the Spirit of truth and being prepared by it for speaking, benefit those who pay attention to them, of whom those called fathers have had experience; because they neither heard nor paid attention to them, they were answered through their works. Just as the Lord has stretched out to do, so it shall happen to them, even if God has stirred them to repentance, so that they might not suffer the things threatened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the fathers suffered what the prophets had warned of.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's works have order and proportion, and the prophet's word is arranged by number, the twenty-fourth day being a powerful square.
comments.comment: In the fourth and sixth month in the twelfth month—this is the month of Sabbath—in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying (Zechariah 1:7). All things happening and being given by God have order and harmony which has proportion, 'doing great and unsearchable things,' 'arranging all by measure and number.' Moreover, the word of the prophet lying before us, becoming visible more by scientific theory than by being heard, is arranged having much certainty according to number in a tetrad … And the twenty-fourth of the twelfth month according to the Hebrews. The number 24 is powerful as a square; for this is divided by its parts thus: half 12, a third 8, a fourth 6, a sixth 4, an eighth 3, a twelfth 2, a twenty-fourth 1. That which is born from 24 according to the composition of its parts is a square, for six times six. And nothing is so certain of forms as the square.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man on the red horse is the Savior who became man, the red horse is his flesh, and he stands between the two covenants, shaded by the depth of their meaning.
comments.comment:
I saw in the night, and behold a man riding a red horse, and he was standing among the two mountains of shade, and behind him red and mixed and variegated and white horses (Zechariah 1:8). … And the man riding the red horse is the Savior who became man. And a red horse is that which surrounds a body; for the human flesh is red by nature, because blood flows through it. But where did he see the man standing, and between whom, and when was the one receiving God to stand watch?

He saw him, then, 'among the mountains of shade.' These two covenants happen to be fruitful and shady because of the density of meanings and the ambiguity of the words concerning theology and incarnation. And since each of those announced in the two covenants has much obscurity with enigma and depth, in a night he saw the approach of the man to the horse, similarly to what was said about him: 'He set darkness as his hidden garment' (Psalm 18:11); for in this expression, that which is hidden is signified by the obscurity, just as in: 'The abyss was as his enveloping garment' (Psalm 104:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the rider is and what the horse and the shaded mountains stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The horses behind the rider differ in color: red for those who handed down the Word's becoming flesh, variegated for teachers suited to different learners, and white for those announcing divine things apart from matter.
comments.comment:
And those following him come behind him; for Moses, the great theophany, not yet being able to see his face knowingly, has been set to see those behind him, that is, those with him, and not other things existing of the creation of God. …

A different color of the horses behind the one appearing is written down, since some of them are men, and others are divine 'spirits, being sent for service for those about to inherit salvation.' For those who have handed over the human things of the Word's appearing and becoming flesh, are red, especially since even he, behind whom they exist, says 'a garment of red from Bozrah,' as it was said to him by those who saw: 'Why are your garments red?' saying his garments which surround the flesh and the blood sprinkled upon it. These things have been made more clear in the commentaries of the prophet Isaiah.

After the red horses behind the one being praised, various and dappled and white horses appeared. And perhaps the various and dappled ones are those who lead the teaching in many ways concerning the sensible and the intelligible, which the divine words say are 'visible and invisible,' while the white ones are those announcing the theological things apart from all matter. It must be said according to another thought that the various and dappled ones are those fitting in teaching to the various condition of those being instructed. Or was not Paul a various horse, being a follower of the Christ speaking in him, when to the Jews he became a Jew to win these, and to the lawless as lawless, to turn them from the lawless disposition, and to those under law as under law, so that he might win them also, persuading them to transcend 'the law of shadow' (Heb 10:1)? After having said these things, he says: 'I have become all things to all, so that I might save all' (1 Cor 9:22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the different colors of the horses stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The angel speaking in the prophet is either the angel of the prophecy or the Savior himself, for a teacher speaks within a listener who shares in him.
comments.comment:
The prophet himself says to the angel speaking in him: 'What are these, Lord?' And the angel speaking in him—that is, the angel standing by the prophecy—is he, or according to another thought, is it the Savior himself, about whom the prophet says: 'His name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel' (Isa 9:6). And the teacher speaks in the listener when he participates in him or is by disposition in him. …

The testimony of the former is: 'But Christ lives in me,' and also: 'Of the Christ speaking in me.' By this understanding also the singer said: 'I will listen to what the Lord God will speak in me,' and Habakkuk: 'I will stand watching to see what the Lord will speak in me' (Hab 2:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the angel spoke in the prophet.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those sent to go around the earth are excellent teachers among men and angels, but not everyone who goes around has been sent by the Lord, for the devil also goes around the earth.
comments.comment:
And the man who stood in the midst of the mountains answered and said to me: 'These are those whom the Lord has sent to go around the earth' (Zechariah 1:10). If anyone were to seek what comes from where, having seen the prophet's horses—red, varied, speckled, and white—the speaking angel promises him what was seen.

Not then, since there is a twofold vision concerning these, one more introductory and one having ascended higher, to the one who has known the introductory showing, the divine instructor promises the more perfect one, having received the perfect love of the revelation. The man who stood in the midst of the mentioned mountains answered twice: 'These are those whom the Lord has sent to go around the earth' (Zechariah 1:10).

According to a second vision, the people from the Hebrews and the nations happen to be overshadowed by two mountains, of whom, standing in the midst, the man already interpreted initiates into the mystery who those sent to go around the earth are. And they are excellent teachers from among men and angels, as it has been said nearby.

It is not in vain that they were sent to go around the earth by the Lord, not all of those promising to teach or those going around having been sent by the Lord. 'Going indeed around the earth' is the devil, as he himself said, in the examining of Job and the other athletes of God, doing this by especially bad intention, but not having been handed over by God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: That the whole earth is inhabited and at rest means that the rational soul, moving well, is calm and stable out of reverence for God and ceases its disordered shaking.
comments.comment:
What then do the sent ones say they have seen in the going around, or that the whole earth is inhabited and is at rest, as the following wording presents it thus. And they answered the angel of the Lord who stood in the midst of the mountains, and they said: 'We have gone around all the earth and behold, all the earth is inhabited and is at rest' (Zechariah 1:11). …

One should consider what it means for the whole earth to dwell and to be at rest. Since the rational soul is self-moving and ever-moving, when it moves well and blessedly, it is calm and rests from disordered shaking, and it bears this stability from divine reverence.

For it is written: 'The earth was afraid and was still when God arose to judgment' (Psalm 76:8-9), and: 'He who dwells on hope is still from every evil' (Proverbs 1:33), according to the inspired writing of the Proverbs. By this understanding, regarding the agitator Cain, moved as if God says: 'You sinned, be still' (Genesis 4:7), he is not only saying: 'Having sinned with disordered shaking, put an end to the disordered impulse'; for then you will be praised to be still, 'turning away from evil and doing good' (Psalm 34:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the earth being inhabited and at rest means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeing the nations believing and the earth at rest, the angel asks how long until Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, now in the seventieth year, are shown mercy.
comments.comment:
The angel of the Lord answered and said: 'Lord Almighty, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you overlook, until this seventieth year?' (Zechariah 1:12).

Having seen prophetically the angel of the Lord Almighty the whole earth dwelling and resting, and all the nations having believed in the Lord who came among them, he deems it worthy to be granted the knowledge of the King of all, until when and when Jerusalem and the cities of Judah beneath it will be shown mercy, the seventieth year of the captivity already having entered, through which they seemed to be passing by.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the angel's question about the seventy years.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jerusalem may mean the perfect soul or the Church and the cities of Judah the lesser souls, and the seventy years, seven decades, bring the perfect rest given by Christ who came to proclaim liberty to the captives.
comments.comment: It has been interpreted, according to each interpretation, that the cities of Judah might also be taken. If, therefore, Jerusalem is the perfect and enlightened soul receiving all things peacefully and steadily—for she is received into the 'vision of peace'—the cities of Judah are the inferior souls still struggling forward. If the name Jerusalem signifies the Church, being the 'holy one standing by Christ,' then the cities of Judah are interpreted as the souls that have not become such. The Apostle makes such a difference when writing to the Corinthians, blessing 'the Church with all those who call upon the name of the Lord' (1 Cor 1:2), as the Church is allegorically Jerusalem, while the cities of Judah are those who call upon the name of the Lord. According to both interpretations, Jerusalem and the cities subordinate to her sometimes suffer the same thing as the mother-city, so that, having received perception from the over-seeing, they may redistribute themselves, so as to suffer no longer the things of the captivity, 'the seventy-year period having come in.' For there shall no longer be laborious work, the Sabbath year having been fulfilled; for the number seventy, having been composed of seven decades, brings perfect rest, providing it through the one having come to 'proclaim liberty to the captives' (Luke 4:18), having risen out of Judah. For concerning the Savior it is announced: 'My King, Judah,' and toward him it is said regarding blessings: 'Judah, your brothers have praised you, your hand is upon the loins of your enemies, and all the sons of your father shall worship you' (Gen 49:8-9). When these divine words are announced, which kind of soul is it that is called Jerusalem, but also confessing, being the cities of Judah—for Judah is interpreted 'confessing'—that they might learn from Jesus 'that he is gentle and lowly in heart, that I might find rest' (Matt 11:29), pure souls heard, the seventy-year period being fulfilled.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord answered with beautiful and comforting words that Jerusalem and its cities would be shown mercy, which encourage and restore those returning from captivity.
comments.comment: To the angel who had spoken, 'How long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah?' (Zechariah 1:12), the Lord Almighty answered with beautiful words concerning the fact that Jerusalem and the cities under it would be shown mercy, and with comforting sayings manifesting and bringing much consolation. For how do they not encourage and restore those returning from captivity, so as to say thankfully: 'When the Lord restored the fortunes of Zion, we became like those having been relieved, we became rejoicing' (Psalm 126:1)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the beautiful and comforting words were.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Zion means a lookout who fixes on eternal things to keep the commandments, Jerusalem a vision of peace, and the Savior himself is the peace and grace given to those he loves.
comments.comment: “But I will be jealous for you.” He pre-announced these things by stirring her up, so that she would not fall to the threats, guarding the justice of the household undefiled. Zion and Jerusalem call the one being zealously loved so that she might no longer be exhausted by those attacking her toward evils, because of the virtues having come to her. For Zion is interpreted as a lookout, a settled commandment, and Jerusalem as a vision of peace; Zion is called by upward movement the one who looks not at the temporal things but the eternal things in order to do the commandments having been given. Following such a state is the unmixed and undisturbed nature of those succeeding. And peace is seen, that of which Jesus says: “My peace I leave to you” (John 14:27). And this is given with divine grace from God the Father and Lord Jesus Christ, as Paul teaches. And both these things, peace and grace, I say, the Savior is. For it is said concerning him: “He is our peace” (Eph 2:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is very jealous for Jerusalem and Zion and angry with the nations that attacked wildly after a short time of discipline, so that those who see God's people abandoned should fear and turn to piety.
comments.comment:
And the angel who was speaking in me said to me: 'Declare, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been very jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and I am very angry with the nations that are attacking, whereas I was only a little angry, but they have attacked for evil' (Zechariah 1:14). …

He says that a prophet is to be given a command by the angel of the Lord Almighty to cry out formally: 'Thus says the Lord: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, bringing great anger upon the nations'—those who are suffering, since, after the guardian had led them on for a little and short time of discipline and return, they attacked wildly and crudely. …

It is necessary for those seeing the ones belonging to God being abandoned to be struck with fear, to be flogged for the evils they committed, and to be struck with piety, lest they suffer the same things …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God meant to correct Israel by measured chastisement, but Babylon, though brought in for that, was merciless like a wild beast, and so God accuses it.
comments.comment: Yes, and with very good reason. For the God of all willed to rebuke Israel when he had turned aside to apostasy, and by measured chastisements to persuade him to run back to the worship he was used to, I mean the worship of the Law. But the Babylonian, though brought in for this purpose, was merciless like a wild beast and gave free rein to his fury. So he is accused, as God says plainly: “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that join in the attack; for I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack for evil” (Zechariah 1:14-15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God was angry with the nation he had used to punish Israel.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's words come with a 'because of this' tied to what people did, and so he returns to Jerusalem in mercy, pitying her like a protector and father after the enemies attacked for evil.
comments.comment: Since nothing happens by chance by the one providing for all things, because of this, causal conjunctions are often placed before things happening, God saying to those subject to his administration: instead of “these things you said or did,” “these things shall be brought to you.” Immediately indeed, even in the present word, there is carried the word having this manner: “Because of this these things says the Lord of hosts.” What is this, or the “I will be jealous for Zion and Jerusalem with great zeal” (Zechariah 1:14)? Since, “after my being angry a little, they attacked toward evils” (Zechariah 1:15) the enemies of those being envied, “I will return to Jerusalem in mercy” (Zechariah 1:16), pitying her like a protector and genuine helper, for he is a “father” to this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The house rebuilt in Jerusalem is the Church of the living God, and also the body of Jesus and each believer, while measuring the city shows God's mercy treating it as fruitful again.
comments.comment:
The manner of having mercy on Jerusalem is immediately announced: 'For my house shall be rebuilt in it' (Zechariah 1:16) and in its midst, so that by dwelling and walking among its citizens, He may perfectly have mercy on it, no longer allowing it to be desolate or plundered, proving Himself a zealot and one to be remembered, stretching out a measure over it again as before when it had prosperity and fruitfulness. For a desolate and neglected land that is not being surveyed, the land being pitied by God is instead measured like a fruitful land. And the city is measured, being laid out into groves and squares, and cut into gymnasia. …

The house being built in the midst of the pitied Jerusalem is the Church of the living God, in which it is fitting for the Healer of God, sanctified according to law, to dwell. This the Apostle speaking in Christ cries out to Timothy, writing thus: 'If you are delayed in seeing how one must conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, a pillar and foundation of the truth' (1 Timothy 3:15).

According to another understanding, the house being rebuilt in Jerusalem, which is Jesus, who was brought forth from Mary, having been built by the wisdom of God, has according to the proverbial decree thus: 'Wisdom built a house for herself' (Proverbs 9:1), concerning which the building wisdom said to the opponents: 'Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up' (John 2:19); this, he says, 'was speaking about the temple of his body,' as the evangelist wrote. Regarding the things said, each of the faithful is also a house being raised up to be a temple of God. 'For do you not know, he says, that you are a temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you?' (1 Corinthians 3:16). And the Savior himself says this clearly: 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and I will love him, and we will come to him and make a dwelling with him' (John 14:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the house rebuilt in Jerusalem means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The four horns stand for the many evil powers against which the saints struggle, and the prophet saw them with the eyes of his mind so that he might put on God's armor.
comments.comment:
And the four horns lying over the citizens of Zion and Jerusalem are builders. There are no others among those enemies about whom the Apostle and the rest say: 'Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers and authorities and the cosmic powers of this darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness' (Ephesians 6:12). Consistent with the multitude of the powers of the evil ones against which the struggle is for the saints, and the singer who says regarding the one overcoming the enemies: 'He shall mount upon a shield and a basilisk, and shall trample the lion and the dragon' (Psalm 91:13). And since each of the said evil ones rises tyrannically, he says they rule lawlessly.

These horns, promised through enigma, the prophet saw, lifting up the eyes of his mind, so that from having seen the preparation and the power of them, he might put on the invincible panoply of God. Who then are the builders sharpening the presented horns? It is possible to learn from the following, having such knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The horns were brought only to scatter Israel and Judah from the holy city into captivity, outside unity and harmony.
comments.comment: And he said to me: These horns which scattered Judah and Israel have ascended. The responding angel, showing to the prophet the clarified four horns, the work and the need for which they were brought, says to the one being enlightened, that the horns were brought for no other reason than to scatter Israel and Judah from the holy city, so that, having been scattered into captivity, they might become outside of unity and harmony. It was said previously as Judah confessing; but he, seeing God in his mind, is called Israel.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the four horns are said to have done.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not every craftsman is praised, for the horns are a workshop of unfaithfulness and crudity, but those God shows coming are craftsmen of mercy toward neighbors and of faith.
comments.comment: The seer, being pleased by the multitude of approaching enemies, is shown by the one pointing out the numbers called for help that the craftsmen are praiseworthy; for not all who fashion appropriate works are praised, but some are also counterfeit, whom they send away from one another according to the proverbial rule: 'Good men fashion mercy and faith; evil craftsmen do not know mercy and faith.' This worst workshop of the craftsmen is nothing other than the four horns, being an instrument of all unfaithfulness and crudity. Those whom God shows coming are craftsmen of mercy and faith, performing practical virtue through mercy toward neighbors, loving them as themselves, and fashioning faith through pious and scientific contemplation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the four craftsmen are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The four builders may be the four evangelists, or angels who gather the elect from the four winds, shown by God against the proud and against the fallen who lift up no head.
comments.comment: I read an explanation of someone having taken that the four builders are the four evangelists. Whether it is so, let those encountering the one who wrote thus judge. It is possible to say the four builders are 'to gather the sent angels to gather the elect of God from the four winds,' that is, from the four climates of the inhabited world. In order that the four builders might be understood, they are shown and led by the Forethinker of all things, God, against those lifted up with audacity and arrogance, and against those having fallen by God's judgment, not lifting up the head, neither of the captor nor of the captives, the holy builders being set in opposition. It is also worn away in custom that those acting badly do not lift up the head.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The craftsmen come to sharpen the horns, the nations raised against God's earth, so that none of the afflicted can lift his head, yet the horns prove too weak to tear apart those handed to them.
comments.comment: Having seen those shown to him and coming by God, he asks the one showing him what they will do having come, and God answers him that they come to sharpen the nations raised against God's earth, the four horns, in order to take the ones being handed over into captivity, so that they may scatter Judah and humble Israel, so that no one of the afflicted is able to lift up his head or defy the approaching enemies. But the word of the horns presents a greater weakness, for even after sharpening, it has not become possible for them to tear apart the ones handed over to them, even while the craftsmen who are sharpening them are present.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner is led down from on high to the depths, and one handed over to an unapproved mind cannot lift up his head to the things above.
comments.comment:
It is carried in the manuscripts instead of 'they brought down Israel,' as 'they led Israel down,' showing also by this word that the one sinning is brought from on high to below. And many are the writings that show this, such as: 'How has the morning star fallen from heaven, rising in the morning?' (Isaiah 14:12) and: 'They shall enter into the lowest parts of the earth' (Psalm 63:9). And other myriad words are revealing that the diligent ascends and is elevated, but the lover of pleasure descends, having a material choice, as to become 'fleshly, having been shaped by sin. …

And if the mind is sometimes signified by the name of the head, even this is not lifted up when someone 'is delivered to an unapproved mind, having not tested God to have in knowledge' (Romans 1:28). For how can he who has been held in an unapproved mind still think of the things above or split the heart in heaven, not having treasured in heaven? It corresponds to the scattering of Israel being recognized or being led away, that which is announced with full force by those having scattered against those having seized by force: 'Our bones have been scattered by the underworld' (Psalm 141:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man with the cord is the Savior, the builder of the spiritual Jerusalem, who lays its foundations and measures it, with angels and holy men building beside him as skilled craftsmen.
comments.comment:
This man [the man with the measuring cord], being a builder of Jerusalem, architecturally measures its width and length, having previously laid its foundations and having been cast down, and after the destruction which he underwent from the coming of wars and those capturing her, so that he may lay the foundations in the proper places, symmetrically and in order, upon which it was fitting for her walls to be raised.

And there was shown to the prophet a geometric measuring line, woven from various architectural threads, so that the previously prophesied might be fulfilled in: 'And a measure shall be stretched out over Jerusalem yet again' (Zechariah 1:16). And not far from the Savior being the architect, according to what was said concerning 'the city of the Lord of Powers,' that: 'God has founded it for eternity,' the apostle Paul is writing in concert concerning this divine city, which is expected by all those having pleased through faith, thus: 'For they received the city having foundations, of whom God is the craftsman and builder' (Heb 11:10).

The angels and holy men who rebuild with him, like excellent craftsmen, hold the aforementioned geometric measuring line in his hand called the practical power. Paul indeed writes concerning himself: 'As a wise architect, I laid a foundation' (1 Cor 3:10).

Furthermore, in Ezekiel, a man is seen holding a builder's rod and a reed to measure and found the holy temple of God (Ezek 40:5). In such a way he measured and crafted the building, it is possible to know, the one reading the prophet.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the man with the measuring line is doing and for whom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lifting the eyes means the inner man looking at fitting sights, and the man with the cord measures Jerusalem so that it can be rebuilt, perhaps the same as the rider on the red horse.
comments.comment: It has already been shown many times how one lifts the eyes of the inner man for the understanding of fitting spectacles. In the same manner as what was said, even now the prophet, lifting his eyes, saw a man holding in his hand a geometric cord, for the purpose, as a most excellent architect, of measuring how great the breadth and length of Jerusalem is, so that, the foundations being laid, its rebuilding may take place after it suffered demolition by enemies. Who the man seen by the prophet is, it is time to see. And see whether he is not the same as 'the one mounted on a red horse, standing between two shady mountains' (Zechariah 1:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the man with the measuring cord is and why he measures.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one with the cord measures the city's width and length so that its temples, streets and squares are laid out in harmony, and this applies to the soul, the Church and the heavenly city.
comments.comment:
By chance, one holding the geometric cord approaches to measure how much the width and length of Jerusalem is. For he is taking care to build well, knowing the location and the opportunity of the plots, so that each of the parts of the city, having been taken with appropriate width and length, may place the divisions, temples, monasteries, streets, and squares in harmony, so that in these streets the wisdom of God may carry itself with boldness, being proclaimed on the edges of the city walls according to what is philosophized in Proverbs, as if to say to those guarding this holy city to proclaim Him within it and upon its walls, day and night, by no means being silent but always speaking things for the salvation of its citizens.

Thrice Jerusalem has been often assigned by analogy, both of the visible soul and of the 'glorious Church not having a pillar or a support' because of holiness and fullness, and of the heavenly city of the living God, in every way to have its width and length measured by him having the geometric cord in his hand, a man being assigned by him having the reason of wisdom and knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Another angel comes out to give the message, since such things are shown not to a mere man but to a young man, as the holy man is young beside the divine angels.
comments.comment:
And behold, the angel speaking in me stood. And another angel was coming out to meet him, and said to him, saying: 'Run and speak to that young man there, saying.' He says that he saw the angel standing speaking in himself, and another angel coming out saying to him: 'Running, say to this young man what it is time to say.'

In many ways it has been interpreted before what it is that is spoken in the prophet by a divine angel and how this is made manifest, especially when the promise comes from another angel coming out. For it is not possible for the things being announced to be heard while remaining within and by oneself, but by coming out through condescension. Indeed, the showing of the things of the mystery happens not toward a man but toward a young man. For just as the holy man is a young man toward the divine angels, especially when he exists clothed as a young man, as it was said concerning him in the divine Proverbs such as this: 'A young man with the holy one, and his way is straight.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who walk in holiness are young in mind and taught by the angel who goes out, whose going forth, like the Lord's coming out for his people's salvation, leads the one cast out of paradise back in.
comments.comment:
Is not the way of the one traveling with holiness straight? Regarding those having such a participation in virtue, John in his epistle addresses them, saying: 'I wrote to you, young men, that you are strong and have overcome the evil one.' (1 John 2:14). Each one, and only the one, who is thus young in mind is taught by the angel who goes out to speak the things made clear next.

And see if the going forth of the angel is of the same power as what is said by the choir of the saints: 'You went out for the salvation of your people, to save your Christs,' and to him: 'I went forth from God and I have come.' For salvation and divine enrichment become the race of men cast out from paradise, having trodden the divine laws, when the 'angel of the will' of the 'great' God comes forth in order that he might lead in through obedience and divine instruction the one cast out, saying: 'Today with me you shall be in paradise.' The one coming forth promises to show great things concerning the spiritual Jerusalem, which the following word, having such a character, signifies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As the trees of paradise bear much fruit, the holy city is inhabited abundantly, for those who dwell in God's house and are nourished by the divine light cannot fail to bear fruit.
comments.comment:
Jerusalem shall be inhabited abundantly from a multitude of men and beasts in its midst, and I shall be to her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I shall be in her glory in its midst (Zechariah 2:4-5). In whatever way all the trees in paradise bear much fruit, so also the holy city Jerusalem is inhabited abundantly, having a multitude of men and beasts in its midst; for it is neither fitting nor possible for the divine and holy city to be found unfruitful, the unfruitful tree being cut off and given out to the fire.

Such was the one to whom the holy one cries: 'Therefore God brings you to an end, to uproot you and to transplant you from a dwelling, and your root from the land of the living' (Psalm 52:8), while everyone remaining in the house of God says thankfully: 'I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God' (Psalm 52:8). For how can the one dwelling in the house of God, nourished by the divine light, not bear fruit, in doing what is necessary and thinking the pious doctrines?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Jerusalem is inhabited abundantly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wall of fire consumes the thorns and briers that bear destructive fruit, and the Lord is around his people as around the holy city, which he glorifies by his presence.
comments.comment:
It [the wall of fire] consumes, 'a consuming fire,' especially those thorns and briers that bear fruit, and even more so those that are cut off and thrown out because they do not make good fruit but destructive and poisonous fruit. Similarly to the holy city, the Lord is said to be around the people in one of the songs of the ascents: 'The Lord is around his people' (Psalm 125:2).

Just as a wall of fire has become around Jerusalem the fallen, and has risen up as a glory in its midst, due to the being glorified by divinity and blessedness of those dwelling in the holy city which is encircled by God, about which the hymn-singer said, rather towards it: 'The city of God was spoken of as having been glorified' (Psalm 87:3), and also: 'Great and exceedingly praiseworthy is the Lord, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain' (Ps 87:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the wall of fire around Jerusalem does.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, the wall of fire around the holy city, would make those wise in the law hard for demons to assail if they lived rightly.
comments.comment: Consider, then, the Jews, who dwell in the holy city, of which the God of all says: ‘And I will be to her, says the Lord, a wall of fire round about, and I will be the glory in her midst’ (Zechariah 2:5). And besides this, they had been made wise by the law. That is why they used to say: ‘Blessed are we, the sons of Israel, for what pleases the Lord is known to us’ (Baruch 4:4). Would you not say, then, that the assaults of the demons would find such people very hard indeed to break into, if they chose to live rightly and to submit to the divine laws?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: When the nations around the holy city are punished, it will dwell secure, guarded by the Almighty as a wall of fire, as when those besieging it fled.
comments.comment: When the peoples around the holy city experience punishment, it shall be inhabited as it is by itself, guarded by the one who built it and chose it, according to what was said concerning its safety: 'Mountains are around it, and the Lord is around his people' (Psalm 125:2). Concerning such a guard, it is also brought forth in the present prophet as the Pantokrator: 'The Lord as a wall of fire' (Zech 2:5) shall be around it, which was made clear in the beginning of Zechariah, when Jerusalem is being inhabited as it is, and those who militarily besieged it have fled, according to what was said by the one dwelling in it: 'All the nations encircled me, and in the name of the Lord I defended them' (Psalm 118:10)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fleeing the land of the north means turning from evil and holding fast only to what is good, as the apostle advises.
comments.comment:
'O, O, flee from the land of the north,' says the Lord (Zech 2:6); 'for from the four winds of heaven I will gather you,' says the Lord; 'be saved, you who dwell in the daughter of Babylon' (Zech 2:6).

The word stirs up those scattered 'in the north, where the evils are burned up from the face of those dwelling in the land,' concisely desiring the flight to take place from the hands of the enemy, which is signified by the name of the north, doubling the epithet of the exhortation, saying: 'O, O, flee from the land of the north.' … The same as fleeing from the land of the north is: 'Turn away from evil,' and: 'Cease from your evils.'

And this is fulfilled when an abstinence from every kind of evil occurs, with only the good and praiseworthy being held fast, according to the exhortation of the apostolic advice: 'Test all things, hold fast to the good, abstain from every kind of evil' (1 Thess 5:21-22). And he alone and everyone flees from what is harmful, he who considers the good to be the good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what fleeing the land of the north means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Spirit calls like a herald to leave Babylon for Zion, where God is hymned, and God gathers from all climates, while the winds may also be taken as false teachings that toss the immature.
comments.comment:
And since it is not possible to hymn and sing to God while inhabiting the daughter of Babylon and the north, the Holy Spirit cries out like a herald, saying: 'O, oh, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord; be restored to Zion, you who inhabit the daughter of Babylon, because from the four winds I will gather you,' that is, from all climates of the earth's surface. This is equivalent to: 'From the four winds I will gather you,' which the Savior said in the Gospel, 'to send the angels to gather the elect from the four winds' (Matthew 24:31).

When Zion and the daughter of Babylon are allegorized, the winds must also be allegorized, namely, as fleshly powers or the various winds of false teaching, tossing and carrying away into atheistic mindsets and uncertain practices those who are infants in intellect, which is not praiseworthy; for the Apostle writes about such a state: 'Lest we be infants, tossed and carried about by every wind of teaching in cunning' (Ephesians 4:14). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Holy Zion is the safe place of return for those who lived in Babylon, whose name means confusion, so that all whose mind is disordered should be restored there to sing to God.
comments.comment:
The flight becomes unobstructed from the north when the Benefactor and Provider of all things gathers the citizens of the beautiful city of Jerusalem, who were scattered among the four winds. By providing an easy escape, He makes it manifest where and in which city salvation occurs for those fleeing from the harsh and cold north wind; for it is written about it: 'Boreas is a harsh wind' (Proverbs 27:16), and again: 'A cold north wind shall blow' (Proverbs 27:16). Holy Zion is the place where those who formerly inhabited the daughter of Babylon can be safely restored. The multitude of those inhabiting her is her daughter.

And since the name 'Babylon' is taken to mean 'confusion,' everyone whose mind is disordered and poured out is Babylonian; he who is to be separated and of a disposition to have love for Zion ought to be restored, so that he may hymn and sing to God, since there it is fitting to hymn God, and it is right to sing a harmony to Him. For it has been said: 'A hymn is due to You, O God, in Zion' (Psalm 65:1), and: 'Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion' (Psalm 9:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Babylon and Zion stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God was sent not as Almighty but by descent, and he who touches God's people touches the apple of his own eye, harming himself, as Cain, Saul and Absalom did.
comments.comment: An apostleship occurring to men follows the glory of the one called God, being Almighty; for he was not sent as Almighty, but in the manner of 'emptying himself' and 'taking the form of a servant' by descent. What is being pre-announced to those still at their peak while being plundered by nations? 'He who touches, he says, of you, touches the apple of his eye' (Zechariah 2:8), harming himself rather than striking the righteous or those he intends to harm, similarly to the one striking the apple of his own eye. This theory gathers from many places of Scripture: Cain, wishing to harm, exposed himself before he intended to murder (Genesis 4:8). The same happened to Saul pursuing David in order to kill (1 Samuel 24:1-22), and to Absalom attacking his father tyrannically (2 Samuel 15:1-14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why touching God's people is touching the apple of his eye.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To touch here means to bring harm, not simple contact, so the verse speaks of one who touches God's people for evil.
comments.comment: And as for 'to touch,' let it not mean here to strike instead of bringing affliction; for we commonly have this expressed in Scripture. For 'do not touch my sheep' does not forbid simple contact, but the audacity against the saints to harm them. And 'he who touches you touches the apple of his eye' (Zechariah 2:8) similarly means one who touches for evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'touches' means in this verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rulers who crucified the Lord of glory, not knowing they were destroying their own order, destroyed themselves, as the saying about touching the apple of his eye foretold.
comments.comment: But Paul interpreted who the rulers are: those who became the cause of the Lord being crucified, of whom he says there are many wisdoms. And he says: 'If they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Corinthians 2:8). If they had known that they were bringing about the destruction of their own order, they would not have dared to do this. As we previously said prophetically regarding 'he who touches you touches the apple of his eye' (Zech 2:8): they, having laid hold of the Savior, destroyed themselves; and they rushed to kill him, thinking they would end his rule. On the contrary, it turned out for them: they themselves were destroyed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To touch God's people means to harm them, and such harm falls on the harmer, who becomes plunder to those he plundered, and then they know the Lord Almighty has sent the Almighty Word to men.
comments.comment: In the present prophetic text it signifies harming through touching, and especially through those whom God himself says to those attacking murderously against his own people: 'Touch not my anointed ones, and do evil to my prophets' (Psalm 105:15). To touch lightly lies in: 'It is good for a man not to touch a woman' (1 Corinthians 7:1), signifying approaching shamefully and licentiously. From this verb it is also shown that to touch well is to join through contact, as in that said by Jesus: 'Someone touched me' (Luke 8:46), when the woman with the issue of blood, desiring to be healed, touched by grasping the hem of Jesus' garment. Having fallen so many interpretations upon the present voice of 'touching,' the now present prophetic word signifies harming through maltreatment. But he who intends evil against those guarded by God touches the apple of the eye of the inner man. And it is manifest how he who touches the servants of God touches the apple of his own eye, because of the saying: 'I will lay my hand upon them' (Zechariah 2:9), making manifest the disciplinary power, so that they become plunder to those they formerly plundered, leading them into captivity, so that they serve those against whom they formerly ruled tyrannically. Which event leads to 'you shall know that I am the Lord Almighty' (Zechariah 2:9), having been sent by the Lord Almighty, is the completion of the things pre-announced. The God Word is being sent Almighty from the Almighty, coming to men by the good pleasure of the Father.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sabaoth in the Hebrew is rendered Lord of Powers or Pantokrator [Almighty], and the Son, through whom all things were made, speaks in Zechariah as the Almighty sent by the Almighty.
comments.comment: It should be noted that those who have been precise regarding the Hebrews say that the voice of Sabaoth is lying in the Hebrew. The Seventy translate into Greek either 'Lord of Powers,' 'Lord of Armies,' or 'the Pantokrator.' They say, indeed, that in this place where Sabaoth is located, the translation into 'Lord of Powers' has occurred. But if Sabaoth lies concerning the Savior, it is also translated into 'the Pantokrator,' so that it is fitting the voice of the Pantokrator should be attributed to the Savior; for if all things came into being through Him, and He is before all things, and all things consist in Him, and He holds providentially all things having come into being through Him, and He is before all things consisting in Him, it follows that He is called Pantokrator. For it is His face speaking in Zechariah: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been sent after glory' (Zechariah 2:8), and 'You shall know what the Lord of hosts has sent me to you' (Zechariah 2:11). For the Son is the Pantokrator being sent by the Pantokrator, being sent by the Father. And most clearly in the Apocalypse of John, the Savior is called Pantokrator: 'These things says the Lord, the faithful and true witness, the one who was and the one who is and the one who is coming, the Lord God the Pantokrator' (Rev 1:8). For these things have been said about the Son without dispute.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Son is Almighty as the Father is, being one with him and holding all things by the same word, and 'beginning of creation' means the reigning kingdom over all creatures.
comments.comment: For by the same word by which the Father royally holds all things he made through his Word, by this also the Son holds all things and reigns, pre-existing the things constituted in him. By whom the Apostle says 'the visible and invisible were created in Christ,' being before them and all things constituted in him: 'For he is before all, and all things are constituted in him' (Colossians 1:16-17). And it is nothing strange if Almighty is from Almighty; for God is from God and light from light. For being consubstantial with the one who begot him and one with the begetter according to 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), all things the Father has are the Son's. The Father has being God, light, holy, Almighty. These are the Son's. Almighty, therefore, from Almighty is the Son, all-king from the one reigning over all. Indisputably in John's Revelation the Savior is confessed as Almighty, he himself saying thus concerning himself: 'Thus says the faithful witness, the beginning of God's creation, the one who is and who was and who is coming, the Lord God the Almighty' (Revelation 3:14). Being Almighty, the one saying these things is not a creature, lest he also hold himself. For this is absurd: the same one creating and being created by himself, and reigning and being held. But even if the theologized one is called 'beginning of God's creation' in the quoted voice, as royally ruling and being Almighty by this very fact, he is the beginning of creation — that is, the reigning and leading kingdom over all creatures.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophet begins his cry with joy because sorrow is hateful and joy longed for, telling the captives to rejoice greatly since the one who brings them back has come.
comments.comment: Since sorrow is hateful to people and joy is longed for, he begins his cry with joy, saying: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion” (Zechariah 9:9). “Rejoice greatly,” the prophet cries to those in captivity. “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). Why “Rejoice”? And why “greatly,” and “be glad and delight” (Zechariah 2:10)? Because He who brings you back has come, as the father of the King who brings you back foretold, saying: “When the Lord brought back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted; then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with gladness” (Psalm 126:1–2).
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The delight commanded is the fruit of the Holy Spirit, love, joy and peace, and those returned from captivity rejoice because the Lord has tabernacled in the midst of Zion.
comments.comment:
The Lord has come and has tabernacled in her midst, the temple having been raised again and God dwelling in it. 'Rejoice and be glad,' says the prophet, 'daughter of Zion.' In many places of the Scripture, the daughter of each city is called, meaning the citizens who fulfill her. The delight and the gladness which the divine word commands to have is the same as the joy which happens to be the fruit of the Holy Spirit, arranged together with divine love and blessed peace, which the holy Apostle makes manifest writing thus: 'The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace' (Galatians 5:22). Having experienced this stability, those delivered from captivity say: 'When the Lord turned the captivity, we became as those who are returned; then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with shouting' (Psalm 126:1). And in another Psalm it is brought in harmony: 'When the Lord turns the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad' (Psalm 14:7).

For those who mourned, being torn away from their own fatherland by the law of captivity, follow a return to it, to delight and be glad because the Lord has tabernacled in its midst, the cause of the delighting and the gladness. And what is the cause of the gladness and delight—is it the enjoying of the currents of the river filled with waters, about which it is written: 'The river of God was filled with waters,' and also: 'The currents of the river make glad the city of God; God is in its midst, it shall not be moved' (Psalm 46:4-5), no longer departing or abandoning, but because of goodness remaining with it?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the command to rejoice and why the Lord's dwelling in Zion causes joy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many nations fleeing to the Lord in the day of the sun of righteousness will be received as his people, no longer without hope, called a holy nation and royal priesthood.
comments.comment:
And what good and salutary will attach to the indwelling of the Lord in the midst of the beautiful city, or the 'fleeing of many nations' repenting 'unto the Lord in the day' when the sun of righteousness is grasped, of which the patriarch Abraham, having received light, seeing it, rejoiced, and with him the sons and children of him who are according to faith and his works having become, as saying thanks: 'This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it' (Psalm 118:24). And the 'many nations having fled unto the Lord' shall receive the people to enrich the one to whom they have fled, no longer atheistic and without hope. …

concerning these things God says in the prophet: 'I will call him who is not my people my people, and he himself will say: Lord my God you are' (Hosea 2:23), so that they may be addressed as 'a holy nation, a holy priesthood, a race of God' (1 Peter 2:9).

For he says to those fleeing to God in the same manner as mentioned by him to whom they have fled: 'You shall be to me an elect race, a holy nation, a royal priesthood, my people, through whom I shall display my virtues' (1 Peter 2:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the many nations that flee to the Lord become.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The people of God will know that the Lord Almighty sent the Redeemer, Jesus anointed to proclaim release to the captives, and the All-King will first inherit Judah, those who confess.
comments.comment:
What then follows for those who have become the people of God, or the dwelling in the midst of the heavenly and blessed Zion? For then then it will be known, by divine and accurate vision, 'that the Lord Almighty sent' (Zechariah 2:11) the one redeeming her, saying concerning his own Father: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me to preach to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives' (Luke 4:18).

For because of preaching to the poor, Jesus, who dwells in the midst of Zion, was anointed with the Holy Spirit and the power of God, proclaiming release to the captives held by unseen enemies, her children. For thus the All-King, the benefactor of her, will inherit Judah, those who confess. For the confession of Judah is interpreted. And so he will first inherit those called unto salvation; for from of old they were part of him and before that they suffered dispersion and captivity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord inherits Judah upon the holy land, honoring his Father and loving the Church, his Mother, who is Jerusalem, having come down to seek and save the lost.
comments.comment: But where will he inherit Judah being part of him, except upon the holy land in which he will be long-enduringly well-suffering, he who honors his Father God and his Mother the Church being Jerusalem, whom he still loves, taking again and reigning in her midst, knowing that he has come to dwell in her midst, sent from the Lord Almighty, when bowing heaven he descended to us humans, saying: 'I have descended from heaven to do the will of him who sent me' (John 6:38), 'to seek and to save the lost' (Luke 19:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The chosen city is the pure soul that sees the peace surpassing understanding, the glorious Church of Christ, and the heavenly Jerusalem.
comments.comment: In many ways, the identity of the chosen city of God is revealed. For the pure soul that sees "the peace surpassing all understanding" (Phil 4:7) is called Jerusalem, and so is the glorious Church of Christ, "the holy and immaculate, having no spot or wrinkle" (Eph 5:27); and through an elevated allegory, it is the heavenly city of the living God, according to it having been thus written: "Come up, O Zion, mountains and city of the living God, Jerusalem, heavenly and with myriads of angels, in festival" (Hebrews 12:22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the city the Lord chooses again stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Flesh' has many senses in Scripture, and here it means humankind, which, being rational, is called to stand in awe before the face of the Lord.
comments.comment:
The term 'flesh' being homonymous signifies many things, as it stands for the God-breathed writing itself. For when it is said in the Psalms, 'To give food to God to all flesh' (Psalm 136:25), it stands for all mortal animals being sustained by food in living, as also in: 'All flesh is gathered according to its kind'. And when the Apostle writes: 'For who has ever hated his own flesh? But nourishes and warms it' (Ephesians 5:29), the body joined to the rational soul is signified, as it is possible to learn from the apostolic word itself having this: 'In this manner men ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. For who has ever hated his own flesh?' (Eph 5:28), and the following. …

But there is also when only men are revealed by the designation of flesh, as in: 'Hearken to prayer, to you all flesh shall come' (Psalm 65:2). And it comes to God in relation and disposition, not the irrational, but the humanity, being made worthy of the bountiful gift of the Holy Spirit by the one saying: 'I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy' (Joel 2:28). … This so-called flesh, being rational, is receptive of divine awe; for indeed, 'to stand in awe from the face' of the one appearing to it is commanded, concerning which the pure of heart, saying, send up a prayer: 'Appear your face and we shall be saved' (Psalm 80:3). And he gives the reason hereafter for why all flesh ought to stand in awe before the face of the Lord God, bringing forth: 'Because he has been raised from his holy clouds' (Zach 2:17).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy clouds are the divine prophets who pour out the spiritual rain of righteousness, and the Savior came forth from them to fulfill the law and the prophets, so that all flesh should stand in awe.
comments.comment:
But holy clouds are not those that cause sensible rain, but those that bring the spiritual downpour, according to that said in Isaiah concerning Israel, by way of allegory called a vineyard, from the face of the Lord: 'I will command the clouds not to rain upon it' (Isaiah 5:6), because of the thorns and not having grapes as fruit. … For of the vineyard being allegorized, the clouds were also taken up in harmony, sometimes raining to water, sometimes being prevented from doing this. Concerning such rain-givers, again in that same prophet, it is commanded by God:

“Let the clouds rain down righteousness.” For since righteousness is a virtue of the rational soul, it is not the sensible clouds that pour rain, but the divine prophets, being called clouds by upward analogy.

Since therefore the Savior has come forth from these clouds to fulfill the law and the prophets, for this reason “let all flesh stand in awe from the presence of the Lord” (Zechariah 2:13) the God, which was predicted and shown when the prophecy having this character was fulfilled: “The God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Psalm 84:7), and he shone so that “we might behold his glory, as the only-begotten from the Father” (Jn 1:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the holy clouds are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The light cloud on which the Lord comes is the flesh of Jesus born of the virgin, light because sin, which weighs down the soul like lead, had no part in it.
comments.comment:
Having come forth from the holy clouds, which were interpreted to be Moses the great hierophant and the prophets who possessed the Holy Spirit, he arrived upon a light cloud, having mounted upon the world which is among us, Egypt which is called by analogy. And the prophecy concerning these things begins from this place: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and he shall come into Egypt, and the works of her hands shall be shaken” (Isa 19:1).

Having been transferred from Egypt to the place concerning the earth, in harmony the light cloud shall be raised to the humanization of the Savior, the God the Word sitting upon that which had gone forth from Mary.

For what light cloud does not have the weight of sin, or the flesh of Jesus which did not consist of the union of man to woman being heaviest, but from the Holy Spirit having come upon the virgin not having experience of man, and upon whom the power of the Most High overshadowed, to make the born one holy without marriage. And even more the lightness and thinness of the lordly cloud is revealed from the fact that it was not made by sin nor did the soul of Jesus know it.

For nothing else drags and weighs down the soul of men like lawlessness, being compared to a talent of lead, because it searches and drags down those practicing it; but the soul of Jesus was not tried by this weight, “having loved righteousness and hated lawlessness” (Psalm 45:7)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God shows the prophet the great priest standing not in a human way but divinely before the angel, the truly great priest ordained forever, standing firm so that all who come may drink.
comments.comment:
But God shows great and superlative things that happen, which are neither sensible nor human. Because of this, God shows to the prophet the great priest Joshua not standing humanly, but standing divinely before the face of an angel of the Lord; not merely the son of Josedech as is shown through him, but the truly great priest, who had traversed the heavens, ordained 'according to the order of Melchizedek,' not according to the power of a fleshy commandment for a certain time, but according to an unpassable priesthood; for it has been said of him: 'You are a priest forever' (Ps 110:4). Jesus the great priest was not shown merely as it happened, but standing unshakeable and firmly established, similarly to what was said in the Gospel: 'Jesus cried out saying: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink' (John 7:37).

For everyone coming to him drinks, because he stands ready.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the high priest Joshua stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil stood at Judas's right hand because Judas had given him place, but he stood against the great priest to oppose him, as when he sought to sift Peter, and those who hope in God suffer no harm.
comments.comment:
And he stood also at the right hand of Judas, as it is said in the 108th Psalm: 'Set the sinner against him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.' But see the great difference in the words; for regarding the one betraying the Savior, he stands at the right hands having already taken them, 'having given place to the devil.' For it is said that 'he cast into his heart to betray' the one who had chosen him as best teacher and also Savior. And after the casting into the heart, he had entered into him in order to work the things of betrayal in him as he works in the children of disobedience. For it is written that 'after the morsel Satan entered into him.'

But the great priest did not stand at the right hands any other way than by opposing him, especially when he attempts to seize those being helped and instructed by him; does he not stand opposing from the right hands when he seeks to exclude those called to faith and the rest of virtue, according to what was said: 'Behold, Satan has asked of you to sift you like wheat, and I have prayed for you,' O Peter, our disciple, 'so that your faith may not fail' (Luke 22:31)?

Regarding not being harmed by those whom he opposes, and they receive authority against him, so that they tread upon all the power of the one opposing hostily, they suffer no harm at all because of hoping in the one who is being crushed under the feet of the saints, the standing and muddy devil; for it is written: 'Everyone having hope in God' will remain without infirmity and undefeated, not fainting, not falling away.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the devil standing at his right hand to oppose him means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil stood at the right hand of both Judas and Jesus the priest, but against Jesus to make war on his right side, where he does his works, while Judas's right side was already his.
comments.comment: Regarding Josedech: 'the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him' (Zechariah 3:1). And see that for both Judah [Judas] and Jesus [Joshua] the priest, the great, the purest and holy, the devil stood at the right hand. But concerning Jesus it is said: 'to oppose him.' He stood in order that, being positioned against his right side, he might wage war against him, because he performs practical matters on the right and has such a disposition. But regarding Judah, it is not so. The right side of Judah was already seized. He gave a standing to the devil in these things. And here 'they stood opposite.' For this reason they drew near, in order that they might harm and trouble.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord rebuked the devil when he joined to himself by his word the man he loved, and the Jerusalem he chose is our Jerusalem above.
comments.comment: It is also clear from the prophecy of Zechariah, having prophesied long ago concerning this name, for he says, 'the Lord showed to me Jesus the great priest, standing before the face of an angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: the Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you' (Zechariah 3:1). For when did he rebuke him? When he joined to himself by word the man loved by him. 'The one who has chosen,' he says, 'Jerusalem,' making it clear that this is our Jerusalem, concerning which the apostle says, 'but our Jerusalem is above; for this one serves with her children' (Galatians 4:26).
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: An ember torn from the fire is half-burnt wood, weakened and no longer fruitful, yet saved from being wholly consumed and kept for other uses, like a captive freed from the fire of captivity.
comments.comment:
What will result from "rebuking the Lord against the devil" (Zechariah 3:2) is made clear; for it says: "Is this not like an ember torn out of the fire?" (Zechariah 3:2).

An ember is half-wood, having reached the point of turning into charcoal, no longer possessing the strength and hardness of wood. Such were also the enemies of the King of the Hebrews, concerning whom God said to him: "Do not fear, nor let your soul faint because of these two smoking embers" (Isaiah 7:4).

Just as these appeared weak, having fallen under the punishment of fire, so also the one receiving rebuke from the Lord who chose Jerusalem has become weak, as if no longer bearing fruit, having been deprived of vital power, according to the ember torn out of the fire; for a plant thus scorched can no longer bear fruit, even if it was torn from the fire so that it might not be wholly consumed and turned into ash, being useful for other needs, for which God takes it, for the sake of beauty to those being fashioned, being molded and beaten out as silver and gold vessels (2 Tim 2:21).

For how can the one liberated from the fire of captivity—by the one proclaiming remission and descent to the captives and giving it to the fatherland which he formerly inhabited before the enemies came, seized and scattered them—not be torn from the fire?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the ember torn out of the fire stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The priest, mourning with the fallen captives, is clothed in filthy garments, which are lawless deeds, and the angel orders them removed as the iniquities are taken away.
comments.comment:
And Joshua was clothed in filthy garments, and he stood before the angel. And he answered and said to those standing before him, saying: "Take away the filthy garments from him." And he said to him: "Behold, I have taken away your iniquities, and clothe him in festive attire, and place a clean turban upon his head." And he clothed him with festive attire.

Regarding the spoken words set forth concerning Jesus [Joshua] the high priest, who iconically demonstrates the truly faithful high priest, possessing an unassailable priesthood. For since the saints are found to be loving, they sympathize with those in misfortune, weeping from sympathy, 'weeping with those who weep' (Romans 12:15).

Because of this, while the fallen Israel is still at its peak in captivity, the priest who holds the care in his hands, mourning and suffering with them, is clothed in filthy garments, which the angel present with him protects should be removed from him. And the filthy garments are the deeds performed without law; for after it is said, 'Take away his filthy garments' (Zech 3:4), it is harmoniously brought forward: 'Behold, I have taken away your iniquities' (Zech 3:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the filthy garments are and why the priest wears them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Once the iniquities are removed the priest is clothed in a tunic to the feet and a clean mitre, and Jesus the great high priest, whom he prefigures, was clothed in the sins of all mankind without himself sinning.
comments.comment:
Once the iniquities having been taken away—which are filthy garments—he is clothed in the foot-reaching, priestly tunic, adorning even to the feet the one wearing it, and a clean mitre is placed upon the head of the one priestally healing 'the Lord who has come and dwelt in the midst' (Zechariah 2:10) of Zion and Jerusalem.

Upon the restoration and rebuilding of the city and the temple, the leader of those liberated from captivity is clothed in a 'garment of salvation and a tunic of joy' (Isa 61:10), having cast off the filthy garments so as to no longer mourn, but to rejoice and be glad, having been saved from the captivity of those who were tested by it. …

Regarding the things said, apply them to the explicit narrative, and those to be contemplated by intellect.

Jesus the great high priest, of whom the iconic Jesus [Joshua] passing through Babylon with the captives carries the type, was clothed in filthy garments, the sins of all mankind, not himself sinning nor being tested by sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the new clothing and how the priest points to Jesus.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The house God judges is not a building but the Church, the sum of its members, whom Jesus distinguishes as apostles, prophets, shepherds and teachers, like the eyes, hands, ears and feet of Christ's body.
comments.comment:
The Lord's 'distinguishing his house and guarding his divine court.' One must not understand 'house' in these matters as a place or a building, but the sum of those completing it, as the Apostle says: 'But Christ, as a son, upon his house, of which we are the house' (Hebrews 3:6). And to Timothy he writes: 'In case I delay, so that you may know how you ought to behave in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and foundation of the truth' (1 Timothy 3:15).

And this house is distinguished by Jesus, placing in the Church 'apostles, prophets, shepherds, teachers, for the equipping of the saints' (Ephesians 4:11). For it is not as it happens, but with much distinction and arrangement, so that one is placed in the rank of an apostle, another in the place of a prophet, and others to tend the flock of Christ and to exert the divine instruction for other saints who are well-disposed toward learning. Similar to this is that which has in the Psalms thus: 'God has stood in the congregation of gods, and in the midst he distinguishes gods' (Psalm 82:1).

The house of God, thus utilizing members according to another thought, becomes the body of Christ, composed and being equipped from many members; his eyes, indeed, are those seeking the contemplative life, just as his hands are the practical ones, working the works of virtue, and the ears are called the prudent listeners of this body, of whom each one says: 'The instruction of the Lord opens my ears' (Isaiah 50:5). Appropriately, the feet of the body of Christ would be said to be 'those not sluggish in haste.'

Consequently, regarding the distinguishing of the Lord's house, it is also the distinguishing of the divine body, so that one may be an eye as previously mentioned, and another a vigorous hand, of whom it is good to work and to be useful.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the house God judges and its distinctions are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those standing are the firmly established in holiness and faith, and Jesus, who turned about among humans, gives a model to those who live and contemplate divinely to follow among them.
comments.comment:
What is the contest of the one distinguishing God's house and guarding his court shown in: 'And I will give you those turning among these standing ones'? (Zechariah 3:7). For 'standing' shows those firmly established according to holiness, having received a permanent position according to faith, to whom the Apostle writes speaking: 'For in faith you have stood' (Zechariah 3:7). The Savior says in the Gospel, signifying those 'founded and rooted' perfectly 'in love': 'There are some of those standing here.'

Among those thus standing, those turning according to a divine manner of life and a contemplation of the truth are given by Jesus through God. Among those humans who truly become according to the image and likeness of God, Jesus, having received them from the Father, turned about among them, 'having appeared on the earth in order that he might turn about with humans,' providing a pattern and a model for those previously mentioned to imitate him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Standing' may also mean the angels who minister to the Savior, among whom those who live in celibacy turn about, and who will be equal to the angels after the resurrection.
comments.comment:
By a second meaning, say that 'standing' shows the dancing angels being gathered according to 'thousands of thousands and myriads of myriads,' praising the All-King Savior and ministering to him. These, who are shown turning among their own Creator, are given to become equal-angels after the resurrection, no longer marrying or being married, no longer able to die, the succession of marriage and child-rearing having ceased, since 'their corruptible put on incorruption and their mortal immortality' (1 Cor 15:53-54).
