For how does he who perfects celibacy not turn about among the standing immortal angels and the other divine powers, always being 'mindful of the things of the Lord, without distraction' (1 Corinthians 7:32-35), desiring to serve him priestically and to serve him nobly, being 'a fellow-worker,' so to phrase it, having set this before him. Similarly, also 'the virgin, being holy in spirit and body,' is without distraction pleasing to the divine bridegroom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those near the high priest are the spiritual priests under him, especially those who serve God in celibacy, and those sitting before his face are the apostles seated in the regeneration, perfect men.
comments.comment:
And to say collectively, all those approaching the Savior turn about in the midst of those standing always and continuously in holiness to share in him. One of those turning about in this way sang to the King of all: 'Against angels I will sing to you.' …

The angel testifying to Jesus [Joshua], the great priest, says these things: 'Hear, you, Jesus, being the great priest; and let those near you and those sitting before your face hear also, being men who watch for wonders, that I call my servant East, because upon the stone which I gave before the face of Jesus, seven eyes are upon it.' …

To this great priest the angel of the Lord says: 'Hear then, O Jesus, the great priest, you and those near you' (Zech 3:8), the spiritual priests, those having been appointed under you being high priest, to whom also in Isaiah it is said they are righteous ones: 'But you shall be called priests, servants of God' (Isa 61:6). And they possess this promise especially, those who through all-pervading holiness in celibacy serve God.

Not only, however, do these hear of the angel with Jesus the great priest, but also those sitting before his face. These are those in the regeneration according to the resurrection of the dead sitting before the face of the Savior, being judge and king, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

These who hear the divine words of the angel with Jesus are not others than the apostles; being near him and sitting before his face, they are not found to be infants or children, but perfect men having encountered the perfect man of the fullness of the knowledge of the Son of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who those near the high priest and those sitting before him are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus the great priest is 'faithful to him who made him', which means certain and unshakeable in his office, not that the Son was created, as the faithful commandments and the faithful blessings of David show.
comments.comment:
The great priest Jesus, who was previously given according to the order of the priesthood of Melchizedek, concerning whom the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: 'Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, understand the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, being faithful to him who made him' (Heb. 3:1).

And see that those able to understand how faithful he is to him who made him, the apostle and high priest of our confession, are found to be holy, partaking of a heavenly calling. For it is not for everyone to see how faithful he is to him who made him, the apostle and priest Jesus, but only for him who is able to speak in all things with wisdom to the perfect, he who is able to say: 'I have seen Jesus' with the eyes of my heart enlightened toward the true light.

Therefore, those not partaking of the heavenly calling are negligent, and from this word they themselves are deceived, having been misled, saying the Son of God is a creature and a work. But the foolish err senselessly, taking 'him who made him' to mean creation and production into being, the writer of the epistle not intending this. For to become the faithful apostle and high priest is made manifest as certain and immovable to be apostle and priest; for one is not always apostle and priest.

He is Jesus, but from the time when those to whom he is sent and for whom he intercedes exist, through whom the descent here has happened of the one sent by the Father, when 'bending heaven he descended' (Ps 18:9) to those to whom he was sent and of whom he is priest.

Many scriptures signify the certain and unshakeable through the faithful. For that which is said about God: 'All his commandments are faithful, established for an age of ages' (Ps 111:7–8), and that: 'I will give you the faithful blessings of David' (Isa 55:3), and even that: 'I will raise for myself a faithful priest' (1 Sam 2:35), declare the certain and unchangeable, of the commandments of God existing faithful according to the spiritual law because of the unchangeable, and of the commandments according to the shadow of the law being transferred from the letter to the spirit and from the shadow to the truth.

By this theory also are those of the true David, in whom the Savior is according to man, whose faithful blessings are to remain forever, the words of him remaining even if heaven and earth pass away; therefore also a faithful priest exists, having an unshakeable priesthood for the age, becoming and having been shown according to the order of Melchizedek.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The stone rejected by the builders became the corner, joining Jews and Gentiles in one building, and believers come to it as living stones built into a spiritual house.
comments.comment:
"The stone which was rejected by you, the builders, has become the head of the corner." Ps 118:22. For how did the two walls not join and complete one single corner: the one being built from the Jews coming to the gospel, and the other from the Gentiles who believed? For when the Church of both Jews and Greeks was gathered, Christ having become its head, He completed one corner, with all those joined to one building in one faith, all people from the two peoples being created into one new man Eph 2:15.

This stone, thus announced as the cornerstone, chosen, precious, which God placed in the foundations of Zion, no longer to be shamed by any sin, having become pure for everyone believing upon it. Those coming to the immortal living Word, living themselves, are being built up as hidden stones, so that a spiritual house may be composed and an intelligible altar, upon which the sacrifice of praise is offered and all things being like it are spiritual.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the stone set before Joshua stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord digs a pit to bring all hidden things to light and search out all injustice in the one day of illumination, the season of the Savior's visitation, when he takes away the sin of the world.
comments.comment:
"I dig a pit," says the Lord of all, "and I will search out all the injustice of that land in one day" Zech 3:9. "On that day," says the Lord of all, "let each call his neighbor under the vine and under the fig tree" Zech 3:10.

"I dig," says the Lord of all, "a pit, in order to make all the hidden things manifest, in order to touch and feel all the injustice of that land;" it is clear that of the one being dug, in the one day of illumination, then most especially when "the Lord God shines" Ps 104:4 the Lord of all "the secrets of darkness, and makes manifest the purposes of the hearts," in order to condemn those having done all injustice.

One day can be called the season of our Savior's visitation, in which the benefactor who shines also searches all the injustice of the revealed land, taking away the sin of the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the pit and the one day in which the Lord removes iniquity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When strife, war and the opposing powers are gone, everyone will live without fear and invite his neighbor under the fig and the vine, as Micah also foretold.
comments.comment:
Because of this, once the cause of all strife and every unjust war has been overcome, there will be a deep peace, such that no one fears anymore, since strifes are dissolved and wars are ended, and the demons and other opposing powers, which are called 'rulers of this darkness', are gone, so that everyone may live fearlessly and invite his neighbor under the fig and the vine.

This peaceful and stable state is being described, and the prophet Micah foretells presciently that day, saying: 'Each one will call his neighbor and his brother under his fig tree and his vine, not being afraid' (Micah 4:4). For how can anyone still be afraid, when all strifes and wars are dissolved?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what sitting under the vine and fig tree means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The vine is the contemplative life, which gladdens, and the fig the active life of toil for virtue, and those who tend both invite one another beneath them in peace.
comments.comment:
What is meant by the mentioned plants, the vine and the fig trees—whether the contemplative or the active life? The vine, producing fruit that makes the contemplative and scientific life joyful, and the fig, being somewhat severe and rough due to the toil and sweat for the sake of possessing virtue. …

The fig is said to be the active and energetic life of good things; likewise the vine should be understood, becoming like a branch of the true vine. For each of the disciples of Jesus is a vine, becoming a branch of the one saying, Savior: 'I am the vine, you are the branches. Every branch remaining in me bears more fruit' (John 15:5).

Those who have cultivated the said trees, becoming fellow-laborers and brothers, invite one another under the vine and the fig tree in peace, to live in luxury.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The seven lamps on the lamp are the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit resting on the Savior, and they are fed with oil, which is the study of the truth.
comments.comment:
… Just as a torch appeared above the interpreted lamp, so also seven lamps appeared above that lamp, being a seven-fold radiance. For just as the manner of perfect luminous intellect is called seven eyes, and seven pillars support the house of wisdom, so also the seven lamps sit upon the lamp, in another manner being that which the Savior took during His visitation, soul and flesh.

For how is this whole lamp not golden, having not committed sin nor known it, upon which sit seven lamps: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of divine counsel, and strength, and knowledge, and piety, and fear of God. And how does each of these stand in relation to the one who ceased rising from the root of Jesse, having been made clear previously when it was foretold: 'A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse' (Isaiah 11:1), and the whole scope of the prophecy announcing these things.

And this seven-shining power of the seven lamps above the lamp is nourished and increases, the oil being dispensed through the seven wicks, flowing as the nourishment and guarding the light. And this is nothing other than the study of the knowledge of the truth. For from studying we bear fruit in memory and a stronger vision.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lamp is a mental pattern like the one Moses saw, and in God's house it may mean the teacher who lets his mind shine through his teaching, or the practical life.
comments.comment:
Since the present theory concerning the lamp is not a sensible but a mental one, see whether this is not that which Moses saw on the mountain according to the pattern shown to him, and not another being of the so-called idea; toward the invisible and mental lamp the sensible one was constructed according to the description of the hierophant Moses.

It is not untimely to write alongside the things seen and that which was said in the Gospel by Jesus: 'No one,' he says, 'having lit a lamp, puts it in a hidden place or under a vessel or a bed, but on the lamp, so that all those in the house may see the light' (Matt 5:15).

It is possible in these things to take the house to be the Church of the living God, becoming His house, in which those remaining and dwelling, standing according to its doctrines, are illuminated toward the lamp placed by the lamp, which is snatched away by the one educating those traversing in the house of God according to the statutes and canons and doctrines of the ecclesiastical opinion. And this teacher illuminates when he lifts up his own mind like a lamp, which he does not hide under a bed or vessel, but places upon his spoken word, being allegorically addressed as a lamp, having 'a tongue of instruction' as it must be said.

It is also possible to call the practical life a lamp, upon which the enlightened mind of the one who has enlightened himself with the light of knowledge rests. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The two oils may be the study of intelligible things and the Spirit's gifts and the study of the world and God's providence, or the teaching on the Son and on the incarnation.
comments.comment:
Upon all those things observed—the lamp, the torch, the seven wicks, and the lamps—two oils were also seen above the lamp, one of which was on the right and the other on the left of the torch. And see if the study concerning the intelligible things and the gifts of the Holy Spirit is oil being harvested from the oil on the right, while that concerning the world and its constitution and the providence from God is pressed from the oil on the left.

They suppose, according to a theory, to say another, an oil being on the right of the torch, to be the theory concerning the Only-begotten Son of God, the one on the left nourishing the Word concerning the incarnation. For this one also shines, but not in the same way as the theory on the right and preceding. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The things shown to the prophet in Babylon were intellectual visions and not sights for the senses, since the house of God and its vessels were not yet built.
comments.comment:
Visions, that is, all things revealed, or those specifically preceding the present word, which is about the whole golden lampstand and the things upon it: a lamp, seven small lamps, and equal lamps, and two olives, one on the right and the other on the left of the lamp.

Regarding the question of whether these are not perceived by the senses, the one asked immediately answered that they are the word of God from the person of Zerubbabel, from which it appears that the things shown were intellectual visions and that this is true. The showing of the revealed things happened to the prophet while he was still in Babylon, in which neither the house of God was built, nor the vessels in it, of which the lampstand and the things upon it are. Since these are thus viewed, one must remain with the interpretation spoken of them or seek something greater than it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophet asked the angel because he wanted to learn what the divine things shown to him were.
comments.comment: 'And I asked and said to the angel speaking in me, saying, What are these, Lord? And the angel speaking in me answered and said to me, saying, This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might nor by power, but by my spirit, says the Lord of all' (Zech 4:6). The prophet says he asked the angel speaking in him, desiring to learn what the divine things shown to him were.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word came to the prophet by the Spirit of the Lord and not by great power or strength, since the power the Spirit gives is the power of Christ.
comments.comment:
The word which... the angel said to the prophet was not done by great power or by the strength of man or of any other creature, but in the Spirit of the Lord it was spoken and was revealed.

The Holy Spirit of the Lord is continually called so in the Scriptures, as also in other Scriptures besides the present one. Concerning Him, a lament and that in Isaiah is announced thus: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me' (Isaiah 61:1). In agreement with these, the apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: 'For what man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, which searches even the mystic depths of God' (1 Corinthians 2:11). And again in Isaiah, the Originator and Provider of all things says: 'A Spirit shall go out from me' (Isaiah 57:16).

By this Spirit, the things shown before the person of Zerubbabel were revealed, but not by great power or strength of any creature. For there is another power provided with the Spirit to those worthy, about which the Savior, in the Acts of the Apostles, says to his disciples, as he was being taken up into heaven to his Father: 'You shall receive power upon the coming of the Holy Spirit' (Acts 1:8). … This power is not a different power from that of Christ, who is "the wisdom and power of God," from which the evangelical preaching has surpassed the apostles, one of whom, Paul, writes: "My speech and my preaching are not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a demonstration of Spirit and power" (1 Cor 2:4), which is sometimes provided by God who has stretched out His hand, as it is said concerning John in the Gospel, "having gone before the Lord in spirit and power" (Luke 1:17).

Understand precisely if the thing announced to Mary by the holy angel Gabriel has the same understanding: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35). In the mentioned Spirit of God, in the words set forth and many others, the announcement has occurred before Zerubbabel and the power joined with him, "and not by any other great power and might" (Zech 4:7). For this is inferior, even if it be divine and highly esteemed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what 'not by might, but by my Spirit' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountain before Zerubbabel and the stone are both names that Scripture gives to the visiting Savior, the Son of God.
comments.comment:
Who are you, O great mountain before Zerubbabel, to level the stone of the inheritance to be equal to its grace (Zech 4:7)? … For many scriptures name him both mountain and stone.

For in "The mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest at the end of days" (Isa 2:2), the Son of God is, concerning whom He spoke at the end of days after speaking through Moses and the prophets. Of Him also it is demonstrative: "Ascend the mountain of Zion, O evangelizer, Zion" (Isaiah 40:9). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountain is the Savior, who is also called the stone the builders rejected, the head of the corner and the foundation on which believers are built into a spiritual house.
comments.comment:
… Even the named mountain, Savior, is called a stone in the saying: 'The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner' (Ps 118:22). Remembering this word in the Acts of the Apostles, the preeminent disciple of the Savior, Peter, most strictly rebuked the Pharisees, scribes, and Sadducees who were listening to the Jewish teaching, saying: 'This is the stone which was despised by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner' (Acts 4:11).

And since it is not only the head of the divine building but also the foundation, God promises concerning it, saying: 'Behold, I lay a cornerstone in the foundations of Zion, chosen, precious, upon which the believer has unashamed hope' (Isa 28:16). Laying out these words, Peter, the disciple of Christ, upon whom the Church is built, exhorts and advises those to whom he has inscribed his epistle: 'To whom approaching the living stone, you are being built up into a spiritual house in which spiritual sacrifices are offered' (1 Pet 2:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the mountain and stone are, with the Scriptures that name him so.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The stone belongs to the inheritance God chose and loved, Jacob and Israel, and above all to the nations the Father gives to the Son.
comments.comment:
Of what inheritance does the stone belong? It is of that inheritance concerning which it is brought forth in Isaiah: 'There is an inheritance to those healing the Lord' (Isaiah 54:17), and of that inheritance concerning which the hymnodist said, singing: 'My inheritance is most strong for me; you are the one restoring my inheritance to me' (Ps 16:5).

See then whether the stone is the inheritance of that inheritance being fulfilled from the God-fearing ones according to each, which is chosen and desired, existing from the cause of all things, according to that which was announced by the spirit-bearing men, apostles and evangelists, prophets and the great high priest of all things, Moses: 'He chose for us his own inheritance,' God, clearly, 'the beauty of Jacob whom he loved' (Psalm 47:4).

It is equal to the voice from the Psalm and that in the great song of Deuteronomy having here: 'Jacob became a part of the Lord, a portion of his inheritance, Israel' (Deuteronomy 32:9).

But especially the stone being hymned is the inheritance of that which is signified in the second Psalm toward this stone: 'The Lord said to me, Son are you, I have today become your father. Ask of me and I will give you nations for your inheritance' (Ps 2:7-8). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountain is the unwedded Mary, and the stone cut from her without hands is the Son she bore without a man.
comments.comment:
Regarding how it is to be carried, it must be said and otherwise that one part is the mountain and another part is the stone. And the mountain of achievement is the unwedded Mary; but the stone coming forth from her, whom she bore as a son without a man, exists. The book of the most wise Daniel initiates us into these mysteries.

For it has been said in it that the striking stone—the various kingdoms and the image completed from them—has been cut and torn away from it without the custom and the practiced way toward the generation of the energy from parents. For as many as have the generation from both parents, they are torn and cut away from the hands of the marriage acts and from those who conceive; but only the one born from the virgin, not knowing the man, has been torn away and cut from her without hands. Before the face of Zerubbabel, it happened that the stone from the mountain was to be cut without hands, so that Jesus is also traced through lineage from it. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The stone brings grace upon grace, for the whole visit of the Savior and the salvation in it came by grace.
comments.comment: But the stone placed outside of the inheritance has grace upon grace, according to the thought of what the Baptist John said, 'for from the fullness we have all received' (John 1:16). For the whole visitation of the Savior and the salvation upon it happened by grace, as the theologian says to those whom he addresses in his epistle: 'You are saved by grace, and this is not from us, but the gift of God' (Ephesians 2:8). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The house in the prophecy is not a building the senses can see, since the prophet received it in Babylon, before the house was built in Jerusalem.
comments.comment: The prophecy of the seen house is not spoken concerning a sensible building. For it has already been said that this prophet, while still in Babylon, with the seventieth year of the captivity already having come, was initiated into the placed revelations. But not in Babylon, but in Jerusalem and after the captivity, the sensible house was built. Therefore, the present voice does not happen to be about it; for as if concerning the temple being present and already having come, it is said pointedly about it: 'This house.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The house raised in Jerusalem is a copy of the intelligible house shown to the prophet in vision, and God speaks in vision to the inner man and not through the ear.
comments.comment:
Regarding the house raised in Jerusalem after the descent of the captivity while in Babylon. Even if these things are said about the sensible building, they reveal the prototype of the visible, being something intelligible, like an idea shaped in resemblance. It was said previously that just as the tent and the vessels in it were constructed according to the pattern of an invisible tent shown on the mountain, that is, of the height of the archetype, so the bodily house raised from sensible stones is a copy and an image of that shown to the prophet Zechariah by way of vision, but not by a collision of the senses.

The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation of this archetype, and its active powers shall complete it. When this happens, you will know toward whom the promise is, that 'The Lord of hosts has sent me to you' (Zechariah 4:9), so that you may be enlightened and intelligently contemplate the things established through divine seeing. And the prophet before us might say the same things as he who speaks in Christ, Paul, having this: 'I will come into revelations and visions of the Lord' (2 Cor 12:1). In agreement with the one speaking in revelations to those who are discerning according to the inner man, the hymnist in the Psalms says: 'Then you spoke in vision to your sons' (Psalm 89:19), not in ears nor by voice to those who have the spirit of adoption speaking the Word of God.

For as a true light, it enlightens the intellect of those whom it wishes to receive its divine conversations; it speaks in vision rather than in ear. Immediately also, regarding Isaiah speaking of God thus: 'The vision that Isaiah saw' (Isa 1:1), it is not visible things, but words are brought forward. For how is it visible: 'Hear, O heaven, and listen, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have rebelled against me' (Isa 1:2)? …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The small days are the few days of the restoration, and the cutting short of days of tribulation in the Gospel means the afflictions will not last long.
comments.comment:
'Why is it that one is making the days small?' These are the days with which the restoration takes place, of those descending to their own fatherland by the law of the captivity having happened in Babylon. And small days are those which are few in number, especially also those which are cut short, not remaining long while the sun is in the upper hemisphere above the earth; the former meaning is more likely to be meant, because the revelations were shown to the prophet in the seventieth year of the captivity, as to say to the prophet himself toward God: 'How long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you see this seventieth year?'

… This theory agrees with that in the Gospel said by the Savior: 'If those days had not been cut short, all flesh would not have been saved.' The cutting short of the days of tribulation signifies that the afflictions will not remain for a longer time, ceasing quickly, so that the strength of those being afflicted may endure for the purpose of bravely contending to obtain prizes and crowns.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'small days' are and links them to the Gospel's shortened days.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The days cannot literally have been cut short, so the small days of the prophetic text must be understood by the Gospel's teaching on the cutting short of days.
comments.comment:
For one should not believe Tatian the heretic, erroneously saying that the former days had become fewer than the present ones, because the hours of the day and night were briefly contracted, due to it being announced by the singer to God: 'By your ordinance the day remains.'

… But since it is impossible according to history for the days to be cut short in this way, one must recover the Gospel teaching concerning the cutting short of the days and that which is lying concerning the small days in the prophetic text.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The long days Scripture promises the righteous are days of growing illumination that come from loving God, and the first gleams are small days beside them.
comments.comment:
… The days of the intelligible realm possess greatness and abundance near the sun of righteousness, and this is due to the difference between those being illuminated and the light itself. For when the Lord says concerning the righteous one who 'dwells in the help of the Most High' (Psalm 91:1): 'I will fill him with length of days,' we do not say that a long life is promised to the righteous one who desires to 'depart so that he may be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23), as he says: 'Woe, that my sojourn has been lengthened' (Psalm 120:5).

Indeed, history also struggles against such a view, since those honoring parents are not becoming long-lived in every way, it having been said to each: 'Honor your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be long of years upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you' (Ex 20:12). For one finds those keeping this commandment becoming short-lived and outside of life in a short time.

Therefore, since the spoken word is shown not to have the meaning as many suppose, that which is said in the Psalms concerning length of days, and as elsewhere in the God-breathed Scripture is like: 'He sought life and you gave him length of days unto the age and unto the age of the age' (Psalm 21:4), and that in Proverbs: 'The righteous shall make many years in wealth' (Prov 10:6).

But that the increasing illumination and length of days is the prophet of the divine laws, Moses, saying to the God-lover: 'This is your life and the length of your days: to love the Lord your God with all your soul and with all your heart' (Deut 6:5). For since love that is attentive to God is luminous, it prepares long and great days, so that those participating in it find themselves having many-dayed and long-lasting existence.

Compared to these days, the introductory gleams are found to be small days, which he who is not undervaluing will easily be tempted by, following the bright progresses. In whichs the one born will rejoice in 'joy inexpressible and glorified' (1 Pet 1:8), existing in 'fruit of the Holy Spirit' (Gal 5:22).

And what follows him who rejoices thus, or to see the tinny stone in hand, that is, in practice, of Zerubbabel, from whom the one from Abraham and David and finally from Mary, Jesus, is genealogically descended, who works through all things to be luminous and discerning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The seven eyes that look over all the earth are God's complete oversight, which watches the righteous, as the many-eyed cherubim also show.
comments.comment:
… He said there are seven eyes, observing and looking upon all the earth, especially when those dwelling on the earth learned to do righteousness, walking without blemish and working righteousness. That these look upon things by the Lord is learned from the Psalmist saying: 'The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears to their prayer' (Psalm 34:15).

The whole has seven divine eyes, being inherently perceptive; in this way also the most holy Cherubim, at whom God attends, according to the vision of Ezekiel, are eyed all over, it having been said they are full of eyes, just as they have eyes on their sides and on their faces for the inspection of superabundant and great wonders. The Cherubim are interpreted as a multitude of knowledge; from which it appears that they see what they know and what they look upon and impose.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The seven lamps are the eyes of the Lord that look on the whole earth, so God sees all things, and Christ gives light to all things and watches over all things.
comments.comment: So the blessed prophet asked, ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the divine angel, after inserting a short account (Zechariah 4:6–10), interprets the vision and refers the making of the lampstand to Christ, saying of the seven lamps on it, ‘These are the eyes of the Lord, which look upon the whole earth.’ (Zechariah 4:10) For if we must say something in rather bodily terms, the Godhead sees us with countless eyes and surveys human affairs, ‘knowing what is in the darkness,’ as it is written, ‘and the light is with him’ (Daniel 2:22). For if God puts light even into us who are in the world, he would surely be rich in it himself, since he has it in his own nature before all others. Or if some suspect that this is not so, it is perhaps time to cry out to those who have chosen to think that way: ‘Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, be wise at last. He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive?’ (Psalm 94:8–9) ‘For the word of God is living and active, sharper than a two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes.’ (Hebrews 4:12–13) Christ, then, gives light to all things and watches over all things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the seven lamps and 'eyes of the Lord' mean, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Christ is called a stone because he is our foundation, and a tin stone because, as tin glues things together, he joins us through himself to God the Father.
comments.comment: He has become for us a base and security, and an unshaken under-step, and an unbreakable foundation; and because of this he has been named a stone. For ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘I set into Zion’s (Isaiah 28:16) foundations a chosen stone, a cornerstone, honorable. And the one believing upon him will not be put to shame.’ … And he has joined us through himself to God and Father, having dissolved the enmity in his body, just as it has been written; and indeed he said toward the Father and God in the heavens, concerning those justified in the faith unto him: ‘Father, I wish that just as I and you are one, so also they may be one in us.’ (John 17:21) He has been called for this reason a tin stone, for with tin the things being glued are glued. And God said somewhere through Zechariah’s voice, showing us his own Son, as about to come and go according to times: ‘And they will rejoice, and will see the tin stone in Zerubbabel’s hand (Zechariah 4:10).’
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse names a stone in Zerubbabel's hand and who it is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The stone in Zerubbabel's hand is faith in the Lord, shown in the practice of the commandments and adorned with the seven energies of the Spirit.
comments.comment: Zerubbabel also holds in his hand a stone adorned with seven eyes. For the Lord too the stone is faith in him; and it is “in the hand” (Zechariah 4:10) because faith in Christ shows itself in the practice of the commandments. The hand is plainly a symbol of practice. So the Lord, bearing the stone in his hand, teaches us to hold faith in him as something done, adorned with the seven energies of the Spirit (Zechariah 3:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the stone is 'in the hand' of Zerubbabel.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet, still a beginner in initiation, could not know what the olive trees and branches were, and asked the angel a second time.
comments.comment:
When the angel speaking in the prophet asked: 'What do you see?' he answered and said inquiringly: 'What are these two olive trees which are on the right and by the olive branches of the lampstand?' An answer not being given to him, he inquires a second time about the two olive branches which are in the hands of the two pipes that pour out and bring up the golden oil-streams. To whom the angel said: 'Do you not know what these are?' 'No, Lord,' saying the prophet, the angel said: 'These are the two sons of stability who stand beside the Lord of all the earth.'

For one having the beginning of initiation, it is not possible at all to know what are those on the right and by the olive branches.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophet asks a second time about the branches because only what can be known in part leads to knowing the olives, which some took to be the teaching on the Son and the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment:
The oil of the lamp; therefore, he asks a second time concerning two branches of the olive trees. It has been made clear in the previous discourses that the divine study is called olive, because of their fruit increasing and nourishing the light. Since it is not possible to perceive through all the trunks and the shoots of the plants in question the one 'knowing and prophesying in part' (1 Cor 13:9), he approaches a second inquiry concerning two branches of olives; for only through these is it possible to have a knowledge that imposes the truth 'through a mirror and an enigma' (1 Cor 13:12), so that, having been benefited from the partial, he might at last be able to know what the olives actually are.

… And since one interpretation of what those who explained the text took as the two olives was the discourse concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, see if the branches of these olives would grasp what is attainable to the one knowing in part. For while there is the olive of Christ, the becoming of the Word into flesh would be a branch; and of the Holy Spirit, his introductory contemplation, which is called his 'earnest money' (2 Cor 1:22).

… Having asked a second time about these, the one receiving God heard from the angel who initiates into the mysteries: 'Do you not know what these are?' To which the one hearing replied: 'No, Lord.' 'These,' he says, 'are the two sons of fatness; they shall present to the Lord all the earth' (Zechariah 4:14).

… For just as, by way of the discourse concerning the Father, which is the lamp above the lamp, as has been interpreted a little earlier, so the discourse concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit is being matched to the contemplation of the Father's fatness, being its sons, as it is possible for one still in the body to know.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The two sons of richness are the believers from Israel and from the nations, who stand beside the Lord and are made rich with the oil of the Spirit.
comments.comment:
… But when, now roused, he at last named them two branches of olive trees and begged earnestly to learn what these might be symbols of, he was taught at once, when the angel said: ‘These are the two sons of richness, who stand beside the Lord of all the earth’ (Zechariah 4:14). By the two sons of richness he meant the people from Israel and also the people from the nations, who, he says, stand beside the Lord of all the earth. So he clearly and plainly sets the craftsmanship of the lampstand as a type of Christ. Its olive branches, on the right and on the left, having as it were their place all around it, are made rich with the oil, which is a type of the Holy Spirit, who waters the mind of those who believe, as it says: ‘You have anointed my head with oil’ (Psalm 23:5).

Palladius: Then why did he call them shoots of olive trees, and not rather olive trees?

Cyril: Because, my friend, those who have believed have been taken like slender shoots and newly sprouted branches from olive trees, and are all but transplanted, with faith, into godliness: some of them come from the synagogue of the Jews, and others have been taken out of the multitude of the nations. For not all those from Israel have believed, nor has the whole multitude of the nations come in. Branches of olive trees, then, are those who have been plucked, as from trees, from the multitude of the Jews and also of the Greeks, who have come to be in the divine light and already in some way delight in the more abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit. For this, I think, is what is meant by the olive branches lying, as it were, in the spouts of the lamps. The blessed Psalmist also mentions them somewhere, singing to Christ, the Savior of all, and speaking of the bride joined to him, that is, the Church, and of her children in faith: ‘Your wife is like a flourishing vine on the sides of your house; your sons are like young olive plants around your table’ (Psalm 128:3). For we are given life by sharing in the Spirit and at the holy table of Christ, once we have received faith in him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the two olive branches and the two sons are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The two sons of fatness may be the two sons of men who hope in the wings of God, one by circumcision and one by the Gospel, or Moses and Elijah on the mountain with Jesus, showing the Law and the Prophets.
comments.comment:
According to another interpretation, the mystical understanding of the God-breathed Scriptures is the fatness of the house of God, according to that which is said in the thirty-fifth Psalm to the Lord God: 'They shall be intoxicated from the fatness of your house' (Psalm 36:8); and it is clear that 'those who hope in the wings of God' (Psalm 36:7) are sons of men, being two sons: the one having come by circumcision, and the other according to the Gospel of Christ.

… Understand, if you are able, to take two sons of fatness having been presented to the Lord, those seen in glory with Jesus on the mountain, Moses and Elijah (Matt 17:2-3), making manifest the Law and the Prophets. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The two sons of firmness are Enoch and Elijah, who were taken up without seeing death, as the prophet read in a secret book.
comments.comment: Just as there is a certain quality of firmness, so too is the word of the prophet who has been opened. He read in a secret book that Enoch and Elijah are the two sons of firmness, as it is fitting because they resemble others. For Enoch was translated so as not to see death, and Elijah was taken up, being carried by a chariot of fire and a horse 'as into heaven' (2 Kings 2:11). Considering these things as being by power like our own, though brief, we set forth the following of the prophet, desiring also to understand them, if the one who enlightens the prophet through revelations should 'give a word by the opening of our mouths' (Ephesians 6:19).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The flying sickle is the curse, the punishment brought upon all the earth to cut down and consume the thief and the perjurer.
comments.comment: Turning from the passing vision, I lifted up my eyes of the mind. And I see a flying sickle, having a length of twenty cubits and a width of ten cubits. This is the sickle which, he says, shows the vision concerning it: this is the curse, that is to say, the punishment, being brought upon all the earth, to cut and consume the thief and the perjurer. And behold the greatness of the instruction occurring through revelation, making manifest from the visible things the things not visible, and from the sensible things the things understood.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the flying sickle and the curse mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sickle flies most quickly over the whole earth, even touching sinners in the air, and destroys the middle of the house, that is, its ruling principle.
comments.comment:
The veil is the scourge, covering those who steal and perjure themselves with it. This sickle flies most quickly, coming upon all the earth. And by a second meaning, it flies so that it touches not only those sinning upon the earth, but also those in the air and those being punished for acting impiously everywhere.

In the middle of the house, that is, the ruling principle, the sickle destroys, similarly to the sword that split the judge of Israel who remained adulterously according to Sophronius. For in this word, that he was split in the middle, it signifies the dividing of his ruling principle.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A false oath brings the sickle's punishment on the swearer's house, so one should not swear falsely, or better not swear at all, as the Savior taught.
comments.comment:
For the one is punished with the altogether anger, and with unmanageable penalty, the sickle completing, according as it has been written, the false-swearer’s hearth, and shaking it down unto the complete: ‘For it will enter,’ (Zechariah 5:4) it says, ‘into the house of the thief, and into the house of the one swearing by my name upon a lie, and will dissolve in the middle of his house, and will complete him, and his woods, and his stones.’ (Zechariah 5:3–4) … Therefore one must swear not upon a lie; or rather not swear at all. For this the Savior taught us, saying: ‘Let your Yes be yes, and your No, no; and the excess of these is from the devil.’ (Matthew 5:37) For there will not be need of an oath at all for those in a reputation of solemnity, and having made virtue as it were house-mate; for among the lovers of piety the life of such ones has been very much honored, and to hate being disbelieved; and if somehow he should utter something, he is at once crowned with the hearers’ faith.

Therefore let our life be well-glorious, and the need of swearing through will altogether somehow be idle, as I think.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: The measuring line that comes out is the full measure of wickedness, which the nations filled before they were punished, and which those who killed the prophets filled only when they put the one prophesied on the cross.
comments.comment:
The one speaking, usually an angel, came out to the prophet, not remaining within, in order to show the iniquity and the measuring line and the talent of the lead being taken out. What each of these signifies, it is good for those having understood to observe.

Therefore, the measuring line being shown to come out is the fullness of all wickedness and impiety; which did not previously exist for the Amorites and the rest of the nations, nor did it punish the named nations, suffering punishment when their sins were filled up, with no kind of iniquity being absent, according to that which was said concerning some: 'Woe to a sinful nation, a people full of iniquity' (Isaiah 1:4).

… And concerning the sorcery of Elymas, the Apostle spoke abruptly, bringing the reproaches most strikingly against him: 'O full of deceit and of all craftiness, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, do you not cease perverting the straight ways of the Lord?' (Acts 13:10). This theory is constructed especially from what the Savior said to those Jews who were speaking: 'If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets. So you testify that you are sons of those who killed the prophets; therefore, you also fulfill the measure of your fathers.' (Matthew 23:32). For even if ten thousand had been killed in a murderous way against the prophets, there remained, in order to complete the measure of the ungodly, the audacity of him who says these things, by which they have branded him on the cross; for only then is the measure of their impiety fulfilled, when they, along with those who prophesied, judged the one prophesied to be dead.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Just as sins have a measure that is filled before punishment, good works have a measure too, and each is repaid by the measure it fills.
comments.comment:
Just as there is a measure of sins for those to be punished, so also there is a measure of good works and of mindsets for those who have taken upon themselves a life of diligence and according to godliness.

And this measure is also fulfilled when no just opinion or piety is lacking. Toward these two ranks, both the good and the evil, the Savior said: 'With the measure you measure, it will be measured to you.' For to those who fulfill the measure of that which is praiseworthy, promises are being measured out which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they risen up upon the heart of man, to be prepared by God for those who love Him (1 Corinthians 2:9). But to those who handle deceitful and fraudulent works of both words and thoughts, punishment is brought in accordance with their worth, such as to go out 'into the outer darkness' (Matthew 25:30), and to depart 'into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels' (Matthew 25:41). Realize whether the Savior spoke by both measures or only of the measure of righteous works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'measure' of the vision, as a measure of sins and of good works.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Through Christ the mouth of lawlessness is stopped, but those who refuse his Gospel take the burden up again, show their eagerness for uncleanness as the hoopoe's wings, and carry it away to Babylon.
comments.comment: The mouth of the lawlessness has been stopped up, noble one, through Christ; for we have been justified in him, and have been freed from every charge, and the cry-down of the lawlessness against us has ceased. … But some disobeyed Christ’s Gospel, and not having accepted the redemption from the sin, bear it again as a burden, having hung it upon their own heads through weakness of mind, and softness of understanding and unmanliness of soul. These are carried about by every evil wind, and being most violently pushed together unto every form of uncleanness they make as much eagerness as possible unto the base things. And a sign of eagerness is the wing, which he also says is of a hoopoe, and this is a form of a small bird, always running round the most foul-smelling of the marshes, and gathering from mire and uncleanness unto food. As many therefore as spend their own eagernesses unto pollution, these would altogether reasonably be said to have the hoopoe’s wings. And they themselves are womanlike, and made soft, and thereafter conformed to the sin tyrannizing against them. For in the manner those under him and with him have become conformed to Christ through sanctification, so also those loaded with the lawlessness, and having chosen to live together with unclean baseness, are conformed and like-formed to it. And they carry the measure away unto Babylon, and seek a house for it there, enigmatically (Zechariah 5:11)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The women's wings, filled with the spirit that works in the disobedient, are like the wings of an unclean bird that feeds on tombs and filth.
comments.comment:
They appeared having wings, filled with spirit, that of which the Apostle writes: 'In whichs also you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the authority of the air, the spirit of the one now working in the sons of disobedience' (Ephesians 2:2). It is perhaps related, though the thing in the lying wings is trivial, to the unclean spirit cast out by Jesus from the man, which having been cast out by Jesus, if returning it finds it idling and having swept the place where it was cast out, having an empty hand and having swept, having all the good things it had been cast away, it takes other seven spirits more evil than itself, enters and 'dwells,' and the last things of that man become worse than the first (Matthew 12:44).

To represent that the wings are seven, the wings of the women were compared and made like the wings of the epic. But this creature is unclean, being a friend of the dead and of human refuse; indeed, it feeds in the tombs and makes a nest for itself out of human filth, so that having settled in the diseased cauldron, it may boil and make new ones like itself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The creature may stand for the devil or the antichrist, and the teaching of the heresies is its feeding on tombs, clean outside but full of uncleanness within.
comments.comment: One must observe what this creature must take by way of ascent, and see if it is possible. It either signifies the devil, or the antichrist. And each of the heterodox must not be unknown. The devil rejoices, and the anti-god antichrist, and the word of the heresies is to feed on tombs, the same being for the graves according to allegory, 'they are covered without, but within they are full of all unchastity,' and of the adjacent thoughts separating from God because they are crooked. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unclean creature delights in bad habits and lives in uncleanness, and the women are those who take on the strifes and rivalries of the flesh.
comments.comment: Regarding the question of whether the remembered creature is unclean and finds joy in bad habits, he builds his own beauty from human toil. What follows this, besides that he himself, whom I call the watcher, and his youths live in uncleanness? For this, observing human things, he received this title; but I say human things are the strifes, rivalries, and false zeal, about which the Apostle writes, rebuking those held by them: 'For where there is strife and rivalry among you, are you not human, and are you walking according to the flesh?' (1 Cor 3:3). Those called such flesh, you might graciously say are women, taking on bad habits, perhaps having been struck and eaten by the said watcher, in an allegorical sense, so as to cast out those seized by fear lest they be destroyed, and to raise filters leading to licentiousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever takes up wings like a dove should keep away from these women and their wings, for to be winged by the Spirit is blessed and lifts one to heaven.
comments.comment: It is proper for the one taking up wings like a dove to abstain from these women and their wings, in which the one spread out rests, finding 'the Sabbath which remains to the people of God' (Heb 4:9); you will understand the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove in the Jordan, whom he holds alone, and everyone who rests between the two covenants, called lots according to: 'If you sleep between the lots, wings of a dove are fluttering about.' To be winged according to these things is blessed; for they take up the one having them into heaven and the things above the world.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The two winged women who lift the measuring line between earth and heaven stand for two evils: moral wickedness, and false glory with the evil powers behind it.
comments.comment:
And now, lifting up the eyes of the inner man as in the previous visions, he saw two women coming forth, winged, and a spirit was in their wings. And their wings were like the wings of a bird called an ephah. These women coming forth thus took up the measuring line, in the middle of which the woman called iniquity was found, and they took it up in the middle of the earth and of the heaven. Having seen these things thus, I desired to ask the angel speaking in me, 'Where are these carrying the line?' And he said to me, 'To build him a house in the land of Babylon, and to prepare it, and they will set him there...'

… One must examine what two kinds of women these are. See if the two evils are the moral evil of the habitual transgression of the divine commands, or the false glory concerning those who are prudent and the evil powers working through them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The two women carry the measure on which lawlessness sits between heaven and earth to Babylon, where a house is built for it.
comments.comment: Of the two women being winged according to the watcher, hovering over the measure upon which lawlessness sits between heaven and earth—for even the sinful angels, and the earthly demons, and men who 'bear the image of the swine' (Matt 7:6) have tested it—the one seeing the revelation seeing it hovering and being carried away with the measure upon which lawlessness sits, says to the angel speaking in him: 'Where are these carrying the measure?' And the angel answering says: 'To build him a house in the land of Babylon, and they shall set him there upon his preparation' (Zechariah 5:11). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One must flee Babylon, where the measure is set, as the divine word calls, and take wings from the Holy Spirit to pass into heavenly things.
comments.comment: Therefore, one must depart and flee from Babylon because the measure [of lawlessness] has been placed there to be found ready for those willing. Thus the divine word cries out like a herald to one desiring to be diligent: 'Come out of Babylon, fleeing from the land of the Chaldeans' (Isaiah 48:20). Having understood the vision of the prophet to be such, let us love to have wings formerly, having been made to fly according to the Holy Spirit; for in this way it is most easy to pass into the super-celestial things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the vision sends the reader away from Babylon.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bronze of the mountains may mean showy, resounding speech, which sophistical and heretical teachers use because they lack the love of God.
comments.comment: Two bronze mountains were said from which the chariots went forth from the midst. And see if by the bronze is signified the conspicuous phrase having much resounding. And the sophistical and heretical teachers use this, becoming 'a resounding bronze and a clanging cymbal,' because of being deprived of the divine love toward God. Which the divine Apostle suspecting writes: 'If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become a resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal' (1 Corinthians 13:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The two bronze mountains stand for the twofold exaltation against the knowledge of God, in practical and intellectual virtue.
comments.comment: Two bronze mountains are said to exist because of the twofold nature of those exalted against the knowledge of God. For it is possible to hold false opinions regarding both practical and intellectual virtue, not being any other than the knowledge of truth; for those from the heresies are impious concerning both kinds of virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Four chariots with differently colored horses come out between two bronze mountains, and the prophet asks what they are.
comments.comment: The prophet, turning to receive also another revelation, saw four chariots from the midst of two bronze mountains. The first chariot had red horses yoked, the second black, the third white, the fourth variegated speckled. Having beheld the four chariots, wishing to learn concerning them, he asks the angel speaking in him what the things seen are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The angel says the four chariots are the four winds of heaven, the four regions of the inhabited world.
comments.comment: And he answers saying they are the four winds of heaven, that is, the four climates of the inhabited world. And the black were seen going forth from the land of the north, the white going forth behind them; and from the south came the speckled and variegated.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the angel's own answer about what the chariots are in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The black horses from the north carry God's wrath for the good of those punished, and the white horses follow them bringing propitiation and joy.
comments.comment: Regarding the black horses coming from the north as vessels of wrath (Zechariah 6:6), 'from which the evils are burned upon those dwelling on the earth,' white horses were shown coming after them. These are the ministers of propitiation and of joy, and of profitable things. Since punishments are brought for the improvement of those surrendered to them, they follow harmoniously behind, clearly following them, weaving and announcing the bright and light-like things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the white horses follow the black ones in the vision.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After the black horses bring rest to the Lord's wrath in the north, the speckled horses go out from the south, and all the horses stand ready to go through the earth at the Lord's command.
comments.comment: When the black horses had come from the land of the north to rest the wrath of the Lord, the variegated and speckled were seen coming from the south; from that, namely, concerning which in the Song of Songs the bride says to her bridegroom: 'Come, south wind,' the cold north wind and harsh wind having been sent away by her. The bride's saying goes thus: 'Awake, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let my spices flow' (Song of Songs 4:16). And good words and pious thoughts are the spices. It was interpreted in what went before who the variegated horses are, and why they were so called. And all the horses stand by the Lord of all the earth, being ready to go around all the earth and to accomplish what the Lord of all the earth commands, or rather of all creation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A soul that has been struck by God's wrath, and bears it bravely, comes through to light and gratitude, and God is angry only for a time and for salvation.
comments.comment:
A soul, having experienced these, having become through perception, cries out most clearly toward that which approaches the destruction of the harmed (Micah 7:8): 'Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again,' meaning, having repented. For even if, having fallen, I was cast down by punishment through the wrath of God, yet having endured and having bravely received the wrath that was incited, I have come into a propitiatory state and a rejoicing intercourse, saying: 'I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against Him, until He justifies my judgment (Micah 7:9); and He will execute my judgment, and He will lead me out into the light, and I shall see His righteousness.'

For even if God is angered for the sake of improvement and benefit, He does not always do this; for He says: 'When the anger of the spirit arises, I will heal again.' He who has been benefited from such providence says gratefully to the one who has chastised for salvation by a little: 'I will bless You, Lord, that You were angry with me for salvation; You turned Your face and had mercy on me.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Just as no one can teach a science without knowing it, no one can truly prophesy unless the Word of God comes to him and opens his eyes.
comments.comment: As it is not possible to speak or hand down scientific lessons without having science, so it is not possible to foreknow truly and according to God or to prophesy spiritual prophecy without the word of God coming to the one foreknowing and prophesying. For the word of the Lord, coming to such a one, gives eyes and illumines for beholding the beauties and mysteries of truth and of God's wisdom. And the word coming to the prophet is not other than the Word of God, who comes to holy men, both angels and principalities and authorities and thrones and dominions, being always toward the Father who begot him. For concerning the Father it is said that the Word was toward him: 'For this one,' it says, 'was toward God,' being God the Word (John 1:1-2). And he comes to be, and is not already, toward the spirit-bearing men, being also then toward them when he comes to be.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the word of the Lord came to the prophet.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one head of Jesus receives many crowns because each virtue is a crown and he holds every virtue, and in him all believers, who are his body, are crowned.
comments.comment:
Many crowns made of the intelligible gold and silver are placed upon the head of Jesus, the one of righteousness—for indeed the name Iesedek is taken into the Greek sound from the Hebrew into 'righteousness'. And see how the one head of Jesus receives many crowns. For he was tested 'in all things without sin' (Hebrews 4:15), having overcome the contests.

… Understand by theory another way how the head of Jesus, the great high priest, receives the crowns of all. All those believing are the body of Christ and members; for it has been said regarding those completing the sum of the Church: 'You are the body of Christ and members of the member' (1 Corinthians 12:27).

… And it is not paradoxical for one man's head to receive all the crowns. For if … each virtue is a crown, and the perfect man has all the best dispositions, following the virtues themselves, the one having all them is revealed by many crowns.

… First, the one taken up by the God-Word was a man; then his imitators, who are themselves called Christs because they are partakers of that of whom it is said: 'The Christ is the wisdom and power of God' (1 Cor 1:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why many crowns are set on one head.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man called the Rising is the Savior, a man born of Mary and the sun of true light and righteousness, and Jeremiah's just rising from David agrees with it.
comments.comment:
'You shall say,' he says, 'to him,' making clear that it is the son of Wisdom; 'Thus says the Lord of Hosts: Behold, a man, an ascending-sun is his name.' But these things are said concerning our Savior who has come among us, being a man according to his being born from Mary, the temple of the God-Word, and being a sun of true light and righteousness.

… What is said in the prophet Jeremiah agrees with the present matter, having thus: 'Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a just rising, and he shall reign and reign, and he shall understand and do judgment and righteousness upon the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell trusting, and this shall be his name, which the Lord shall call him, Joshedek among the prophets' (Jer 33:15).

… For the just rising up from David is that which is shown by the hierophant in the: 'Behold, a man, an ascending-sun is his name.' This same man is called an ascending-sun because of the sun of righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father calls him a man because of the incarnation and the East because he was raised up as the sun of righteousness.
comments.comment: Showing His own servant, the Father says: 'Behold, a man, East is his name' (Zechariah 6:12), calling him a man because of the incarnation, and East because of having been raised up, being a sun of righteousness; for indeed it has been written about him in the last of the Twelve Prophets, from the person of the Father who sent him: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise for you who fear my name, and healing in his wings' (Malachi 4:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse calls him a man and gives him the name 'East'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who rises up builds the house of the Lord, and so do those who obey him by building their lives on the rock, and those who were enemies under his feet and are made friends.
comments.comment:
It rose up like light and offspring. He who, having risen up below according to a theological statement, 'he will build the house of the Lord'—the Church of the living God—especially he who, having risen up below the God-Word during the visitation, is a man. But also those who, having risen up below according to the other interpretations, being obedient to the All-King and good teacher, having changed the commandments of the one ruling and instructing them into practices, built their life like a house upon the rock which is Christ, setting the foundations and bases of the house upon the solid and indestructible faith into the Trinity, a rock so named toward the one confessing it toward the one having been confessed, according to it thus as it is said: 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church', and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it' (Matt 16:18).

But also those who, according to the third interpretation, having been placed under the feet of the All-King as enemies, becoming instead different friends, will build the house of the Lord, 'that he may dwell and walk in them' (2 Corinthians 6:16), having called and having improved them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ receives virtue as the righteousness of God made in men, and each of the faithful offers the virtue of his own calling.
comments.comment:
He who, having risen up below according to the visitation, similarly to: 'Truth from the earth has risen up' (Psalm 85:11), 'shall receive virtue,' is one of those bearing it, those being saved toward him and being led into great glory. For how does he not receive this from the one becoming in him the righteousness of God, he became sin on behalf of them, according to apostolic teaching: 'For he who did not know sin, he made sin on behalf of us, that in him we might become the righteousness of God' (2 Cor 5:21)? For how does he not receive virtue being the righteousness and abundance of peace in the days of his incarnation?

As he intends to receive the virtue being made in men, let each of the faithful bear fruit and offer it; the one preferring to be temperate, decency and temperance, also purity and virginity; the one self-controlled, self-control, 'always carrying the death of Jesus in his body' (2 Corinthians 4:10) to himself. And those 'using the honorable marriage and the undefiled bed' (Heb 13:4) also offer virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The throne of the one who rises is double, one as king and one as priest, and the Scriptures show both.
comments.comment:
The one called the Rising Sun 'is seated and shall reign upon his throne' (Zechariah 6:13). And his throne is double, the one as king, the other as priest, as it is possible to demonstrate from the written words.

… The Pantocrator is made manifest from the recurring decree having it thus: 'When a righteous king sits upon a throne, nothing evil opposes him' (Proverbs 20:8); but also from: 'Your throne, O God, is unto an age of ages; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingship' (Ps 45:6); and from that which is said in the Psalms: 'The Lord King is seated for ever' (Psalm 29:10).

… Concerning the priestly aspect, in the Epistle to the Hebrews; for the one who inscribed the epistle wrote: 'Such a high priest became fitting for us, holy, blameless, undefiled' (Hebrews 7:26), and he says: 'Let us therefore approach with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help' (Heb 4:16), calling the throne of grace the throne of the holy, blameless, and undefiled high priest.

… the one about whom it is said 'is seated and shall reign upon his throne' (Zechariah 6:13) has received 'the throne of David his father, that he may reign for the ages, his kingship having no end' (Luke 1:32-33), but also 'an unshakeable priesthood' (Ps 110:4). For it has been said concerning him: 'You are a priest for ever' (Ps 110:4).

… Upon the double throne he is seated and shall reign, he alone having the throne of kingship and priesthood. When having sat upon the throne he shall reign firmly, thus: 'there shall be a priest at his right hand, in the midst of a peaceful counsel between both' (Zechariah 6:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's king and priest on one throne.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The priest at the right hand is like the Son of God and a priest forever, and so has a peaceful will toward him whom he resembles.
comments.comment: [Of the priest at the right hand of the one enthroned:] He is not a shadowy God-healer, but truly and according to the Spirit, he will be at the right hand of the one sitting and beginning upon his throne. Being made like the Son of God, and remaining a priest forever, he has a peaceful will toward the one whom he was made like; and likewise the Son of God is making peace toward the king of Salem, that is, the king of righteousness, who is this Melchizedek. For how does he not have a peaceful will toward the one to whom he is a priest according to the order, remaining for an age?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The crown is for those who endure with greatness of soul and for the useful and those who have known it, and the crown is the Lord of Sabaoth himself.
comments.comment:
And the true and divine crown is given to those who endure with greatness of soul, according to what was said, of which we also briefly remembered: 'Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for having been proven, he shall receive the crown of life which God promised to those loving him' (James 1:12).

… And this holy and beautiful crown exists not only for those enduring, but also for 'the useful and those having known it.' … [The crown is] The Lord of Sabaoth himself, as it is brought forth in the prophet Isaiah: 'On that day the Lord of Sabaoth will be a crown of glory' (Isaiah 28:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We are called orthodox for holding the Church's knowledge, and the crown is woven not of gold but of right glory about the truth, the unfading crown Peter promises to those who have guarded the faith.
comments.comment: For this is a contest of glory, to be given to those who glorify God in their own bodies; and the pious hold a conception, and of those who are prudent, rather of the pious dogmas. For according to this we are called orthodox, those having ecclesiastical knowledge. And this crown is woven not of gold and costly stones, but of the right glory concerning the truth. And this same is the incorruptible, about which the Apostle writes literally: 'He who struggles exercises self-control in all things' (1 Cor 9:25), but one who, having run the lower and human contests, competes 'so that he may receive a corruptible crown' (1 Cor 9:25), 'but we receive an incorruptible' (1 Cor 9:25), which has also been called unfading by the most supreme Apostle Peter (1 Pet 5:4). … For he is writing to those who shepherd the true flock under the shepherd, concerning which things God promises to give to his spiritual sheep, saying: 'I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall shepherd you with knowledge' (Jer 3:15), and the word of Peter has it thus: … 'I exhort the elders among you to shepherd the flock that is among you, not by compulsion but willingly, so that, when the Chief Shepherd appears (1 Pet 5:4), you may receive the unfading crown of glory' (1 Pet 5:4), to be yielded to those having guarded the faith orthodoxly and to those leading to the end, the command saying: 'Then give glory to our God' (Psalm 68:34), and again: 'Give glory and honor to the Lord' (Psalm 29:1).
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms what kind of crown the verse means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm in the house of the Lord is a word about those who do and think well, to which a timbrel, harp and lyre are due.
comments.comment: This crown is given 'for a song of Zephaniah and a psalm in the house of the Lord' (Zechariah 6:14), about which the hymn-writer says: 'Take a psalm and give a timbrel, a pleasing harp with lyres' (Psalm 81:2). And it is a psalm which it is necessary to take, the word concerning those doing and thinking well, to which it is fitting to give a timbrel, a pleasing harp, and a lyre.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The timbrels and instruments given with the psalm are joined to the powers of the soul and senses, but God rejects false songs, so one must sing and chant in the heart.
comments.comment:
… for the timbrel has the form of a dead skin.

These are beaten and struck by the five prudent virgins, according to that which is sung in Psalm 67:5: 'Princes have gone before, singing in the midst of young women, timbrel players.'

The Hebrew women used the interpreted timbrels after they had departed from Egypt and crossed the Red Sea, of whom the prophetess Miriam, sister of Moses and Aaron, came forth, having taken the timbrels of themselves in hand; singing triumphantly in accordance with the choir leader, they said: 'I will sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously exalted; He has cast horse and rider into the sea' (Exodus 15:1), and the following until the end of the song.

For it is not even probable to think that such a multitude of timbrels could be found in a completely desert place with such myriads of women, it being quite possible that the timbrels spoken of allegorically have already been found in more advanced years among the God-fearing, especially spurred on toward the spiritual dance, from which they have been seen to have happened paradoxically for the sake of becoming outside of Egypt.

And they are given by those having received the psalms with the timbrel and a pleasant harp along with lyres, joined to the powers of the soul and the senses toward the divine melody; but sobriety is necessary so that one does not take false instruments and songs, which God rejects, saying: 'Turn away from me the sound of your songs, and I will not hear the melody of your instruments' (Amos 5:23).

He who turns away from what is rejected by God sings and chants praiseworthily, according to the exhortation of the writing Apostle: 'Speaking to one another in psalms, spiritual songs, singing and chanting in the heart' (Ephesians 5:19).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those far off from the captives will come to the one who proclaimed forgiveness and will build in the house of the Lord, and those who hear will hear the voice of the Lord.
comments.comment:
After the crown into the graces of Zephaniah and into the psalm in the house of the Lord, these existing, those who are still far off from the captives will arrive in order to approach the one who has proclaimed to them forgiveness; and praising, they say 'they shall build in the house of the Lord,' in order that they may serve continually in the manner of priests, according to the blessed prophet Samuel.

And each shall be completed, being fulfilled through vision, when the useful ones, having heard, shall hear the voice of the Lord, and having known the cause of the gap which they waited for for a time.

Those who approached and those being far away, the ones who received benefits in the house, they hear the practical things and the mysteries of the kingdom, the priestly iniquities, the things set forth by the Lord Pantokrator.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
