comments.capsule: The Lord tells those who fasted wrongly that the fast he accepts is not theirs, and he recalls the times when Jerusalem and its country around were peaceful, inhabited and fruitful.
comments.comment:
To those who fasted and cut fasts in the fifths and sevenths not as was fitting, the Lord says: “Behold, seventy years you have spent in Babylon, having been carried away in it by the law of captivity (Jer 29:10); not the fast that I accept you fasted for me, but eating and drinking your own pleasant things, doing nothing according to the words in the hands of the prophets before, when Jerusalem was being inhabited and prospering, and the cities of Judah around her, of which she is the metropolis, and the mountain and the plain were being inhabited?”

For how would the metropolis not have prospered with the cities under it, and the mountain and the plain inhabited around it, bringing deep peace and being ruled with the right law, having driven far away every war and enemy? Thus, regarding Jerusalem and the cities around her making peace and having much stability, there was abundant prosperity while the plain and the mountain land were being inhabited.

It happens for such places to be inhabited when there is much fruitfulness and prosperity, for men to dwell able to live well in the mountain, the planting of trees being full of oaks, and the plain bringing wheat and barley and the other crops. For in places multiplying, a multitude of men loves to dwell, some indeed farming, others enjoying the abundance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jerusalem and its peaceful, inhabited country is a picture of the Church, where the mountain bears the doctrines of piety and the plain bears moral instruction, and whoever longs for this must turn the prophets' words into deeds.
comments.comment:
Jerusalem being inhabited and prospering, and the cities around her, the Church finds this by analogy, and the orthodox views; of which the mountain, producing fruits, is the doctrines of piety and of the orthodox faith, having much abundance of products in the moral instruction in the low plain.

… Since this abundance and all-fruitfulness is of a spiritual nature, how could the mountains and the plains not be inhabited by men, along with the true word which makes them so, to the point that they might cry out and sing thankfully to the God who has granted so many things?

… And a sign of a painless habitation in the mountains and the plains is that the rams of the flocks have put on fat-footed steps, because the pasture has been made to grow abundantly in the places of the mountains and the plains.

… When the longing for this spiritual enjoyment of prosperity enters, let him listen to the words given by God into the hands of the prophets, transforming them into actions, so that also from his own practical powers the spring of life may rise up, 'water leaping into eternal life,' by the grace of the Savior who provides all these things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judges who favor one side through bribes or friendship are unrighteous, as the Psalms, Isaiah and Habakkuk complain.
comments.comment:
… to each of the rulers of the people: "Judge a just judgment" (Zech 7:9), as there is one who judges unjustly through bribery and grants favors through friendship, and even when there is a bribe toward someone being judged. To such complaints the divine word cries out to those: "How long will you judge injustice and accept the faces of sinners? Judge the orphan and the poor, justify the lowly and the needy" (Psalms 82:3). Such are also those concerning whom the prophet Isaiah speaks: "Those justifying the ungodly because of gifts and removing the right of the righteous" (Isaiah 5:23).

Concerning those who lawlessly act thus, the prophet Habakkuk cries to God: "Judgment has become contrary to me and the judge takes bribes; therefore the law is dissolved and justice does not go to its end, because the ungodly oppresses the righteous" (Hab 1:4). It must be said to those examining things in this way, who dispute among themselves, that they are not to be considered just judges, but altogether unrighteous and lawless judges.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A judge should look to the facts and not to wealth, rank, friendship or a bribe, since the judgment belongs to God and not to him.
comments.comment: For it is fitting that no one should observe the judge, whether he prefers wealth, status, or lineage, whether he prefers friendship, or looks toward a bribe, but rather toward the facts of the things being judged. The priest who receives God proclaims these things to those being ordained to judge in this way: "Both the great and the small you shall judge, you shall not accept a face," "and the poor you shall not show mercy in judgment," "for the judgment of God is." It is not right to distribute and measure the things of God to whoever happens to be. For of their own things, let each have authority to grant to whomsoever it may seem to him; not of his own, but of God is the judgment according to the divine law.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a just judgment means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law looks at deeds and not at wealth, rank or poverty, so the poor and the widow are not favored if they act unjustly.
comments.comment:
… even if the one being judged is rich, even if he has honor and rank. For the law of those being judged does not count the abundance of wealth and poverty, nor rank and dishonor, but works and deeds having been performed according to virtue or malice.

… Just as therefore it is not necessary to take advantages from the wealth and rank of those being judged, so also you will not lack wealth and the lowliness of dishonor; 'For you will not show mercy to the poor in judgment' (Exodus 23:3). For the just judgment and the things of the poor must be examined. For in this way someone will justify an orphan and a widow, and a poor man and a needy person, not granting him the just right if he acts unjustly, so that the legal judgment may not be perverted.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After commanding just judgment the word forbids oppressing the widow, orphan, sojourner and poor, and one who truly visits them in their affliction cannot judge them unjustly.
comments.comment:
The righteous word, having commanded that a just judgment be brought forth, proceeds to forbid: 'Not to tyrannize the widow, the orphan, the sojourner, and the needy' (Zechariah 7:10). For it is not proper to impose punishment tyrannically against those deprived of human help, but from the opposite to reach out to them with righteousness, according to that which is commanded: 'Become, he says, as a father to orphans, and instead of a husband to their mother' (Sirach 4:10), 'judging orphans and justifying widows.'

For this is unassailable and according to the will of the one who composed all, as James writes in the epistle in which he addressed the believers thus: 'Pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world' (James 1:27). He who thus serves God, how could he unjustly judge these whom he visits in their affliction, filling up their lacks through almsgiving and other help and protection as they may need?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's command about the widow and the poor.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those without protection, the widow, orphan and sojourner, are to be helped and not harmed, and in the allegory the widow and orphan are those who have left the devil and sin and are lifted by God.
comments.comment: In the same way as one must not oppress a widow and an orphan through a husband or parents, one must not likewise oppress a sojourner staying with those to whom he has taken refuge, whom they consider a stranger and a non-native. If any of those named—a widow, an orphan, or a sojourner—is deprived of resources, one should share equality with him, not by oppressing or by harming him in any other way. … It is indeed good and pleasing to God to stand up for those who are in such a state according to history, but especially according to allegorical interpretation. … A widow is praised according to theory if she has cast off the evil husband she had, meaning no one other than the devil or some other evil spirit. Likewise, an orphan is good if the father who sired him through sin has died. … The divine Bridegroom, being also a Father, lifts up those souls who have thus become widows and orphans, according to what is said in the Psalms about him: 'He will take up the orphan and the widow.' For 'the Father is the judge of orphans and widows,' according to what is said in another Psalm, also caring for sojourners who have left idolatry and turned to piety, enriching every poor person and needy one because of us, according to the apostolic word that stirs up those who suffer well, saying: 'Know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that being rich he became poor for us, so that through his poverty we might become rich.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not to hold a grudge in the heart means forgiving from the whole heart, as the Savior shows in the parable of the servant who owed ten thousand talents.
comments.comment:
Having taught how one must not oppress those in need of protection and help, he harmoniously brought forward also that one must not be vengeful, not only in word but from the depth of the mind, saying: 'And let no one be vengeful against his brother in your heart.' What was said by the Savior in the Gospel is equal to the prophetic: 'If you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your trespasses. … The Savior makes this perfect forgiveness of whatever one has done sinfully manifest in the parable of the servant owing ten thousand talents; for this is chosen by the master who forgave the debts to the 'unworthy servant' for all of us: 'So also will your Father do if you do not each forgive from your heart those who owe you' (Matt 18:35).

… Taking the whole parable in hand, understand its words and its meaning precisely, so that, being benefited toward goodness, you may forgive the debts from your whole heart to all those who owe, remembering no more those things by which the one who wronged you sinned against you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means by bearing no grudge in the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who keeps God's words in heart and soul, speaking of them at home and on the road, will not refuse to pay attention to them.
comments.comment:
Since God has given a divine law to the people of the Hebrews, an exhortation from the one who gave it was brought forward in the seventy-seventh and seventy-seventh Psalm thus: 'Pay attention, my people, to my law' (Psalm 78:1). He who follows the exhortation in this way 'meditates on the law of the Lord day and night' (Ps 1:2), according to what is philosophized in the first Psalm, which Moses the high priest previously established saying from the face of God:

'All these words, as many as I command you this day, shall be in your heart and in your soul, and you shall speak of them sitting in your house and walking on the way, looking and wandering, and you shall touch them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be unshakable'—or 'unmoving'—for the scripture is carried either way—'before your eyes' (Deut 6:6-8).

To the one thus keeping the given commandment, paying attention and obeying the legislation follows. For how will one who has the holy words in heart and soul disobey in paying attention, as speaking of them while being at home and walking on the way, looking and wandering?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who turns the words of God into works and keeps them before the eyes of the heart will not be inattentive or disobedient.
comments.comment:
He who is thus zealously disposed toward the words of God, having turned them into works, grasps them upon his practical power, the hand called allegorically, so that having them before his eyes, he may contemplate the beauty of their thought, whether they be shaken or unshaken—for I said there are two kinds of writing of the word. And the words and the meanings completed from them are shaken before the eyes of the heart when we act according to what has been legislated.

Or are the words grasped upon the hand and understood and practiced not shaken, indicating the other writing of the unshaken, which is said before the eyes of the legislated, the permanent and certain of the established things, agreeing with the prophetic here: 'The word of the Lord remains forever' (Isaiah 40:8), and with the words of the Psalmist: 'All his commandments are sure, established unto the age of ages' (Psalm 111:7-8). According to this thought, 'the words of Jesus shall not pass away, even if heaven and earth pass away' (Matthew 24:35).

He who is secured through all the things contemplated, having the words of the Lord in heart and soul, and speaking in them while being at home or walking on the way, looking and fasting, will by no means be inattentive or disobedient, nor again 'will he give heed to one acting foolishly.' How then will he who is disobedient in paying attention give heed to one acting foolishly?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who neglect God's words dishonor the Lawgiver and turn away from him, and some have gone after idols.
comments.comment:
It happens that they stumble and disregard those to whom the words of God have been given as a matter of neglect, just as they have turned away from the very one to whom the words belong. For each of those persisting thus and cutting short, dishonors the Lawgiver God, transgressing what has been legislated, as the Apostle says regarding the one who falsely and with deceit claims to have the truth and guards what God has legislated: 'He who boasts in the law, by the transgression of the law, dishonors God' (Romans 2:23)

… Not only did these wanderers not do this, but they also showed neglect with an unslumbering eye to the overseer, having gone entirely after Baal and regarding all idolatry as to worship and adore evil demons, those hidden among soulless statues, enjoying itching and smoke, and incantations and other things, being burned upon altars built lawlessly and most impiously.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man makes the ears of his soul heavy by his own choice, not the ears of the body.
comments.comment:
… 'For they made their ears heavy, he says, not to listen, and they set their heart disobedient, not to listen to the divine law and words of which the Lord the Pantokrator spoke in his Spirit' (Zechariah 7:12).

… For someone makes his own ears heavy, not those of the body, for this is not upon us, but those of the soul; by pre-choice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that they made their ears heavy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heart of one who despises God's kindness grows hard and heavy with lawlessness, as a weight of lead, and so stores up wrath.
comments.comment: … Perhaps the heart of the one who despises is hardened and becomes heavy, having received lawlessness, being weighed down like a talent of lead. The Apostle writes to the one who despises the existing fountain of goodness: 'Do you despise either the wealth of his kindness and his tolerance and his patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?' (Rom 2:4). 'But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are treasuring wrath for yourself in the day of wrath' (Rom 2:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse speaks of a hardened heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Pharaoh's heart was hardened by his own lawlessness and not by God, and we should ask the one who removes stony hearts to give us hearts of flesh that obey.
comments.comment:
In this way Pharaoh and his heart were hardened. For, while being repeatedly subjected to great powers of those becoming rich in kindness, which are exhorting, but rather coercing, to come to recognition, the insolent man remained in audacity and roughness; the insolent man was being hardened, his heart being weighed down by the talent of lead, there being nothing other than lawlessness, whence, having enriched himself with the lead of lawlessness in like manner, 'he sank like lead in rough water,' as it is carried in the triumphal ode against him.

Since, therefore, no such heart was raised by God, but rather those having it possessed it by themselves, because of the hard and contrary, and being called stony—as we have such a ruling principle by ourselves—let us approach thus by choice to the one who removes the stony hearts, so that instead of them he may place fleshy hearts, tractable and well-guided, so that we may be able to keep his commands and ordinances, obeying the spiritual law, our heart changing from disobeying and not obeying the divine law into doing all things with persuasion that must be fulfilled according to law and the sent words in the Spirit of the Lord of the Pantokrator …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is angry in proportion to each man's deeds, greatly with great sins and a little with small ones, and he does not bring wrath every day.
comments.comment: The Lord, giving to each of the men according to his deed, to those committing many and great sins he is greatly angry, and he does this in part to those stumbling a little and few. For it has been said by him concerning the vessels of wrath being found fit for punishment: 'I indeed was angry a little, but they themselves persisted in evils' (Zechariah 1:15). And those accusing themselves for the things in which they acted lawlessly cry out to the merciful and compassionate Master: 'Do not be greatly angry with us.' For just as the way is 'being a just judge, strong and long-suffering, he does not bring wrath on every single day' (Psalm 7:11), so in part he is angry with those being judged, not observing all their lawlessness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a great wrath from the Lord means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since God does not change, human passions must not be attributed to him when Scripture speaks of his wrath.
comments.comment: These things said concerning God of the Scriptures, let us not fall into such impiety and foolishness as to approach human passions toward the one saying: 'I do not change' (Mal 3:6), to whom the theologians say, the one is: 'You are the same,' and the other concerning him: 'With whom there is no change or shadow of turning' (Jas 1:17). For if he is the same, not changing, not being altered, not having a change of turning or a shadow, how would he stretch out for punishment? For nothing else is wrath or the stretching out for punishment. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is jealous for Jerusalem as a husband is for a wife who strayed and now returns, and so he comes back to dwell in her midst.
comments.comment:
Thus it happened: 'The word of the Lord of Hosts came, saying: These things,' he says, 'says the Lord of Hosts: I have envied Jerusalem and Zion with great zeal, and with great wrath I have envied her. Thus says the Lord: And I will return to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called a true city, and the mountain of the Lord of Hosts a holy mountain' (Zechariah 8:2-3).

As the presented matter might be made clear toward a literal sense thus: There came a word of the Lord of Hosts saying the following things made manifest: 'These things,' he says, 'says the Lord of Hosts: I have envied Jerusalem and Zion,' recalling her to himself after she had been cast out and pushed away, as if she had been insulted by strangers. Not just by chance did I envy her, but in great wrath. From cohabiting women the example was taken for men. The woman who set aside the marriage rights, and strayed from the bed in love toward strangers, no longer being under the guardianship of the former cohabitant, is henceforth neglected, so that it is said to her by the slighted husband: I will no longer spare you, nor be jealous. For how could one be jealous or care when the marriage is dissolved? Even if, then, the one who despised the marriage bed becomes an outcast, having a place of repentance, returning to the one she left, she becomes an object of jealousy again, the former cohabitant receiving her with great goodness.

But from the case of women we must pass to the contemplation concerning Zion and Jerusalem. By Jerusalem and Zion I mean not the places, but those dwelling in them. God led her to cohabitation, bringing her up from Egypt, providing laws and ordinances as a dowry, so henceforth to care for and spare the wedded one, and to chamber as fitting with the cohabiting bride. After the harmony thus made according to laws, setting aside the marriage laws, she set aside the protecting and helping husband, as it says: 'As a wife sets aside her companion, the house of Israel set me aside' (Jeremiah 3:20), so henceforth to go to guilty demons and unclean spirits, and to be insulted harlot-wise.

And those coming together with her are Babylonians and Assyrians according to allegory. When these things happened for long, Jerusalem and Zion, coming to themselves, remembered the one who of old had taken her as a companion, so as to wish to return to the one from whom she was unyoked. She uttered these voices: 'I will return to my former husband, for it was well with me then rather than now' (Hosea 2:7). Receiving such repentance of hers, he to whom she began to return and come back says: 'In that day,' when the return is confirmed, 'she shall call me: My husband,' as henceforth, as protector and guardian, to be jealous over her with great wrath, avenging those who insulted her. Having been jealous over her with great wrath, so as to desire to be with her as before, when she had not yet strayed from the bed, therefore returning to her: 'I will dwell in her midst' (Zechariah 8:3). But he speaks as concerning one, Zion and Jerusalem; for Zion is part of the metropolis.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the marriage picture behind God's jealousy and his return, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the soul has strayed, God in great wrath drives away those who defile her and turns back to her prayers.
comments.comment:
Concerning the so-called Jerusalem of the discerning soul—for Jerusalem is taken to mean 'vision of peace'—having slipped and now being outside the divine chamber, a separation has occurred from that which previously dwelt with her, so that she is henceforth being dragged away in a prostituted manner by opposing powers, called in spiritual ascent Assyrians and Babylonians, so that her suitable husband no longer shows pity for her.

But since the matters of free choice do not remain in this state, for just as a turning occurs from virtue into vice and from piety into impiety, so likewise a change occurs from worse and harmful things into better and profitable ones, so as to find again the divine chamber that had left, so that, as before being cherished, he himself zealously pursues her while driving away those who adulterously defile her. And in great wrath he works this, intensely indignant against those dragging her away, so as to say clearly: 'I have zealously guarded Zion and Jerusalem' (Zechariah 8:2).

In spiritual ascent, the soul is aiming at the unseen and the eternal, and a soul seeing peace has the rhythm of the following of virtues and divine understandings, for whom, having zealously cared in great wrath for her, he turns back to himself, and at the same time to her, attending to her supplications in providing what for which she prays unceasingly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jerusalem is called true because it is again a city full of people and buildings, and the mountain holy through worship.
comments.comment:
What exists when I say, 'when I turn back and dwell in the midst of it', or the calling again of that city 'true', no longer being a desert, but full of citizens and buildings, the temple and the houses having been raised up, to have as before cloisters, streets, cut-out squares and narrow ways.

Thus, Jerusalem having explicitly been called true, and the mountain of the Lord Pantokrator shall be holy as it was before the captivity, through the regular sanctifications there, and the hymns and praises being raised up according to the words of the Psalmist, where it is said: 'To you is due praise, O God, in Zion' (Psalm 65:1); and where: 'Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion' (Psalm 9:11). After these things have appeared according to history, it is a time to contemplate those things regarding the spiritual ascent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountain of the Lord is no earthly mountain but the presence of the Son of God, who takes away the sin of the world.
comments.comment:
In harmony with the holy city being called true, the mountain of the Lord Pantokrator shall be holy and shall prosper. See if the mountain of the Lord Pantokrator is the word of the presence of the Son of God, concerning which in a certain song of ascents it is brought forth thus: 'Those having trusted in the Lord as Mount Zion' (Ps 125:1). For let our mind not be so impoverished as to think it is to be compared to or made like a sensible mountain, those having trusted in the Lord, having a vast virtue, as being shown to have spiritual blessings as blessed ones. For it is written in Jeremiah the prophet: 'Blessed is the man who has trusted in the Lord; and the Lord shall be his hope' (Jer 17:7). And in the Psalms: 'It is good to have trusted in the Lord or to have trusted in man' (Psalm 118:8).

Since therefore it is not a sensible mountain, being a refuse of the earth, those having trusted in the Lord imitate—what must they think, or that concerning which Isaiah said: 'At the end of the days the mountain of the Lord shall become manifest' (Isa 2:2), shining and having been revealed 'at the completion of the ages, in order to abolish sin,' having loosed and made it vanish, having received the judgment of the Lamb. This mystery illuminating, John the Great said, showing Jesus: 'Behold the Lamb of God, the one taking away the sin of the world' (John 1:29).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Literally, Jerusalem is restored to deep peace, so that the old sit in its streets and children play there without fear of enemies.
comments.comment:
The Lord of all says: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet elders and elders shall sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each having his staff in his hand, from day to day. And the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets' (Zech 8:4-5).

As for a literal sense, the prophet's proclamation declares that Jerusalem is being restored to a deep and tranquil political state. For since there is no disturbance and all wars are shot away far from the beautiful city, with no fear of enemies expected at all, those having the age of elders from long duration and many days, men and women alike, shall yet sit as before the captivity in the streets, having staffs in hand; first the elders, and let it be known if also the elders women; for the staff is a symbol of honor.

Thus, those preceding in age being seated, the streets shall be filled with boys and girls playing, not being restless in the streets due to the bringing of infants, or enemies lying in wait, or expected wars.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the verses promise: peace, old people seated, children playing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Church is the city of God, whose streets are the virtues and their actions, and where the Most High dwells unshaken.
comments.comment:
Regarding the showing of an ascent, Zion must be turned back through a high allegorical understanding, calling the things philosophized by the one speaking to the Hebrews the true Jerusalem, writing: 'You have ascended, Zion, mountains and city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem, and church of the firstborn, who celebrate festivals with myriads of angels' (Heb 12:22), for which reason they are 'written in the heavens,' having been granted citizenship in the holy and heavenly city. …

The glorious Church is a spiritual city having streets, concerning which it is announced to the one holding it, the King of all: 'The city of God was spoken of as having been glorified concerning you' (Psalm 87:3). … The streams of the river gladden the city of God; the Most High has sanctified its tabernacle, God is in its midst, it shall not be shaken' (Psalm 46:4-5). For the Most High, having sanctified its tabernacle, dwells in the midst of the peaceful city being spoken of, never becoming outside of it, but remaining unshakeable within it. …

The streets of this beautiful city exist as virtues and their actions, about which the wise man reports proverbially, characterizing wisdom thus: 'Wisdom is praised in exits, leads to boldness in the streets, and is proclaimed upon the edges of the walls.' For how could the wisdom of God not lead to boldness in the streets of the spiritual city, again saying another wise saying: 'Desiring wisdom, observe the commandments, and the Lord will supply it to you' (Sirach 1:26), each commandment being called a wide street because of its breadth, as to say to the hymn-singer toward God: 'Your commandment is exceedingly broad'?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bride in the Song of Songs, left without her beloved, goes about the streets and finds him in the churches.
comments.comment:
One must observe whether it is said according to this thought by the bride of Christ in the erotic drama: 'On my bed in the night I sought him whom my soul loved and found him not; I called him, and he did not obey me. I will arise and go about the city, in the markets and in the streets, until I find him' (Song of Songs 3:1-4). For in the time of conjugal union and resting, whom he allegorically called night, having thought the divine bridegroom was present with her, she sought and found him not, and having called and not having him listening, it was so that something useful happened to her by being distanced, so that she might be more wounded by love toward him; for the love toward him is more raised by the distancing of the one being loved. …

Having suffered this, therefore, she arose, rousing herself, and seeks him nowhere else but in the churches, which are holy marketplaces. There the appointed apostles and prophets and teachers discourse on the rites and mysteries of the truth of the kingdom of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The boys and girls in the streets stand for the different stages of the inner life, from forgiven little children to strong young men.
comments.comment: Concerning all those strolling in the streets of the highly-praised city, it is brought forward like a single dance in one of the Psalms: 'Young men and virgins, elders with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord' (Ps 148:12). Concerning the various ages of the inner man, and whom Jesus loved, he writes to the disciple: 'I write to you, little children, that your sins are forgiven you through his name' (1 John 2:12)—that is, the Savior—'I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning; I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have overcome the evil one' (1 John 2:13-14). He calls 'little children' those who have just received the forgiveness of sins, whatever age they might be according to the outer man; he names 'fathers' those who are expert in the theology from the beginning; and 'young men' those having strength, remaining unassailable with the word of the exhorting one remaining in them, even if the struggle be 'against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness' (Eph 6:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: What seems impossible to men is not impossible to God, whether the restoring of ruined Jerusalem or of the Church in persecution.
comments.comment:
Thus says the Lord of hosts: If it seems impossible in your eyes... Will the remnant of this people not be able to remain even before me in those days? says the Lord Almighty (Zechariah 8:6).

Having undergone destruction by wars, the visible and lower Jerusalem—as its citizens underwent much captivity—was seen by those unfaithful to the promises concerning its restoration to be being abandoned, as they considered it impossible for it to be inhabited brilliantly again, as if it were to have inhabitants of the mountain and the plain, and to have elders and elder women still sitting in its squares, with boys and girls playing in them.

But since 'all things are possible to God' (Mark 10:27), and He leads from narrowness to breadth, and from hopelessness to abundance, even if there be added to the remnant of the people surrounding here many who have died, it is not impossible for God, which is appearing impossible to them.

Just as when the metropolis of Judea was being sacked and undergoing extreme desolation, men lacking the resurrection of the soul thought it impossible to restore it to its former glory and prosperity, even though God had promised and was able to bring the preordained things to an end, so also the unfaithful and the poor in mind, seeing the Church having been driven into a corner most wretchedly during the persecutions against Christians, as if an upright corpse had fallen, thought it impossible to be restored, enjoying a deep peace toward the peace of the known ones: 'My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you' (John 14:27).

Therefore, instilling courage in those to whom He will give, He promised stability and a calmed peace; 'Take courage,' He said, 'I have overcome the world' (John 16:33); therefore, even if you have tribulation now, take courage, for you are to expect relief. For truth is a friend.

Those who attacked the Church and Christianity were so incensed as to want to dash the gathering places to the ground and consume the sacred books with fire. After such brutality held out for a little while, the small-minded thought it impossible to recover it to glory again.

But even if to those it seemed hopeless and unmanageable what happened, it has been proven possible and even easy for the one who has not despaired. For one can indeed see the places once dashed down restored to height.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says and why God can do what seems impossible, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God promises to save his people from east and west, and these are not only the circumcised but all the nations who believe in the Savior.
comments.comment:
The word provides faith to expect those things that seem to be lost in despair, for the Lord of all said he would perform them. Zechariah says: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the west, and I will bring them in and cause them to dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and they shall be my people and I will be to them a God in truth and in righteousness' (Zechariah 8:7-8).

Just as a man who worships and serves God is addressed as a man of God, so his people is the one being filled by those who are God-fearing according to their respective capacities. He becomes his people, whom he saves from all the inhabited world and its ends; he promises, saying: 'Behold, I save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the west, says the Lord of hosts' (Zechariah 8:7). This is not only the one from circumcision, but belongs to all the nations who believe in the Savior according to the Gospel.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who God's people are and the meaning of 'east and west'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Once only the Hebrews were God's portion, but now the calling reaches all the nations, who come from east and west to worship him.
comments.comment:
For in the past, only one nation, that of the Hebrews, was a part and a lot of the Creator, according to the testimony of the hierophant saying: 'When the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered the sons of Adam according to the number of the angels of God, there was made a part of the Lord Jacob, a portion of his inheritance Israel,' through beauty of character and life, according to the testimony brought forth by the saints in the forty-sixth Psalm: 'He chose for us his inheritance, he loved the beauty of Jacob' (Psalm 47:4; LXX 46:4). …

Concerning the simultaneous joy and delight of all men, it has been written: 'Rejoice, O nations, with his people' (Deuteronomy 32:43), no longer of one single Hebrew nation, but of all at once worshiping and serving God according to what is announced in the Psalms, where: 'All the nations shall serve him' (Psalm 22:27); and where: 'All the nations, all those whom you have made, shall come and worship before you, and shall glorify your name, Lord' (Psalm 22:27). And again: 'The ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and the patriarchies of the nations shall worship before him, because the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and he is ruler of the nations' (Psalm 22:27-28).

Concerning the calling of all men, both Jews and Greeks, as the one people set forth by the prophet clearly announces, the Lord of all saying: 'Behold, I save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the west, says the Lord of all' (Zechariah 8:7). Concerning the dance being gathered from all the climates of the inhabited world, the Gospel signifies the Savior having said: 'Many shall come from the east and the west of the sun, and shall recline in the kingdom of the heavens with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' (Matthew 8:11). In harmony with the calling from everywhere, in the forty-ninth Psalm, the singer of the seventy-first says: 'God, the Lord of gods, has spoken, and has called the earth from the rising of the sun even unto the west' (Psalm 50:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is truth and justice, and a people is made his own in truth and justice when it is enriched with good works and true knowledge of him.
comments.comment:
What remains to be contemplated regarding the mentioned virtues? Mercy meets with truth, 'justice and peace have kissed' (Ps 85:10). For since the truth of God is great and has been lifted up, it is necessary that mercy be granted from the God who is the source of goodness, so that it may exist for men. But also justice, dissolving all injustice, the mother of all stability and of all war being averted, proclaims peace and harmony. Someone has also said that among the wise of men, peace and justice have harmony with themselves; for among all those justly pursuing the right, if it should happen so, every uprising and enmity will be driven out, as when peace prevails, equality and justice reign.

Having these things thus, the Almighty Lord is of truth and justice. For it has been said in the thirtieth Psalm, by him having the Lord as hope according to the beginning of the song: 'Deliver me, Lord God of truth' (Psalm 31:5); and in the fourth Psalm: 'In calling upon me you heard me, O God of my justice' (Psalm 4:1). It is in harmony with God being truth and knowledge, as the blessed mother of the holy Samuel said: 'Let not arrogance come out of your mouth, for God is a Lord of knowledge' (1 Samuel 2:3). When we strive to enrich a people through good works and through true and pious knowledge of God, the Victorious One will also be our God, being made our own in truth and in justice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hands are strengthened when the teaching of the prophets is turned into works.
comments.comment: Thus says the Lord of hosts: 'Let your hands be strengthened, you who hear these words from the mouth of the prophets, from the day that the house of the Lord of hosts was founded, and the temple from which it was built.' … Hands prevail in words when moral teachings are converted into works. For only then do the active hands of the soul convert into energy, when works with virtue happen to be woven together with the words, for those hearing, being not only hearers of law but also doers of work.
comments.selected_reason: Says what 'strengthened hands' means: words carried out in action.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The house of the Lord is being founded when the people of God act and think with piety, as the Church is the house of God.
comments.comment:
When, indeed, these things are practiced with sincerity and godliness, or when the people of God act and think with the word of piety, the divine house being founded and the temple being built according to the present days. The house of the Lord is being founded and the temple is being built, the fulfillment of that said in Proverbs: 'Wisdom built a house for herself, and raised up seven pillars' (Prov 9:1). Concerning this house and temple, the Lord who became man says to the Father: 'But a body I will complete for me.' Since the foundations of the house thus exist as if a holy temple having been built, the hands—that is, the practical powers—prevail according to the preceding luminous theories, called days.

Know if the glorious Church, about which the Apostle writes to Timothy his own disciple, happens to be a house founded and a temple built: 'But if I delay, so that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, a pillar and foundation of the truth' (1 Tim 3:15). This is also submitted to the mind by the prophetic voice of Isaiah having it thus: 'He who says, Jerusalem: It shall be built, and I will found my holy house' (Isaiah 44:28). When, however, will this be, or when all those having adhered to the gospel will 'be built up on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone, into a holy temple in the Lord, into a dwelling place' (Eph 2:20-22)?

In view of the things seen, and for each of the god-fearing, the house is being founded and the temple is being built, according to the testimony of Christ declaring: 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come, I and the Father, and we will make a dwelling with him' (John 14:23).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophets' words were fulfilled when the Savior was born of the virgin, and with God among us the hands of the hearers grow strong.
comments.comment:
The Gospel proclaims that the Savior has fulfilled the law and the prophets, from which point the house was founded and the temple was built, upon the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the most holy Virgin Mary, the power of the Most High having overshadowed her. For then truly the words of the prophets before us were fulfilled, having reached the outcome which was decreed.

How then do the hands of those hearing the words of the prophets not grow strong, when there is born from the virgin her whose name shall be called 'God with us' (Matt 1:23)? For when the Lord is with us, our hands at once grow strong as if to shout in praise: 'The Lord of hosts is with us, our God is the help of Jacob' (Psalm 46:7).

For having received the one who fans away evil, that is, Jacob, having acquired the surpassing strength of God Almighty, let us shout in triumph: 'God is with us. Know, O nations, and be humbled; listen, even to the ends of the earth. For if you are strong, you shall be humbled again, and any word you shall speak shall not remain with you, because the Lord God is with us.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the house and temple of the verse are fulfilled in Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Before the days of the restoration men's labor was unprofitable and there was no peace from affliction, because they were set against one another.
comments.comment:
Because before those days the wages of men will not bring profit, and the wages of cattle shall not exist, and to the one going out and the one coming in there shall not be peace from oppression; and I will send all men, each one to his neighbor (Zech 8:10).

Having foretold many things concerning the coming glorious restoration to the benefited people and the rising of holy Jerusalem, the holy house being founded upon it and the temple being built for the benefit and joy of the people, whose hands grow strong in the prophetic words, before the days of the promise, when the city was laid waste, held by those who had captured it, the wages of men by no means had profit, vainly striving and acting without purpose. …

He said: there is by no means peace from affliction for the one coming in and the one going out, the work of men and cattle being useless and unprofitable; the wage of rational mortal animals shall be in vain and the wage of cattle shall not exist, as men rise up against each other, all stability and harmony having been fled due to the ferocity and wildness of hatred existing from passion and without moderation.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the verse describes: fruitless labor and strife before the restoration.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wage of men and cattle shows that those who act without reason or understanding earn nothing, while God pays a wage for works of virtue.
comments.comment:
The word says: it is for the purpose of bringing back to reason men, because they seem to use reason while toiling and striving in vain, not to have the wage as a burden, but also not having the wage of those who are more beast-like through habit, from whom he forbids irrationality, and commands habit and forbids wildness: 'Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding' (Psalm 32:9).

For how can there be a wage for those not having understanding, doing all things with irrationality? Even if some men seem to be doing all things with bad skill, working without pay and uselessly, they do not have a profitable wage, because of 'wisdom not entering into their bad-skilled soul, nor dwelling in the body of sin which uses things wrongly,' having the wage of toil for that which is above virtue and piety.

For the soul that is acting, 'which remains for eternal life as food' and turns the holy commandments into works, the 'paymaster' God says: 'There is a wage for your works' (Jeremiah 31:16). Equally with this comparison, concerning the unseemly workers, the Apostle Paul in Christ writes: 'Each one will receive his own wage according to his own work' (1 Corinthians 3:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Men sent against their neighbors are marked by deceit, and where they live in strife there is no profitable reward and no peace.
comments.comment:
Of the one going out and coming in, of men being sent against one another, while he rules peacefully, 'each against his neighbor,' always killing and troubling one another. The hymnodist describes such a wild state in Psalm 11: 'Each spoke in vain in his heart; deceitful lips in heart, and in their heart they spoke.' Similarly, Jeremiah says concerning those lying in wait against one another: 'Do not trust in friends, and upon brothers do not rely, for every brother flutters and every friend will act deceitfully; they will not speak truth, their tongue has learned to speak lies.' Concerning such things also the psalmist David cries out: 'To me they spoke peaceful things, but in themselves they deliberate words of wrath.' And the prophet again says: 'He speaks peaceful things to his neighbor, and in himself he holds enmity,' making the treacherous and deceptive man manifest.

Of those striving thus and doing 'the works of the flesh' (Galatians 5:19), even if they seem to be men, the reward will not be to beasts, nor will the reward of the more beast-like exist. Cattle are to be rebuked in these things, the lovers of pleasure and lovers of passion, but men who profess the pseudonymous knowledge and 'the wisdom of this age and of its rulers' (1 Corinthians 2:6), having no profitable reward, are to be destroyed and not remain after this age and the life according to it. For when the light of the true one appears in the coming age, every deception having sophistry and irrational pleasure will be dissolved, so that their reward, which until now seemed to be, will no longer have or be to beasts, the one going out and coming in having no peace at all from the exhausting tribulation, each man being sent against his neighbor, so as to pursue and harm him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God promises the survivors of his people peace, with fruit from the vine, abundance from the earth and dew from heaven, as when the captives returned.
comments.comment:
And now I do not do according to the days that are before for the remnant of this people, says the Lord of all, but I will show peace; the vine will give its fruit and the earth will give its generations and the heaven will give its dew, and I will bequeath all these things to the remnant of my people (Zechariah 8:10-12). …

He says to those left of the people, as in the former days when the enemies ruled, having survived those whom they had captured, that he grants peace, and there will be prosperity and abundance, with the vine-bearing plants bearing much fruit, and the earth producing generations in abundance, and the sky giving dew, as God will inherit all things for the survivors of this people.

As a spoken word, the preceding things were promised at the time of the return of the captives, according to which the well-off, giving thanks, said: 'When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are encouraged' (Psalm 126:1), when God no longer does to the survivors of the chosen people what happened in the former days when Jerusalem was desolate, but instead provides the peace of God, for which they sent up a prayer saying: 'Lord our God, give us peace.'
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what God promises the remnant.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The restoration promised surpasses the return from captivity, since Christ's peace is for all nations and his abundance is without limit.
comments.comment:
But the things of the bright restoration have surpassed this intellectually when he came, the one saying: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach to the poor, he has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind, to heal the crushed in heart' (Luke 4:18). The same is promised also in the prophet Amos, saying: 'I will restore the captivity of my people Israel, and they shall build the ruined cities and replant them' (Amos 9:14-15).

Of these graces and gifts given by the Magnanimous, there will be peace, having risen with righteousness, in the days of the visitation of the one receiving from God the judgment of a king, concerning whom it is said: 'Justice and an abundance of peace shall rise in his days' (Psalm 72:7), so that his peace shall have no limit, since it is not for one nation but for all the nations and the whole inhabited world being ruled by him, having spoken to those known to him and those wishing to serve under him: 'My peace I give to you,' he said, with much tranquility prevailing; and not doing only what happened in the former days to the survivors of Israel, he will prepare an exceeding abundance, giving the fruit of the vine and the native generations of the earth, and the appropriate dew of the sky.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: That God will 'inherit' all things for the remnant can be read two ways: Israel is God's inheritance, and God gives his gifts to the remnant by grace.
comments.comment:
And since it is said passively that God will inherit all things for the remnant of the people—namely the fruit of the vine, the generations of the earth, and the dew of heaven—both ways it must be invoked, actively and passively.

Actively, it is said thus: Israel is a portion and an inheritance of God, through nothing other than virtues that approached, being chosen, done, and seen through voluntary action. The same thought holds for: 'Ask of me, and I will give you nations for your inheritance' (Ps 2:8), regarding all men inheriting from the Savior through pious faith and works of virtue.

If 'to inherit' signifies a passion passive reception by the falling verb, the understanding will be this: God will inherit all the aforementioned things, giving them in the manner of an inheritance to the remnant of his people, who are those saying according to the prophet Isaiah: 'Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a remnant, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah' (Isa 1:9). And with others: 'If the number of the sons of Israel were as the sand by the brim of the sea, the remnant shall be saved' (Romans 9:27). Having received these prophetic voices, the Apostle brings them forward saying thus: 'And in the present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace, not of works, for if it were of works, grace would no longer be grace' (Rom 11:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Curse and blessing come from men's own sin or righteousness, so that God, who did not relent in punishing their fathers, is now set to do them good.
comments.comment:
And just as you were a curse among the nations, the house of Judah and the house of Israel, so I will save you and you shall be in blessing.

Be courageous and strengthen your hearts. For the Lord of all says: 'In the way I intended to harm you by provoking your fathers,' says the Lord of all, 'and I did not repent; so I am now set out and intend in these days to do well for Jerusalem and the house of Judah' (Zechariah 8:15).

To fall into afflictions and curses comes from nothing other than sin and impiety, since blessing is given by God to the righteous because of what they do and think rightly. For humans being self-determining, having free and autonomous choice, they do to themselves either punishments or the bringing of divine promises. Therefore, the way in which they undergo curses is the same way in which they undergo prosperity and blessing.

Immediately, indeed, He says He is the cause of all good for Judah and Israel: 'Since your fathers were impious and lawless, as to provoke me against them, I did not repent, but I brought what was likely for those who provoked to suffer; so now I am set out and intended to save those of Judah and Israel, and I did not repent' (Zechariah 8:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Judah was a curse and why God now turns to bless, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God threatens and disciplines only to improve those he has set to bless, and so his people can be courageous and expect his gifts.
comments.comment:
The one who has grasped these saving things will not fall away from the promise, being led into the divine promises by the one saying: 'I have set to bless Judah and Israel, and I have not repented' (Zechariah 8:15). He remains by his grace so as to do well and to lead into eternal salvation those for whom he has not repented, confirming what he promised: even if your fathers provoked him through sin and impiety, and a curse spoke, he did not repent of the threat, nor did he grant you reconciliation from the evil you had through recognition, but therefore both now let your heart be courageous to expect the gifts from me.

For they shall certainly be of my willing and having set to bless you; for it shall be well with you, as you belong to Judah, the one confessing, and to Israel and Jerusalem. 'For wanting to save all men and to come into the knowledge of truth' (1 Tim 2:4), I threaten, I lash those opposing the knowing of the truth of the super-arrogant salvation, subjecting to a little pain those whom I want to improve and to do well. For thus, having been easily benefited, they shall be saved, my having set without regret to save and to do well those whom I have chosen, so that they may be part of and my inheritance.

If we also wish to have God in a propitiatory relation so that he may dispose well toward us, let our intellect, called the heart, be courageous, having made care for excellent works, so that the things of well-being and endless salvation may exist certainly and irrefutably, having been described and having been made manifest from all things, the curse which held on for a little. Therefore be courageous without doubt, expecting what the truthful God promised; for he having said: 'Be courageous' (Zechariah 8:13), without doubt the hoped-for good things are to be received.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The people of Nineveh turned and God relented from the harm he had announced, while the Sodomites, because of their remaining impiety, did not receive the same.
comments.comment: The inhabitants of Nineveh once sinned and were impiously excessive, as the cry of their evil rose to God requiring punishment, as to say to the Provider and Judge of all: 'In three more days, Nineveh shall be overturned' (Jonah 3:4). Having learned this, the guilty ones, following the path of the one who threatened toward repentance, arrived at a state to confess and to do what would undo the preceding evil. Thus, those having changed their minds, the one who had pre-proclaimed the harm against them repented, receiving the cause of blessing; this did not happen regarding the Sodomites, because of the remaining impiety and sins of theirs, even though the merciful God wished to find a starting point for well-doing among them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's 'so that I may know' means he waited to see whether they would remain in virtue, since he blesses those who keep his law.
comments.comment:
We consider that the present prophecy has not been bypassed in vain; for this has risen to clarity because of the unclearly spoken thus: 'I will come down so that I may see if they are complying according to their cry that is coming; but if not, so that I may know.' For it was necessary to reveal by what meaning it was said by God: 'So that I may know.'

God did not repent, having thought to punish and to expose the insolent upon something, remaining in the judgment against them; but from what source He repented, to see the opportunity in innate goodness.

Not having known His intent to bless Judah and Israel, He waited for their remaining in the virtue with which they took up their task from the exhortation of God and of His law; for it is said in one of the Psalms: 'He will give blessing to the lawgiver' (Psalm 84:6), that is, to those guarding His divine law. Equally, it is brought forth in another Psalm, beginning from here: 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in His holy place? He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. This one shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior' (Psalm 24:3-5).

For having been said spiritually: 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in His holy place?' an answer is given, delineating who is and what kind of person is the one about whom the question is, that he is by hands, that is to say, by action, innocent through purity of heart, not at all having taken his soul in vain, or deceitfully swearing to his neighbor, receiving upon these manly deeds both blessing and mercy from God his Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some words of God are given to be done and others to be contemplated, and speaking truth to one's neighbor is to be done, so that a peaceful judgment follows.
comments.comment:
… Since a prophet is at hand, named Malachi; and his word has it thus: 'The lips of a priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek law from his mouth,' Malachi 2:7 desiring to learn from a divine teacher what must be known: orthodox doctrines and mysteries of the kingdom, and a law forbidding injustices and protecting the teachings of virtues.

… Having learned what kind of words become practical for those to whom they belong, let us understand what kind of words possess knowledge and truth. … Moses teaching that 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth,' Genesis 1:1 said this word so that we might truly know the creation and its Creator; and whatever other words of the Cosmogeny were written, they were said not so that we might do them, but so that we might contemplate them; and upon every inspired scripture this instruction has prevailed. … And the Savior himself, in the Gospels, in some places commands those things which must be done, and in others hands down those which it is proper to know and contemplate. For that which is said by him: 'Learn from me, for gentle I am and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls' Matthew 11:29; and again: 'If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me each day' Matthew 16:24, are said for the sake of doing, as also that: 'Have mercy, and you shall be shown mercy' Luke 6:36, and as many other commands of his same power. … But that: 'I am in the Father, and the Father is in me' [John 14:10], and that: 'I and the Father are one' [John 10:30], and also: 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' [John 14:9], and as many other things which are theologized in both Testaments, were spoken and written so as to be contemplated and to have true and pious knowledge. … The Holy Spirit showed which words must be done, and each one declares this individually and according to its kind. For that: 'Let each one speak truth to his neighbor' Ephesians 4:25, is written so that it may be practiced in this way. Paul in Christ, clarifying this, exhorts the believers to the keeping of the commandment, saying most clearly: 'Having put away falsehood, let each one speak truth to his neighbor' Ephesians 4:25. … And before the Apostle, the Savior also handed down the speaking without law, saying: 'But I say to you, do not at all swear, but let your yes be yes, and your no, no' Matthew 5:34-37.

This is most strictly guarded by each person speaking the truth to their neighbor; for in this way every false word and oath will destroy that most precise and perfect brotherly love.

If each person speaks the truth to his neighbor, a peaceful judgment will occur, without those striving to covet and do wrong still causing dissension. For how can they think that conflicts and injustices are still being raised, if each one announces the truth to his neighbor?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'speak every man the truth' commands and how it leads to peace.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words of this verse belong to moral virtue and are given to be done, as Israel promised to do all God said and as Jesus calls wise the one who hears and does his words.
comments.comment:
These are the words which you shall do: each one speak truth to his neighbor and judge a peaceful judgment in your gates. And let no one reckon the evil of his neighbor in your hearts, and do not love a false oath, for I have hated all these things, says the Lord of all (Zechariah 8:16-17).

Of the words of God, those concerning moral and practical virtue are able to be put into practice, those having the contemplative and initiatory aspect to be viewed among the initiatory and discerning men.

For God, having commanded many things through the hierophant Moses so that works according to virtue might happen, those understanding the given words loudly confessed to pass over into the works that were given.

Having been told, they said to the deacon of divine blessings: 'All things which God has said we will do and we will listen.'

… Since it is proper that moral words have a connection to doing and to having a thought of them, so that justly the just may be pursued, and soberly the sober, and bravely and prudently the brave and prudent things—for in this way practical virtues might be raised up along with thought—it is therefore necessary to not neglect listening to and doing the words of Jesus, him himself forbidding this: 'The one coming to me and listening to my words and doing them will be made like a prudent man' (Matt 7:24), and the following.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A teacher is called great when he does what he teaches, and his moral lessons must be shown in works.
comments.comment:
Then especially the words have the capacity to happen among the hearers when the teacher does what he tells others; concerning such a thing the Lord says: 'Whoever does and teaches men, this one will be called great in the kingdom of heaven' (Matt 5:19), the one not doing what he exhorts others to do being of the least, since he, while saying not to commit adultery, is seized by this very thing, and while forbidding theft, he also sacrileges the idols, being loathing them.

… Or does not he who harms through scandal those who have dedicated themselves to godliness by breathing life into divine statues commit sacrilege? For he who harms such people will act with his hand and truly sacrileges through impious thoughts by transgressing the law in which he seems to boast, dishonoring God. If, therefore, no one is an evil teacher, let what he teaches moral lessons be shown in works; for in this way he will be an 'unashamed worker' (2 Tim 2:15). …

With this opinion the Apostle writes to his own disciple 'to have incorruption, dignity, a healthy word, unsearchable' (Titus 2:7). Or does he not have a healthy, unsearchable word? For doing what he dictates to others and thinking what he prepares others to be praised for, he has a healthy, unsearchable word of the teaching.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judgment is given in the gates so that the guilty are cast out and the pure kept in, and it is peaceful when wrongs are forgotten.
comments.comment:
And since they always hate those who have believed in rebuking in the gates, the word promises to restore in the gates a judgment for the good and the useful, through a change occurring. If anyone were to seek for what reason the judgments and rebukes were performed not in some other place or part of the city, but in its gates, it is because what is to be spoken honorably and convincingly—since through the gate is the exit from the city and the entrance into it—it is fitting that the judges sit there to examine the lives of the citizens, so that they might easily cast out those being rebuked for what they are accused of, while those having a pure citizenship, once their state has been made manifest by the rebukes, remain within, and the city becomes even more inward.

Raised to the intellect, those having received from Jesus 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven' (Matt 16:19) are worthy of the presidency and the seat of judging, so that they might cast out those who have fallen worthy of being bound, but those not gripped by the bonds of sin, but being strengthened in them, they might lead in. Then most especially the peaceful judgment is fulfilled, when 'each one does not count the evil of his neighbor' (Zechariah 8:17), through an absolute forgetting of wrongs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why judgment is in the gates and what a peaceful judgment is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months, which the Lord commands, are fixed by the Hebrew months.
comments.comment:
'And there came a word of the Lord of Hosts to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of Hosts: The fast of the fourth, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be to the house of Judah for joy and for gladness and for good feasts; and you shall love truth and peace.' …

The word of the Lord of Hosts having come to me, says the prophet, commanded to fast on the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth of the month, making the month evident; for it is not possible for a tenth to be a Sabbath, as we previously noted. And it is indeed likely that the Lord of Hosts commands these things regarding the Hebrew month, in which the so-called day of atonement and humiliation is fulfilled, which the Jews observe as a public fast, having purified themselves during the fourth, fifth, and seventh fasts before coming to the public fast.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fasts become joy and good feasts for those who confess, and the feasts are good only when Jerusalem lives in peace and not while enemies prevail.
comments.comment:
For those who have confessed, called the house of Judah, will receive joy, gladness, and good feasts as a well-being, celebrating them by thinking and doing what is necessary, according to what is said in the Psalms: 'A voice of joy and confession, the sound of those celebrating' (Psalm 42:4); and again: 'Establish a feast among those crowding to the horns of the altar' (Psalm 118:27). This is confirmed by what is announced in another psalm: 'A man's remembrance shall confess to you, and the remnant of a remembrance shall celebrate for you' (Psalm 76:10). …

Good feasts are fulfilled when the spiritual Jerusalem lives peacefully, being a vision of peace, not when the feasts occur propitiatorily while enemies prevail. For when things are thus, God says: 'I have hated, I have despised your feasts, and I will not be fragrant in your assemblies' (Amos 5:21). And even further threatening: 'I will turn,' He says, 'your feasts into mourning and your songs into lamentations' (Amos 8:10). …

May these painful things perish from the fellowship of the faithful, so that, having been called into joy and gladness, they may celebrate good feasts.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the fasts turn to joy and when feasts are truly good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A festival is truly kept when peace and truth are loved, for truth appears where thoughts are tranquil.
comments.comment: We perform a divine festival, loving deep peace and with it the truth. For where there is tranquility of thoughts and a settled state of soul, the delight and beauty of truth appears. Truth is seen most when serenity leads through the following of virtues and peace presides, with those having attained such well-being rejoicing and being propitious.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The seventh month of the Hebrews holds the fast and the feasts of trumpets and tabernacles, as the Psalm and Zechariah's end show.
comments.comment: It is reasonable to ask from where we estimated the seventh month according to the Hebrews, in which the four days and the others were arranged to be fasts until the tenth day, or from what is written at the end of the prophecy of Zechariah set out for examination: 'And you shall celebrate the feast of the tabernacles' (Zechariah 14:16); for this is lawfully performed not in any month other than the one mentioned, just as the feast of trumpets and the fast are. For it is clearly learned from the Psalm that even the new moon of the seventh month is a festival of celebration, having it thus: 'Sound a trumpet at the new moon, on a day of solemnity, our feast' (Psalm 81:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The peoples will again come to Jerusalem from all the cities, as the law required, after the festivals ceased in the captivity.
comments.comment:
The Lord of Hosts says these things: 'Yet many nations and many people dwelling in many cities shall come, and they shall gather, dwelling in many cities, into one city, saying, Let us go up to entreat the face of the Lord and to seek the face of the Lord of Hosts; I also will go. And many nations and many peoples shall come to seek the face of the Lord of Hosts in Jerusalem, and to seek the atonement of the face of the Lord' (Zechariah 8:22-23).

As the prophet explicitly announces, following the word of the Lord of Hosts having come to him, the coming restoration shall be propitious and festive for the multitude of the Hebrews, for the cities of Judah, and for the mother-city, Jerusalem. God commanded through Moses all Israel to celebrate three days of the year to Him in the place from which He brought them out, which was not any other than Jerusalem, from which it happened to hasten immediately from all the cities and villages of Judah to the mother-city, in which all sanctities and important mystical festivals were performed, all of which reached an end in the time of the captivity, outside of the nourishment of almost all the Hebrews. …

The prophet Jeremiah, being utterly devastated, says in the book of Lamentations: 'The ways of Zion mourn because no one comes to the festival; all her gates are destroyed, and her priests groan' (Lam 1:4-5). For how could the ways of Zion not mourn, having been deprived of those walking, with no one still hurrying for the sake of celebrating and making a festival in Jerusalem, and the gates being destroyed, torn away by those who seized them tyrannically?

In this desolation, the priests necessarily followed with groaning, seeing the time when God, whom He chose, was being treated without all pleasing readiness. These unpleasant things cease to be, as Zechariah says before pronouncing it: 'Many peoples shall still come' (Zechariah 8:20), making it clear regarding Jerusalem; for the seventieth year of the captivity is already entering, as we learned clearly from Him saying to God: 'How long will You not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, this seventieth year?' (Zechariah 1:12).

Immediately after the Lord of Hosts has relented, the peaceful leading of Jerusalem is revealed to the one who prayed, such that, just as before, many peoples will come seeking the face of the Lord of Hosts, beginning again the words: 'Three times in the year all your males shall appear before me' (Exodus 34:23), and 'Nothing shall be absent before the Lord your God' (Deuteronomy 16:16), meaning bringing sacrifices for the liturgy and other gifts and the festive offerings.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the prophecy promises: the pilgrim feasts restored after the captivity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The end of the holy assembly is to seek the Lord's face, and the pure in heart see God.
comments.comment: For such a diligent holy assembly, an appropriate end exists: to seek the appearance of the Lord of Hosts through litanies and holy prayers, Him looking and revealing Himself to the one who is lucid in mind and partaking of holiness, according to what was said in the beatitudes by the Savior: 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matt 5:8). In agreement with this thought, the lawgiver Paul writes to the Hebrews to 'pursue peace and sanctification, without which no one will see the Lord' (Heb 12:14), appearing to those who do not disbelieve in Him and shining forth to those who keep His commandments.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'seeking the face of the Lord' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ten men who seize the skirt of a Jew are the nations in the days of Christ's coming, and the Jew is the one from Judah whom the Lord raised up.
comments.comment:
'Thus says the Lord of hosts: In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations will take hold of the skirt of a Jewish man, saying: We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'

The prophecy marks the time when many peoples and many nations will come to seek the face of the Lord of hosts, seeking nothing other than the visitation of the Savior to men, through whom Emmanuel was born of the virgin, remaining God among us; in the days of him having appeared on the earth and having lived among men, there will be a calling for all people … To understand the will of the expressed prophetic word, first it must be observed who is the one Jewish man specifically named; I think it is none other than whom the Apostle signifies writing to the Hebrews: 'Manifest that from Judah our Lord has risen' (Hebrews 7:14), to rule and reign over the Jews who are in secret, by spirit and not by letter, being circumcised not in the flesh but in the heart; for concerning him we grasp that which is said in hymns by each one of discerning insight: 'My King, Judah.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Jew from Judah is the expectation of all the nations, and they follow him as leader, worshipping in spirit and truth.
comments.comment:
The same understanding is applied to the blessing said by Jacob having this content: 'Judah, your brothers have praised you' (Genesis 49:8); and with others: 'A ruler shall not depart from Judah, and a leader from his sides, until he comes for whom it is reserved, and he himself is the expectation of the nations' (Genesis 49:10). For it is not the expectation of one nation, but of all nations together, the fulfillment of the prophecy concerning the calling of all people having this content: 'There shall be the root of Jesse and the one standing to rule the nations, upon whom the nations shall hope' (Isaiah 11:10). …

Because he is a true Jew from Judah, ten men from all the languages of the nations, seizing the edge of the garment, say to him as a leader and general, rather a high priest and king of kings: 'Let us go with you, because we have heard that God is with you.' It is evident that for the Jews according to the intelligible, those who worship God in spirit and truth (John 4:23), it is not in Jerusalem or on the Samaritan mountain. For just as the angels worship the Son of God in a place, about whom the Holy Spirit says: 'All the angels of God shall worship him' (Hebrews 1:6), so also the worshippers of God from among men do not worship in any place, but act intelligibly, 'in spirit and truth.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The number ten is not literal, since the multitudes of the nations who believe are the ten, like the ten virgins in the parable.
comments.comment:
Having these things set forth, a pattern is established to show how from all the languages of the nations ten men shall seize the edge, that is, the body of the spiritual Jew. The number ten mystically lies here through allegory, just as in other divinely inspired oracles about which we shall say next: first, saying how it is impossible that from all the nations and all their languages, though there be myriads and many people, only ten men, according to the number being readily taken, have followed Jesus; for he himself is the true Jew, having risen from Judah.
