Might it be, then, that all the multitudes having come to the gospel from different nations and languages, and having knowledge of the Holy Trinity mystically, happen to be ten, similarly to what was said by Matthew of the parable by Jesus: 'Then the kingdom of heaven shall be like ten virgins' (Matthew 25:1); of those who have believed, all of whom happened to be the ten virgins, let the understanding be such.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ten men with the true Jew are those who keep both kinds of senses pure, or who turn the Decalogue into works, or Christians, since the name of Jesus begins with the tenth letter.
comments.comment:
… Therefore, all who are ever disciples of the gospel, when they possess their senses incorruptible, both the external and the internal, they become ten virgins reigning under Christ; but if ever some, through laziness, leave the internal senses of the man to act only through the mortal ones, they will become five foolish virgins, returning only to the perceptible things, as if their own light were not being nourished, which will be an extinguishing and a remnant of oil.

According to the spoken manner, ten men are found traveling with the true Jew from all languages and nations, having kept both kinds of senses pure and incorruptible, according to what was said by the Apostle: 'Grace' and peace shall be 'with those loving our Lord Christ in incorruption.' It is probable that the lovers of the letter are ten men who have converted the Decalogue ministered by the great Hierophant into works; but also Christians having the name of Jesus beginning from the tenth element among both Greeks and Hebrews; for the tenth is in the elements not only of the Greeks but also of the Hebrews.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Barrenness is a blessing when it ends a woman's destructive births and lets her receive God's seed.
comments.comment: … Because so much has been managed for Gaza, which is being severely afflicted, and for Akko, which is being described as a barren woman, for thus it is interpreted: that her piercing hope will bring shame. And since the offspring is understood in two ways by way of ascent—one being that which comes from those able to speak to God: 'From your fear we conceived in the womb and labored and brought forth' (Isaiah 26:18). And the other being the praiseworthy one, having the Bridegroom Word as her seed, being a pure one as opposed to one standing with adulteresses. … When the succession of children is thus divided in two, it is a blessed thing to undergo barrenness, she who was giving birth destructively from the invisible evil lovers; for this barrenness is for the sake of good, as she takes up the seed from God, from which a generation of offsprings shall be saving, as the result of the bride having been blessed and having become a many-child dwelling in the house of the husband …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The barren woman stands for the Gentiles, who bore children to the true Bridegroom once the synagogue grew weak.
comments.comment:
… The scriptures received are most pointedly alluding to the two calls, both the one from the circumcision and the one from the Gentiles. For the one had the law regarding the husband, bearing children from him; but the barren one was a desert of children, when, being godless, she had no hope at all in the world, according to what was written by Paul concerning idolaters (Romans 1:21). Having these things, when the true Bridegroom arrived, the barren one became a mother from him of divine offspring, seven named because incorruption and purity were coming forth, possessing these virtues of the mystical seven; nevertheless, the barren one having borne seven, she is settled by the husband, a mother of rejoicing children. …

Because the synagogue of the circumcision has grown weak due to the coarseness of the children, although it has a man, the law, the one called mother from the Gentiles has become, although she was previously barren; the seven children having been made clear as 'reborn not from corrupt seed but incorruptible through the living and abiding word of God,' so as to be a multitude of children of the desert rather than of that living by law, to a man called allegorically. Through the showing of different children and their parentage according to the divine pedagogy, it will be for good that the soul having the readiness to give birth to children of destruction be made barren, it being a ruin and harmful to be made barren of the quick-grasping soul from the seeds of the God-Word. Therefore it is proper to avoid such a barrenness, so that a generation of heavenly and good children may exist. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When what is evil is taken away, those made in God's image and likeness remain and confess to our God.
comments.comment:
Whatever is removed, those freed from the murderous insolence remain to the Lord. For when all evil joined to mankind is taken away, the image and likeness in which they were created by God remains.

Since 'man, being in honor, not understanding' (Ps 49:20), fell in a manner 'as if cast down to the mindless beasts' (Psalm 49:20), when bestiality and the beastly state are removed, the honor 'remains to our God,' the rational being revealed in the man who has become upright, the many crooked thoughts being excluded; for God having made man upright, they themselves sought vain thoughts, existing in many through coarseness.

Immediately indeed in the present prophetic word, the things that happened according to what the Ashdodites, the citizens of Gaza, and the inhabitants of Accacre did having been taken away, those created according to the image and likeness of God shall remain and they themselves shall sincerely confess to our God, as if 'making Judah thousands'; for one is taken into confessing. And each one, sincerely confessing with princely choice, is a thousand-leader. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that a remnant stays for our God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God fortifies those he has benefited so they never wander back to old sins, and the enemy who drove them out is overturned.
comments.comment:
… These things having happened, God builds an anathema for those having been benefited, having a high fortress, so that remaining within, standing firmly, they may not wander any more here and there being carried about lawlessly, nor even turning back again to those sins which they have left behind, 'forgetting them, stretching forward to those things before' (Phil 3:13), to reach 'the prize of the upward call' (Philippians 3:14). These things having been achieved, more so the gifts of God, no longer does an enemy exist to drive out, all the things lying about wildly having been destroyed.

The tyrant of the spiritual Egypt once pursued the people of God, speaking boldly and arrogantly: 'Having pursued, I shall seize; dividing, I shall scatter the curs; I shall fill my soul; I shall ascend by my sword; my hand shall rule'; and still speaking these things arrogantly, he has become a coward, all his proud words having been overturned, so as to no longer be able to drive them out. …

Having threatened the enemy, he was immediately removed, and much of his army was laid waste in a single hour by one angel, just as the Scripture declares, saying that one angel had removed one hundred eighty-five thousand 2 Kings 19:35, so that the people of God might no longer be driven out to perish. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God says he drives out no more because he has seen with his eyes, which are the angels and the contemplative men who oversee human affairs.
comments.comment:
… The Benefactor and cause of all blessed salvation says: 'Therefore it is no longer driving out, because I have seen with my eyes,' referring to the contemplative power, concerning which the Apostle writes: 'All things naked and laid bare to the eyes of God' Hebrews 4:13 and His word. It must be said a second time that those seeing are the eyes of God, which are the supervising angels of human affairs, about whom the Hymnodist says: 'His eyes look upon the nations' Psalm 86:8.

Nor did he fail to call the contemplative men, whose visions the divine have inscribed, the eyes of God; for since the body of Christ, which is the whole Church of the saved, is participating, there exist discerning eyes, as the apostolic word makes manifest. …

This should also be attributed to the prophecy: since the eyes had seen the Savior coming for the benefit and salvation of all, the one driving out was released, 'being given authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and all the power of Satan' Luke 10:19. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The daughter of Zion is the soul that contemplates good things, the daughter of Jerusalem the soul that sees God's peace, and each is told to rejoice or to proclaim.
comments.comment:
… The daughter of Zion is the contemplative soul of good things, observing the unseen eternal things; for Zion is interpreted as a place of observation, and a settled commandment. For how could the contemplative soul of truth not perform the divine commandment, taking hold of it for works, as it has been emboldened to say: 'The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes' (Psalm 19:8); and again: 'Your commandment is very wide' (Psalm 119:96) 'and your servant loved it.' Just as such a soul is the daughter of Zion in the said manner, so might someone also be the daughter of Jerusalem, a soul seeing 'the peace which surpasses all understanding' (Phil 4:7).

The word commands both, the one to rejoice intensely at the arrival of the true King, the other, as having ascended above, to proclaim the coming All-King. For Jerusalem precedes Zion, and therefore the daughter of Jerusalem precedes the daughter of Zion, as the one is commanded only to rejoice, the other also to proclaim. For one can rejoice having only accomplished a practical life, whereas the one rejoicing and proclaiming has contemplation, because the Word of wisdom and knowledge has received the superabundant gift of the Holy Spirit. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king who comes just and saving is Jesus, the Savior of the world, born of a virgin and announced at Bethlehem.
comments.comment:
… Prophecy commands that at the arrival of a king, one must proclaim him, who is simultaneously saving and found to be just, being no one other than Jesus. For who is so saving and a savior of the world as 'God with us, Emmanuel,' born from the experience of a woman not having a man, fulfilling the prophecy that says: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son' (Isa 7:14). The angel named the child Jesus, marking this mode of the virgin bearing without a man, and giving the reason for this designation thus. For this, he says, he shall be called Jesus, 'for he will save his people from their sins' (Matt 1:21).

Immediately after Mary gave birth in Bethlehem, a great angel appeared: 'A savior has been born to you today,' he said, 'who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David' (Luke 2:10-11). Those proclaiming his descent here were arranging themselves around the born Christ, according to Isaiah: 'Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, a savior is coming to you' (Isaiah 62:11); and this is no other than he who announced about himself, Jesus: 'The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost' (Luke 19:10); and again: 'Just and saving, there is none beside me' (Isa 45:21). …
comments.selected_reason: Says who the just and saving king is and why he is called Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The coming king is gentle, as he says of himself, and whoever bears his kind yoke is subject to the king mounted on the colt.
comments.comment: … Regarding the coming king being just and saving, he also stands gentle, mounted upon a colt and a foal; for he himself says about himself in the Gospel: 'Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is kind and my burden is light' (Matt 11:29-30). Everyone who carries the kind yoke becomes a subject of him upon whom the gentle king has mounted.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the king is gentle and what the colt and yoke mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The new colt stands for the nations, and the king who mounts it makes the two peoples one Church.
comments.comment:
And since the Savior is not only the one for those yoked under his good yoke, but also for those just called, and he has mounted a new colt, which was still untamed and without a bridle, so that he might also tame it, as the most skilled horse-tamer would.

In this understanding, both the called peoples are signified by the word: those from circumcision, yoked under the yoke according to the letter and the shadow of the law, called a heavy yoke; and the one immediately called from all idolatry and superstitious handling. Because those yoked to the law according to the letter bore a heavy yoke, the apostles say about it in their own Book of Acts that 'neither we nor our fathers were able to bear' (Acts 15:10) the heavy yoke of the law. …

Likewise, the gentle king has mounted the new colt mentioned, 'so that he might create the two into one new man in it' (Ephesians 2:15). For thus one people and one Church shall be composed from both the callings.

Equally in the Gospels it is written about the colt released from the opposite village, so that he might come to Jesus, being tamed by mounting upon him by the Savior (Matthew 21:2-7); for it is said that not yet had any man sat upon him, which is shown by the word that the Gentiles had not yet transitioned for any didactic reason; for they were atheists in the world, having no true hope; but even if before the faith they were an unbridled colt, yet since the Christ rising from Judah has shone upon them, expectation has risen for them, according to what is said about him: 'And he himself shall be an expectation of the nations' (Genesis 49:10), and again: 'Nations hope upon him' (Isaiah 11:10). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the colt and the donkey as the two peoples the king gathers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He begins with joy, telling the captives to rejoice greatly because the one who brings them back has come.
comments.comment: … Since sorrow is hateful to people and joy is longed for, he begins his cry with joy, saying: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion” (Zechariah 9:9). “Rejoice greatly,” the prophet cries to those in captivity. “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). Why “Rejoice”? And why “greatly,” and “be glad and delight” (Zechariah 2:10)? Because He who brings you back has come, as the father of the King who brings you back foretold, saying: “When the Lord brought back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted; then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with gladness” (Psalm 126:1–2). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse opens with a command to rejoice.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The chariots of Ephraim that the king destroys are the gatherings and teachings of the heterodox, since Jeroboam, who led the schism, came from Ephraim.
comments.comment: … Having been greatly benefited by the two callings from the mounting of the righteous and saving and gentle king upon them, the chariots of Ephraim are destroyed (Zechariah 9:10), and the horse from Jerusalem, and with them the bow of the most brutish and wild wars … The collections of the heterodox and their irrational dogmatizing are the chariots of Ephraim. It has often been shown that heresies stand by the designation of Ephraim, because Jeroboam, who led the ninety-five schisms, was from the tribe of Ephraim; just as the Savior is called Judah because he is called from the same tribe to be a ruler of the Church, so the leader of bad doctrines is called Ephraim, promising much fruit by persisting in the deceived. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The waters poured out to the sea are salty and undrinkable words that falsely claim the sweet rivers of the earth.
comments.comment: … If all things interpreted by the Great King are taken away, this too shall be: 'The waters shall be poured out unto the sea,' making them manifest to be salty and not drinkable, and 'the outbursts of the rivers of the earth,' waters flowing down to the sea. The words there are impious through saltiness, falsely claiming to have the outbursts of the sweet and drinkable rivers of the earth. Such are those of Pharaoh, who, sitting enthroned, boasts saying: 'The rivers are mine, and I have made them.' The drinking of these is forbidden by God in Jeremiah the prophet: 'And now, says he, what have you to do with the land of Egypt, to drink the waters of Gihon? and what have you to do with the land of Assyria, to drink the waters of the rivers?' (Jeremiah 2:18). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The humble king destroys the chariots of Ephraim, meaning the devil's kingdom, and in the letter the Jewish kingdom, which lasted until Christ.
comments.comment: … “Gentle, and mounted on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden” (Matthew 21:5), that is, humble-minded, and in His humility “destroying the chariots of the kingdom of Ephraim” (Zechariah 9:10), that is, the kingdom of the devil, who reigned over Israel and over the nations. According to the letter, too, He destroyed the kingdom of the Jewish people; for the anointing and the kingdom of the Jews lasted until Christ, and then ceased. “And the horse,” he says, “from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:10), that is, all the pride of their rule, by means of His humble colt. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the chariots and the horse in plain terms.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The waterless pit holds many saints, such as Joseph, Daniel and Jeremiah, whom God brought out unhurt, and symbolically it is Hades, which has no life-giving water.
comments.comment:
… The word commanded by the one in the prophet, or rather God, to Zion and Jerusalem—to the one to rejoice exceedingly, and to the other to proclaim the coming king, saving and strong and being gentle—turns the word toward him who is coming, saying: 'And you also in blood of covenant sent forth your prisoners from a pit not having water' (Zechariah 9:11). For where was it necessary for the prisoners to be, or to be cast down into a pit not having water by those laboring against them? One finds many of the holy men having been cast into waterless pits by those attacking and murdering against them.

For instance, Joseph, being envied because of the goodness and beauty coming toward him, was thrown by those unjustly envying into a pit not having water. Likewise also the wisest Daniel, the friend of God, was thrown by the Babylonians into a pit not having water, so that he might be shown to be without water, being led through there by the lions, not being able to live if he had been filled with waters. And again Jeremiah, the great prophet, the opponents threw into a pit full of mire. And no one of those thus attacked remained without help, God of them having sent them unhurt out of the waterless pit.

And since these things were being fulfilled symbolically, see lest the pit is waterless, being shown through the symbols, the Hades of the ungodly and sinners, there not being any life-giving water, because there is no praiseworthy moisture there at all. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the waterless pit is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The new covenant is confirmed by blood, as Paul says, and the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience far more than the blood of bulls and goats.
comments.comment: The shadowy image of the calf, the new covenant being confirmed by the blood, as Paul says to those believing in the old covenant: 'If the blood of bulls and goats and the sprinkling of the sin offering sanctifies those who are communing toward the purity of the flesh, how much more does the blood of Christ cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living and true God' (Hebrews 9:14). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prisoners released from the waterless pit sit in strongholds, which are salvations, such as the fear of the Lord.
comments.comment:
… What and what kind of security will there be for the prisoners sent out from the pit lacking water, as the Word declares, saying: 'They shall sit in strongholds' (Zechariah 9:12), clearly meaning the praiseworthy 'prisoners of the synagogue' of the glorious Church, no longer having 'a hole or a wrinkle.' But the fortresses are salvations; there the prisoners of the synagogue sit resting, having been carried out from the waterless pit. …

In the divine writing of Proverbs, reverence is called a stronghold for those establishing holiness and righteousness, thus: 'A stronghold is the fear of the Lord' (Proverbs 14:26). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the strongholds are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Church's wall has an inner side of spiritual law and contemplation and an outer side of historical writing, and faith in the Trinity is another wall.
comments.comment:
… What is the Church? It has an inner wall consisting of the spiritual law and the elevated contemplation, and an outer wall, outside the secure wall, which is the explicit and historical writing.

And still, by another metaphor, there is a wall of the well-fortified city: the faith concerning the Trinity and the Only-begotten Son of God, who is the Word of God, truth and the Wisdom of God, which is appropriately surrounded by this understanding of the Word's incarnation and the birth from the unwedded Virgin Mary.

It can be said that the pious thoughts of the Church according to the doctrines of truth serve as a wall guarding it, while the moral teachings and the keeping of the commandments serve as an outer wall. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever sits in the Church's strongholds receives double comfort for his affliction, as Job did, and a promise of life now and in full later.
comments.comment:
… He who sits in this city and in its praiseworthy fortifications, being a bondservant of Christ, lives fearlessly, expecting to receive double in return for what he has been afflicted with: consolation and comfort; for it has been promised to the benefited multitude: 'Instead of one day of your sojourning, I will repay you double' (Zechariah 9:12), the comfort being doubled for those who have undergone affliction.

Take the sensible image of contemplation from the most manly Job. For just as the things previously taken from him were doubled upon him, so those who have trained themselves perfectly toward piety 'have a promise of life, both of the present and of the coming' (cf. 1 Tim 4:8), not of the life that is near, which only pities those who hope in it alone, but of the life which is able to exist now for those believing, according to what was said by the Savior: 'He who believes in me has eternal life' (John 6:47), and again: 'And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Him whom you sent, Jesus Christ' (John 17:3).

He who possesses this life directed toward him will enjoy it being multiplied when the perfection comes and truth is seen face to face. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the promise of double repayment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the first man's transgression separated body from soul, God repays doubly by raising an incorruptible, strong and glorious body.
comments.comment:
Because the body was separated from the soul by the transgression of the first man, the body was being distressed as if to undergo a long-lasting sojourn; instead of existing for one day, God has doubly repaid by raising and giving the soul its body, so that it does not merely receive the same thing, but instead of a corrupt and dishonorable and weak and psychic body, an incorruptible, strong, and glorious body, and this very body is spiritual.

The one paying attention to the reading of the God-breathed oracles and many other things will understand how God doubly repays the one having been relocated for one day. Regarding what is explicitly said: the people, having been taken into the captivity of enemies, were not only redeemed, but also ruled over those who had seized them; when this happened, those who had been slightly afflicted had joy. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father bends Judah, the Savior, as a bow whose arrows bring salvation, unlike the destroying bow of Ephraim, and the Savior is at once the bow, the archer and the chosen arrow.
comments.comment:
… The Father bent a bow for Himself for the Savior rising out of the tribe of Judah, from which He releases arrows aiming at salvation. And see the difference: the destroying bow of Ephraim is named after being used against the enemy. For it is said in Psalm 78:9 regarding satanic powers of enemies and all the heterodox: 'Ephraim, bending and shooting with the bow, how were they turned in the day of battle,' having grown weak and being overthrown, clearly showing the shattering of the shields? For it is said: 'Their sword shall enter into their own heart, and their bows shall be shattered.' The shattering of the bows is the ruling principle of the combatants, from which evil words are sent, the judgment of unheeded arrows about which the divine word says: 'Their tongue, shooting a missile, is deceitful, their words...'

The words of those promising false knowledge are full of the venom of a serpent, killing those who receive them.

But such are not the arrows of the powerful Savior, about which it is said in the forty-fourth Psalm regarding the blessed and excellent archer: 'Your arrows are sharp, mighty' (Psalm 45:5), which instills divine love in those struck by them, as if speaking like a blessed bride possessing divine love: 'I am pierced by love.' And behold the paradox: the same Savior is the bow, the archer, and the arrow. For in the present prophetic word spoken to Him by God, it is said: 'I have bent you, Judah, as my bow' (Zechariah 9:13); but in the Psalm, those praising Him say: 'Your arrows are sharp, mighty' (Psalm 45:5); and He Himself says about Himself in Isaiah: 'He has made me like a chosen arrow; He has hidden me in His quiver' (Isa 49:2). For how could the one fashioning those who are being pierced as chosen not be a chosen arrow, hidden in the quiver which He possessed from the flesh of Mary? …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the bent bow and the arrows are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the bow is bent, Ephraim is struck, and the children of Zion who advocate the truth are raised against the Greeks who advocate false knowledge.
comments.comment: … Once this divine bow is bent, from which the arrows that strike are released into divine love, Ephraim is struck, being overturned and shown to be weak, according to what was said by the sub-text of the Psalm: 'The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, how were they turned back in the day of war' (Psalm 78:9), when the great God, bestowing grace, raised up 'the children of Zion against the children of the Greeks' (Zechariah 9:13)? The generations of Greeks are signified in these things: those advocating false knowledge and all those having impiety, by which the impious send out destructive arrows against those who have not taken up 'the door of faith.' The children of Zion are those advocating the truth, being raised up by God who reigns over them. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God works salvation in two ways, bending a bow for love and wielding a sword against opponents, and we are struck by the living Word to be made alive.
comments.comment:
… God feels for Judah like a warrior wielding a sword," effecting salvation in both ways: just as a bow was strung for a blessed erotic desire, and just as an excellent general feels for a sword, being a warrior, in order to strike down those set in opposition. It is also written about this in the forty-fourth Psalm: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O Mighty One, with your beauty and your splendor, because of truth and gentleness and righteousness, and your right hand shall lead you wondrously" (Psalm 45:3). For how would the right hand not lead wondrously the one who has girded a sword upon his thigh, the Mighty One, paradoxically striking those being struck? …

And we also have been struck saving-ly by the living and active Word, about whom it has been written: "The Word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword" (Hebrews 4:12), so that having been put to death in the flesh, we might be made alive in the spirit. And let us be struck also by the chosen arrow, sent from the drawn bow; for thus we shall be raised up, happening to be children of Zion upon the generations of the Greeks. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The children of Zion overturn the arguments of the Greeks with spiritual weapons, and the Lord over them unites both into one new man.
comments.comment:
… Many, being children and sons of the Greeks, strove according to the dogmas of piety, as to leave behind many writings; but they were overwhelmed when the ecclesiastical men of God rose up against them.

Let us overturn the contentious arguments of those with confidence, saying: 'The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but are powerful in God, demolishing arguments and lifting up every height against the knowledge of God' (2 Cor 10:4-5). When the children of Zion rise up against the Greeks, the Lord, having accomplished this, will be 'over them' (Zech 9:14), uniting those who rise up with those against whom they rise up, as they are prepared to reign with one mind and one judgment, having created the Greek and the Jew into one new man. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When God draws the bow, a flash like lightning goes forth, piercing to divine love and becoming the light of the world.
comments.comment: … And he will go forth like a flash of lightning, and the Lord God of hosts will sound the trumpet and will go forth in the fury of his indignation; the Lord God of hosts will protect them (Zech 9:14-15). When God has drawn the bow against Judah, a flash like lightning will go forth, piercing and striking toward divine love, so as to become the light of the world, which is able to be called a perfect soul or a glorious Church: 'I am wounded by love.' And it is not only there that the things sent from the divine bow are luminous; in Habakkuk it is said toward God: 'Your arrows shall go forth as light, into the brightness of lightning of your weapons' (Habakkuk 3:11). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the flash of lightning that goes forth in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The trumpet is the loud, clear word that is heard and the lightning is what enlightens the mind, and warning serves to turn people back, as at Nineveh.
comments.comment:
What God gives is one trumpet and another flash of lightning. For since the things announced clearly, piercingly, and loudly are heard, they are likened to a trumpet; but since they enlighten the mind, the eye of the soul, they resemble lightning.

Just as all the divine things are bright and loud for those being benefited by free will and for ourselves, so a warning becomes against those turning back easily; whence it is appropriate to compare the one coming like a lightning bolt to the Lord Almighty blowing the trumpet, that the benefactor might be shaken in warning, with much goodness being presented by God walking in a storm of warning, so that he might not be completely cast out, the warning being at times corrected, as it happened regarding the Ninevites (Jonah 3:4).

For having said the one warning: 'In yet three days Nineveh shall be overturned' (Jonah 3:4), it seemed appropriate to shake them in warning and to cause them to turn, so that the place of repentance, offered outside the warning, might make those who had ceased from what they previously were doing to repent. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's going in the whirlwind of wrath means anger over sins and, as with God walking in Eden, a departure felt by the sinner.
comments.comment: … Similar to this is what is brought in Zechariah, said to the sinners: 'the Lord shall go in the whirlwind of his wrath' (Zechariah 9:14). And the whirlwind of wrath signifies the anger because of their sins, for he himself is... The 'shall go' might perhaps be similar to that said in Genesis concerning Adam, that he heard God walking just as he was sinning (Gen 3:8); through this he receives a sensation of the departure of God because he no longer has anything luminous in himself. For those lengthening themselves from God hear: 'the Lord is far from the ungodly' (Proverbs 15:29), not in place of this being said, but in distancing the one being good and the one being bad from Him. And these things are because of the 'shall go in the whirlwind.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord who seems to depart in warning really protects with his shield, and to blow the trumpet is to make his blessings manifest and defend those he enlightens.
comments.comment:
… And indeed, the Lord is not departing from the Jews when they sincerely kept the law and ministered to the one who gave it, nor has he entirely abandoned them to walk in a storm of warning, saying concerning them: 'I have left my house, I have abandoned my inheritance' (Jer 12:7). The abandonment is clearly shown, Jesus saying in the Gospel: 'Behold, your house is left to you' (Luke 13:35). The purpose and the end are shown to be for the good of those being left, from the coming of: 'And the Lord Almighty will move in a storm of warning,' 'The Lord Almighty shall protect them.' For when it seemed to depart in warning, he helped just so, putting forward for them his invincible shield, concerning which it is said in the Hymns to the one being benefited: 'His truth shall surround you as a weapon' (Psalm 91:4). …

The Holy Spirit protects the herald of the truth, raising his voice like a trumpet, so that his teaching, which he brings to war, might rouse those fighting for God against those arrayed militarily against them, and also to call them to the festive assemblies. These things lie in the God-breathed oracles, sometimes with enigma, sometimes in historical narrative.

To show that blowing the trumpet means making things manifest, the words spoken by Jesus to those wishing to give gifts to the poor in the nearby region are sufficient: 'When you do alms, do not sound a trumpet before you.' For he wants this virtue to be practiced in secret, because vainglory is contrary to it and the praise-seeking is clearly performing it; but the command forbidding it is also transgressed: 'What you hate, do not do to another.' For to give gifts to those in need—so I phrase it—is, unfortunately, not to be a friend to the one being benefited, since the giver follows him and does that which he himself does not wish to suffer.

Therefore, when the Lord Almighty enlightens those being helped by him, making manifest what he grants, he blows in a trumpet, defending those well-disposed, so that they may remain unassailable and unharmed, surrounding them clothed in the invincible shield, having put on the whole armor of their ruler and king.

It would also be for us 'to put on the weapons of the light' and 'to take up the shield of faith,' so as to say with boldness: 'You are my help and my defender; my God, do not delay.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Rebuking words like sling-stones consume the wickedness of sinners, and their wine-like blood becomes joy that makes the altars bowls of gladness.
comments.comment:
… the words of rebuke, like stones shot by a sling, will consume the sinners, so that they are no longer enemies of God, the wickedness having been consumed through which they were opposed to the grace of God, after they were struck down by the stones of the sling being made against them. For just as 'love covers a multitude of sins' (1 Pet 4:8) does not allow them to remain, having hidden the sins by making them vanish from all, so the rebuking and corrective words coming upon them, by which they are sling-stoned, will cover them, becoming their covering, the pouring out of their wine-like blood is a joy, as to gladden and pour out abundantly those who are pouring, so as to become altars, bowls, vessels of joy serving for use.

For how does one not partake of the divine, he who offers a sacrifice of praise and righteousness? For just as those performing the rite in an improper way cover the altar with tears, the most corrective voice saying to them: 'You covered my altar with tears; is it still worthy to look upon your sacrifice, or to receive a gift from your hands?' (Mal 2:13) Let these things be said to those sacrificing after impiety; but to those performing the rite piously, as their sacrifices are to be acceptable, the altars will be bowls making joy, so that, having been made sacred, they may be saved, being revealed in a luminous state, on the intellectual day, when they shall be saved, being transformed into a people of God like sheep. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord saves his guarded people like sheep, and the stones, made light, roll upon God's earth and build themselves into the holy city and the spiritual house.
comments.comment:
… the Lord will save those who stand guard as a people like sheep; for after that, the powerful stones will become movable, having been built up with the divine foundation, so as to roll upon the earth of God, becoming light and movable as the weight and stoniness is lifted from them. For so, rolling upon the holy earth of God, they will build themselves up, harmoniously stepping into the walls of the holy city and the building of the temple of God. …

For the first state of those beginning well and as they ought, is to be led like a flock by the best shepherd, so that after these things, having been promoted from sheep to a people, they might be made kings by the one who was previously their shepherd; those who, after being enriched, shall be a people of the Pantokrator and parts of the city being built by the Lord of Powers.

Stones that were rolling upon the earth of God because they had become hollow and light, being placed upon an immovable foundation, having become stones, build; Peter, the spokesman of the apostles, writes: 'To whom approaching, a chosen precious stone by God, and you yourselves, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house for a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ' (1 Peter 2:5). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the flock and the holy stones rolling on his land.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy stones that roll upon the earth are the holy apostles, such as Paul, and the saints are precious stones for the glory of Christ.
comments.comment: … For those leading peoples bring themselves forward unto adornment for Christ, as some precious stones. Therefore also the prophet making clear the holy apostles for us, ‘Holy stones,’ (Zechariah 9:16) he says, ‘roll upon the earth’; of which sort was the divine Paul, running round from Jerusalem even until Illyricum through the proclamation. Precious stones therefore and unto Christ’s glory are the saints’ company. …
comments.selected_reason: Names who the holy stones are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: Whatever is good and beautiful is from God, as James also says that every good gift comes from the Father of lights.
comments.comment:
… That if there is anything good, it is His; and if anything beautiful, it is from Him, grain for youths and fragrant wine for virgins.

That which is principally acceptable and good exists, and that which is uncontradictedly praised is found, agreeing with the prophetic word in the epistle concerning him: 'Every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from above from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning' (Jas 1:17).
comments.selected_reason: Says in a few words that everything good and beautiful comes from God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord alone gives good things, and faith and knowledge must guard what is received as good and beautiful, since he is tasted and his name is like poured-out myrrh.
comments.comment: … Therefore, this one alone gives good things to those asking him, as he is the one whom the soul finds, and as he is the one raising up desire, the Lord, who fills your desire with good things. Faith and knowledge must stand over his giving of the good, so as not to fall into error. For example, thought is a good thing, and a useful good thing is addressed as beautiful. … 'For if anything is good, it is of him; and if anything is beautiful, it is from him,' in harmony with 'milk for young men and fragrant wine for virgins' (Zechariah 9:17), … For how would the sense of smell and taste not be harmed by not tasting the Lord, according to what was said: 'Taste and see that the Lord is good' (Ps 34:8), and the comprehension of the holy breath of his name, according to: 'Myrrh has been poured out for you, therefore the maidens loved you' (Song 1:3)? …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Drought comes as God's judgment when wickedness prevails, as in the three and a half years without rain in Elijah's time.
comments.comment: … When wickedness prevails, drought occurs often, as God judges; therefore the one raging against such things is to be calmed, lest falling into error, as if instead of God they were flattering demons; it is better to be calmed, as to receive prophecies and dreams from them. Such a deception occurred to the Hebrews in the times of Elijah the great prophet, when rain did not become upon the earth for three years and six months, as all things were driven to despair, as an assurance of death, and other animals were ruined through the scarcity of their fodder. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Israel stopped asking God for rain because the prophets of Baal under Jezebel deceived them with false dreams, so God told the prophet to ask for rain.
comments.comment:
… This harm having prevailed, it was the custom for Israel, having been benefited many times by God in such things, to be surrounded by Him and to ask rain from Him so that prosperity might exist. This they have not done, because deception has prevailed, as those seeking from idols are able to drink in what they are not able to provide. And madness came from Jezebel, the wife of the one ruling the Hebrews, being exceedingly an idolater, as she had ensnared him and her husband.

In her days, therefore, the prophets of Baal increased, being an image of the Sidonians, prophesying and uttering words and this very thing being found by them being highlighted in dreams, always daring to follow predictive paths, variously lying when favorable weather arrived, so as to no longer ask for the provision of rain, 'that rises the sun upon the good and the bad and rains upon the just and the unjust' (Matthew 5:45). Since, therefore, those submitted to me have fallen into such ignorance, God, taking pity on those thus submitted, cast upon the prophet to say: 'Ask for rain' (1 Kings 18:41).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord who heals after his anger visits his flock, the house of Judah, whose name means 'confessing', and shepherds it in strength, as Micah foretold.
comments.comment: … It is also necessary for us to become under the good chief shepherd, who dwells in the place of green pasture for those being shepherded by him, so that entering and going out, applying ourselves inwardly and outwardly to divine words, we may be experienced in blessedness and eternal life. And the Lord God the Pantokrator, being the one who after being angry heals beneficially those who fell by the indignation, will visit his flock, which happens to be the house of Judah, that is to say, of the one confessing; for Judah is interpreted as confessing. The Lord God Pantokrator, being, visits his own flock; concerning which it is also said in Micah: 'And he will stand and see and will shepherd his flock in strength, the Lord' (Micah 5:4), being Savior. And the Lord God the Pantokrator will visit his flock, the house of Judah, and will array them like his well-ordered horse in war (Zechariah 10:3). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the Lord visiting his flock is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord God Almighty who visits his flock is the Son, who gave his life as a ransom and sets his flock in order like a fine horse.
comments.comment:
… That the Lord God Pantokrator is the Only-begotten Son of God, this has been demonstrated previously. For the Trinity being of one substance, the one being begotten being of one substance with the one who begotten, the Savior is Lord God Pantokrator from the Lord God Pantokrator. For how could he not be Lord God, 'who was in the beginning with God' (John 1:2)? And just as 'through him all things came to be' (John 1:3), so also he holds and reigns, as to be for this reason Pantokrator. This, then, is the one being theologized, having arrived to find and save the human race, which having fallen like a sheep from the hundred of the rational beings …

He set his own life as a ransom for which he came to save, as if to oversee his own flock, being the house of Judah, concerning which it is said: 'Judah, your brothers shall praise you' (Genesis 49:8). And since a rapid change of progress occurs for those being benefited, he arranges those completing his flock, like a fine horse, 'all having been equipped with one mind and one purpose,' as if to become a best charioteer from a shepherd, riding salvationally. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: From the house of Judah the Lord arranges a bow whose arrows are words of punishment and threat.
comments.comment: … This good has increased by having sent an embassy of those having longing for his arrival, saying: 'Mount the horses, and your riding shall be salvation' (Habakkuk 3:8). From the house of Judah, from a flock having become a fine horse, he looked out and arranged from it a bow, from which he sends arrows, words concerning punishment and threat; concerning which he who arranged the bow said: 'I will satiate my arrows with blood' (Deuteronomy 32:42), and again: 'My arrows will complete them.' It was also said previously that punishments are called arrows for some profound reason. In the seventh Psalm, indeed, concerning the judge of all, living and dead, it is said: 'He has bent his bow and prepared it, and in it he has prepared instruments of death; he has worked his arrows for those being burned' (Psalm 7:12-13). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who suffer well for the Lord become experienced warriors who tread the mud of the slain, and the Lord fights for them.
comments.comment:
… What then will happen when the Lord God the Pantokrator looks out from Judah and arranges from it a war-bow, or when those having suffered well by him from the people of Judah become experienced warriors of war? He will go out in the same manner, the one going out prepared for war, so that to tread the mud of roads, many falling, as mud shall become from the blood. And this happens to those conquering, but not to those being defeated. For those having turned to flight are pursued and hasten, but those charging and hastening, showing their knees through fear, tread the mud of the blood of the slaughtered, returning like the one going out on horseback.

When these righteous ones exist, the Lord their God will be fighting for them and about them, as to say graciously: 'The Lord of strengths is with us, a defender is our God Jacob' (Psalm 46:7), and again: 'In God we will do strength, and he will bring to nothing those crushing us' (Psalm 60:12). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those arrayed under the Lord have courage against all enemies, including the invisible powers, and say that the Lord is their help.
comments.comment:
Having confidence in themselves, they will line up against those against whom they have the fight and the war, as each one might say thankfully: 'The Lord is my light and my savior; whom shall I fear? (Ps 27:1) The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I shrink in cowardice? (Psalm 27:1) In the approaching of those who do evil to eat my flesh, those who afflict me, and my enemies have grown weak and fallen; (Ps 27:3) if an encampment is lined up against me, my heart shall not fear; (Ps 27:3) if a war rises up against me, in this I hope.' (Psalm 27:3).

Having the same courage, he who sings the third Psalm also was emboldened to say: 'I will not fear from ten thousands of people surrounding me.' (Ps 3:6). To those thus arrayed, the word, encouraging them, says: 'One of you shall pursue a thousand, and two shall put ten thousand to flight' (Deuteronomy 32:30), not of men alone as warriors, but also of the invisible.

To those having the struggle, those fighting for Christ and having clothed themselves in His good fortune say: 'Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers and powers and the cosmic dictators of this darkness and the spiritual things of wickedness.' (Eph 6:12). For, having been surrounded by all these warriors, he who, by the designation of God, is like an unassailable shield, full of courage, says: 'Encompassing, they have surrounded me, and by the name of the Lord I defended myself against them.' (Psalm 118:11). The same thing this one also cries out triumphantly: 'Behold, the Lord helps me; who shall harm me?' (Isaiah 50:9). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who trust in horses are deceived and put to shame, as Pharaoh was, and the riders are undisciplined souls who cannot control their bodies.
comments.comment:
… They are being deceived, having learned through experience that 'a false horse is for salvation.' Concerning those fighting in this way, the choir of the saints says: 'These are in chariots and these are on horses, but we shall rejoice in the name of the Lord; they themselves were overthrown and fell, but we have risen and been set upright' (Psalm 20:7). Similarly to these, the tyrant of Egypt and all those marshaled with him were dejected when they were crushed in the Red Sea, as a victory hymn began to be sung against them from: 'I will sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; he has thrown horse and rider into the sea' (Ex 15:1). Concerning these riders, it is also said in one of the Psalms: 'From your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those standing on horses have been unseated' (Psalm 76:6).

Who, then, are these who are being overseen? If horses are understood to be human bodies, because they are skittish and unruly, souls are found to be riders who are not disciplined, not skillfully subduing the horses upon which they ride; therefore they also endure shame, being tossed about, as the prophetic word says: 'The riders of horses shall be put to shame' (Zechariah 10:5). According to another understanding, the pompous and sophistical men were understood to be horses, upon whom evil powers ride in a disorderly manner, not knowing how to guide with reins but being carried by a disorderly force, who, because they approach the four-footed passions unskillfully, shall be put to shame; they fall into pits because they doze and slumber, not enduring the things of those who ride salvationally. For the soul that subdues and leads the body surrounding it is not a mere passenger, nor a rider, but a horseman, skillfully controlling the hooves. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A true horseman who guides the horse with skill differs from a mere rider, and it is the passengers who will be put to shame.
comments.comment:
… An ancient wise man commanded that horsemen be distinguished from mere riders, calling one false and the other praiseworthy; for he who holds back without skill, not guiding the horse with reins, is merely a rider, as the aforementioned wise man demonstrated, whereas the one practicing the art of horsemanship is called righteous. Immediately, as the great prophet Elijah was being taken up, Elisha the God-inspired one cried out, 'Father, father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen!' (2 Kings 2:12). For the one riding most excellently, having guided his own vehicle, ought to be called a horseman, not merely a rider.

Since this distinction between horseman and rider exists, it is not the horsemen but the passengers who will be disgraced, as they slumber while those riding with skill are sober and watchful, guiding the reins; therefore, those proven as victors bring victory, while the passengers of blameworthy horses are put to shame. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God strengthens Judah and saves Joseph, as the Savior from Judah fed the hungry, and promises to let them dwell because he loved them.
comments.comment:
… Those of Judah prevail, and the house of Joseph lives and will be saved by God, the King of all; from the parallel of Joseph and Judah, the Savior who became man exists, since from Judah he rose up and provided food to those suffering from famine and starvation, so that he might ultimately be shown to be full of bread, having received the greatest prosperity; for it is said concerning the offspring of Mary that those who previously famished because they lacked spiritual food were filled with good things, which their intelligent Joseph provided. Indeed, he has come to such abundance that, just as in the wilderness he nourished those deprived of food into a flock, he fed large multitudes from very few loaves.

Having strengthened the house of Judah and the house of Joseph, God promises to let them dwell, for no other reason than that he loved them. But when will this be? When they are enjoying what they have; he persuaded them with promises, concerning which it is written here: 'Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it come upon the heart, what God has prepared for those who love him' (1 Cor 2:9). And the promised things shall be for them, in the manner of 'I have not turned them away, but I look upon and care for them,' the Lord being 'their God.' For I will hear of them being exceedingly fruitful according to Ephraim (Zechariah 10:7), interpreting fruitfulness as their intellect having eaten and rejoiced, as in wine …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The drinking of the divine wine means joy in beholding the mysteries of the kingdom, and the spiritual children begotten by teachers share it.
comments.comment:
… What results from the drinking of the divine wine? Or is it to be made glad from beholding the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven and other things which possess a high contemplation, by which one will see God, having approached with a pure heart 'by the character of his subsistence,' as he calls the existing one an 'image' and character 'of the invisible God': 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9)?

Not only will these themselves enjoy the promises of the holy visions, but also the children themselves whom they have begotten by divine instruction and imitation of an excellent life. For the Apostle in Christ writes to the Corinthians and the Galatians: to the former, 'Through the gospel I have begotten you' (1 Corinthians 4:15); to the latter, 'My children, whom I again labor for until Christ is formed in you' (Gal 4:19). And Peter, the foremost of the apostles, writes as to his own children the letter he has engraved: 'As children of obedience, not being conformed to the former manner of life' (1 Pet 1:14). And Barnabas also, an apostle with Paul, having been placed at the circumcision, having sent a letter to the faithful according to the gospel, addresses it as to sons and daughters. And the hymnist addresses those being born from him according to virtue: 'Come, children, listen to me, I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days?' (Psalm 34:11).

The children will be made glad in mind, in the heart so named, in no one other than their Lord God, saying to each of those living according to the divine Gospel: 'Enter into the joy of your Lord' (Matt 25:21). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord brings in the captives gradually, by signalling his goodwill.
comments.comment: … The Lord, intending to bring in those alienated by the manner of captivity, does not do this all at once, but by signaling His benevolence to those receiving it. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus invites the weary to take his yoke and find rest, and he redeems those he signals, as Peter says, with the precious blood of Christ.
comments.comment:
The practice of contemplation is especially brought forward in the Gospels; for Jesus, desiring to give rest to souls, says, 'Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and you will find rest for your souls; and take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; for my yoke is good and my burden is light' (Matt 11:28-30). By saying, 'Come to me and I will give you rest,' he signifies how he judges them worthy to receive him into himself so that they might lift off his yoke, which is good, and the light burden. …

For whose sake does he signify and receive them, saying in harmony: 'Because I will redeem them and multiply them, because they were many' (Zechariah 10:8)? He redeems them from the law of captivity of shoulders and unclad tyrants who had led them away from their own commonwealth.

The manner and how the restoration to liberty is exalted lies in other writings. Indeed, one of the saints cried out to the benefactor: 'My joy, redeem me from those who persecute me'; and again: 'Redeem me, Lord God of truth.' Peter, the foremost of Christ's disciples, makes manifest a turning away of those who had rushed from their former wickedness, writing to the faithful: 'You were not redeemed from your futile, ancestral way of life with corruptible gold or silver, but in the precious blood of Christ, the lamb without blemish and without spot' (1 Pet 1:18-19). The Savior, having redeemed, promised this. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's multiplying of his people means excellence as well as number, as Abraham became father of many nations through faith, and it is to be understood spiritually.
comments.comment:
… The statement, 'I will multiply them because they were many,' is necessarily relevant; it refers not only to a multiplication in number, but also to an excellence in honor, similar to the blessing spoken by God toward Abraham: 'I will increase him, and I will multiply him, and I will bless him, and he shall be a blessing; a father of many nations, being revealed as a gift of God.' He becomes a father of many nations not merely according to the flesh, but according to the intelligible, clearly meaning that his children and sons are those who do his works and possess faith.

Indeed, the Savior himself, most strongly rebuking those who claim to have Abraham as a father according to the flesh, said: 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham' (John 8:39). By this understanding, 'the vessel of election,' the apostle Paul writes to the Church, clarifying how the holy patriarch is a father of the nations, asserting: 'As many as are of faith, these are sons of Abraham, being blessed with him' (Galatians 3:7). The same view is proposed by that prophecy brought forth in Isaiah: 'The few shall become thousands, and the least a great nation' (Isaiah 60:22).

Taking these things in a sensory way provokes laughter, since many saints did not bear children at all: namely Elijah and Elisha, and John the Baptist, of whom no one greater was praised in deed or holy knowledge; they in no way bore children, so it is appropriate to understand the multiplication of those possessing such promises spiritually, 'because they were many.' For the righteous did not begin to multiply and become many only in this present life, according to the assigned understanding; for they were many even before this present life. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God will multiply them because they were many.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints are like seeds sown among the peoples, bringing them to their own virtue, as Jesus sent his disciples to all nations.
comments.comment: … These, being many, were like seeds that he sowed among the peoples so that they might partake of their virtue. Just as seeds thrown into the earth transform the lying soil to become offspring and fruit, so those sown among the peoples and the nations bring those whom they have sown into their own quality, as if becoming imitators of their virtue. No one errs in saying that those who heard were sown by Jesus, saying: 'Go and make disciples of all nations' (Matthew 28:19); and even to the same in the Gospel according to John: 'For this reason I said to you,' that is, I appointed and demonstrated, 'that you might go and bear more fruit' (John 15:16) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sowing among the peoples in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints are taken captive among the peoples so that by their virtue they show themselves to be grain of saving seed, and the nations remember and turn to the Lord.
comments.comment: … I think that in this way the saints are taken captive with the peoples and into Babylon and Assyria, so that by imparting their own virtue they might show themselves to be ears of grain and offspring of saving seeds. This will be consistent with the remembering of the Lord by those who had drifted away from him through sins and impiety. Especially these promises fit those who have believed from the nations. For it has been said concerning them in the 121st and 1st Psalm: 'All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, for the kingdom is the Lord's and he is the ruler of the nations.' For how could he not rule and be the master of those remembered who have turned to him, as to worship and glorify the one who holds them as a benefactor? …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who have been benefited will rear their own children with spiritual food, as righteous fathers such as Zechariah, Abraham and Paul did.
comments.comment:
… What will follow for those remembering the All-King, or that it might happen in a non-literal sense regarding 'the city of the living God,' being heavenly, according to what was said: 'You who are far off, remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem ascend to your heart.' Those having been benefited by their own Savior, being as it were servants and many-children by spiritual upbringing, will rear their own children, imparting intellectual food, as it is announced concerning each one according to the writing of the divine Proverbs: 'A righteous father brings up his children well.'

This can be understood toward spiritual upbringing, and also according to history; for being a righteous father, Zechariah reared well John the Baptist, who was his child, just as Abraham reared Isaac, and Isaac reared Jacob; and he himself, Paul the divine, reared profitably and praiseworthily those whom he had begotten through the gospel. For it is possible to hear him writing to the Corinthians: 'I gave you milk.' Similarly Peter writes to the faithful in the dispersion: 'Having been born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible through the word of the living and abiding God, as newborn babes, long for the spiritual milk, so that in it you may grow unto salvation.' In this same way also the evangelist John, having begotten the disciples through him by a way of instruction, writes to the whole Church: 'Children, keep yourselves from idols.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God brings the children back from the spiritual tyrant of Egypt and the ruler of Assyria, who may be one evil power or several.
comments.comment:
… They will find their own children, those who have become fathers, and they will turn them back with divine exhortations and instructions, so that they may no longer be with evildoers in ungodly lands, this being granted by God, as He Himself said: 'I will bring them back from Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will receive them' (Zechariah 10:10), so that they may no longer be subdued by the spiritual tyrant of Egypt, nor be held by the ruler of the Assyrians, called 'the great mind' because of the cunning and absurdity of thoughts, which the common people do not refute, but only those speaking God-wisely say: 'For we do not ignore his thoughts.'

It is possible to call the same tyrant the ruler of the Egyptians and the Assyrians through another energy; and even if different evil powers were signified by various names, it does not grieve, for such a thing is not impossible, with many being 'rulers and powers of this darkness, but also cosmic rulers and spiritual wickedness' (Ephesians 6:12). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those brought into Gilead and Lebanon are those who migrate from wickedness to virtue, from strength to strength, and from the shadow of the law to its truth.
comments.comment:
… The provider of great gifts, having freed from Egypt and Assyria those who are well-rearing their children and those who begot them, promises to bring them into Gilead and Lebanon, with no evil king still bothering them. And see if he brings into Gilead those who strive to have the migration of martyrdom, the movement from wickedness into virtue; for the one repenting from sin into righteousness, from ungodliness into godliness, is being migrated, as the righteous are being migrated in a different way from the introduction of instruction into the following progress, and from that into the succeeding one, until that very end, with which nothing other good exists, being the final object of desire.

In this way, concerning those being migrated, the hymnist says: 'They shall go from strength to strength' (Psalm 84:7). And they are also migrated from the shadow of the law into its truth, those having ascended above the killing letter (2 Corinthians 3:6) and becoming in the life-giving Spirit. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sea stands for human life, and the saints are fishermen and steersmen who work in its many waters and see God's wonders in the depth.
comments.comment:
… Continuously in the divine words, the manner of the earth and the cosmic movement of the sea are brought forward. The evangelical parable concerning the net indicates nothing sensible, all of it pronouncing an ascent; for the net cast into human life upon a field of the fishes in it, so named allegorically, is the God-breathed scripture, manifoldly woven by 'the manifold wisdom of God.' But the sea is the condition regarding us, widening and broadening for the greedy and the passion-loving, near to those remaining in the motionless; for the fish does not leave a voice, nor does it have a distinct appearance, since even its sensation is not precise.

Even if the fishes being caught by it have nothing manifest, because of the weakness of their soul and sensation, nevertheless the holy men, being fishermen and catchers of fishes, do work and in the multitude of the water of the sea. Concerning them indeed it has been written in divine hymns: 'Those descending into the sea in ships, doing work in many waters, they themselves saw the works of God and his wonders in the depth.'

Human lives descend into the surging, salt-filled swell in human ships, which are bodies, in order to do work in many waters, fishing and steering; for each of the intelligent ones has steering, being one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For it has been said that 'the comprehension and the steering' of the Holy Spirit is a gift. In being a pilot, the intelligent one and fisherman exists, having that art about which Jesus said to the known ones: 'Come after me and I will make you fishers of men' (Matthew 4:19).

Those doing work in many waters see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the depth, approaching as if to the judgments of God, encountering a great abyss. For even if they are unsearchable, but having the Spirit of God who searches its depths, they see in the depth the wonders and works of God.

See also another work of those descending into the sea, being announced in the prophet Isaiah: 'They shall be cast in ships of foreigners, they shall manage the sea at once' (Isaiah 23:3); saying ships of foreigners regarding the bodies because they are of a different nature from the souls that are sailing …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture often uses the cedars of Lebanon to signify the haughty, and this verse speaks of the great ones in this life.
comments.comment: Often he signifies the haughty ones by this wood: 'And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.' There are also praiseworthy cedars. But concerning the great ones in this life, he signifies by this name: 'Open, O Lebanon, your gates; fire consumes your cedars' (Zechariah 11:1). … So there are also praiseworthy cedars, but the word is not concerning these now.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The command to open the gates of Lebanon is an enigma: it is spoken not to the mountain or its woods but to arrogant and proud men.
comments.comment:
Likewise, the present word of the prophet, being brought forth enigmatically, brings forth a concealed teaching. An enigma is this: 'Open, Lebanon, your gates' (Zechariah 11:1).

For it is not toward the perceptible mountain, which is soulless, nor the woods within it according to sense and imagination, that the command is made, so that the gates of Lebanon might be opened and the fallen cedars of the pines might crash; but toward men, arrogant and proud, falling into lawless idolatry toward 'the ruler of this age' (John 12:31).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Lebanon and its cedars stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The trees of the prophecy are great tyrants, and naming rational beings after trees is no wonder, since God's wisdom is called a vine and the Tree of Life.
comments.comment: Having large branches, imitating both firs and pines. … For how could they desire and imitate such great tyrants, to the point where it is possible to perceive them as tangible woods, in whose side-branches and limbs all winged creatures dwell and wild beasts give birth? … And it is nothing wonderful that the names of woods are categorized among rational animals, when even the wisdom of God is sometimes called a true vine, and sometimes the Tree of Life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The weeping shepherds and roaring lions are the leaders of the peoples, who lament because the gains and the cover of ferocity they trusted in have been taken from them.
comments.comment: Their greatness has been brought to misery; it is the roar of lions, because the thicket of the Jordan has been ruined. … The leaders of the peoples, who are shepherds of them both priestly and teaching-wise, turn out to be like sheep, while there are those presiding kingly rather than tyrannically as lions. And since both types of rulers are called shepherds and lions, it is necessary for all the subjects to be brought as sheep and other cattle, having a tendency toward the shepherds who graze, and toward the lions for the cattle. It has been said indeed in Proverbs: 'A lion is stronger than cattle, who does not turn away nor falls upon every cattle' (Proverbs 30:30). … Having fallen into misery, those under the teachers—rather, false teachers—and those lying tyrannically over them, the shepherds lament, not being sparing of the flocks, but having been deprived of shameful gains and for the sake of seizing pleasures, so that they might not serve the Law-giving God and Him who has given them to rule, but rather their own bellies. Concerning the heterodox, the divinely-inspired Apostle writes, correcting the peoples of the Church: 'Do not be carried away by strange and varied teachings; for it is good to be established by grace' (Hebrews 13:9), and again: 'For such teachers serve their own bellies, not Christ, deceiving the hearts of the simple through exploitation and greed' (Hebrews 13:9), appearing as pastures through simplicity. These, having suddenly come into perplexity, lament the things they desire to be pleasant, their greatness having been brought to misery, which they thought they had deceitfully; likewise also those who rule tyrannically roar, the Jordan having been ruined where they spoke and were hidden, thinking they had cover and safety through ferocity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some shepherds of the rational flock preside by God's will and others impiously, and the command to shepherd the sheep of the slaughter is addressed to the good ones.
comments.comment: Thus says the Lord of Hosts: 'Shepherd the sheep of the slaughter, which those who owned them were slaughtering and did not care, and those selling them said: Blessed is the Lord and we have become rich, and their shepherds suffered nothing upon them' (Zech 11:4-5). … Regarding those appointed to instruct and shepherd the rational flock, some preside according to the will of God, while others preside impiously and erringly. Concerning both of the ranks of shepherds, it is possible to gather testimonies from the Scripture. … Concerning those who excellently perform the oversight they were handed, it is said by God: 'I will give to them'—clearly to the flocks—'shepherds according to my heart, and they shall shepherd them, shepherding with knowledge' (Jer 3:15). … Having separated the good law-keepers from the handlers, a command is given to those who are skilled, having this character: 'Shepherd the sheep of the slaughter,' either those already slaughtered or those worthy of this suffering or those unjustly being plotted against. The latter is shown in the one hundred and nineteenth Psalm, of those being plotted against unto death, saying toward the benefactor God: 'Because of you we are being killed all the day, we were counted as sheep of the slaughter' (Psalm 44:22), and also: 'You gave us as sheep for food' (Psalm 44:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the shepherds are and who the sheep of the slaughter are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who shepherd with knowledge are the apostles, prophets, teachers and evangelists of the Church, while the impious shepherds mix in foreign doctrines and subject people to demons, as Jeremiah and the Psalms testify.
comments.comment:
… Concerning those who thus shepherd the flock with knowledge, the Christ-bearing Apostle remembers those placed in the Church with the apostles and prophets, as teachers and evangelists. And perhaps apostles and prophets, teachers and evangelists, are those who gnostically and prudently instruct the assembly of Christ, shepherding those possessing a practical life and presiding over good works, not unskillfully returning the faith and the understandings of Christians, while those who oppose the skilled shepherds through faultiness are named impious; the God...

For he says regarding them and that other wickedness is at work: 'The priests did not say: Where is the Lord?' And those holding to my law did not believe me, and the shepherds were impious toward me,' and the following.

… Those impious in this way and fornicators turn out to be, perhaps also licentious, but certainly also mixing with diverse and foreign doctrines, they subject people to demons and to 'the wisdoms of the rulers of this age' (1 Corinthians 2:6). Immediately, for instance, 'those not having tested God to have in knowledge, having been handed over to a reprobate mind (Rom 1:28), do what is not fitting, licentiously reproaching one another, men performing indecency with men, but also their females having abandoned the natural use of womanhood contrary to nature and suffering, but also women licentiously approaching women.'

… Regarding the impious shepherds' sensual licentiousness toward God, and lusting with evil powers, according to that which is said in the Psalms toward the provider of piety: 'Behold, those distancing themselves from you shall perish, you having destroyed all the fornicating one from you. But for me to cling to God is good' (Psalm 73:27-28).

… Concerning the impious law-keepers, in Jeremiah it is brought as being announced toward the fornicating soul: 'And you had many shepherds as a hindrance to yourself' (Jeremiah 3:3), and also: 'You have fornicated with many shepherds; and you returned pretending toward me, says the Lord' (Jeremiah 3:1). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Shepherds who think they own the flock sell it for shameful gain and boast of being rich, and so feel no sympathy with it as the Apostles did.
comments.comment: Those who think they are owners and not shepherds of the flocks entrusted to them, slaughtering the sheep with a knife—and this is their sophistical discourse, proclaiming impious attitudes—did not regret or repent for what they acted in robbery and murder. For they carelessly sell those things which are not their own as if they were theirs, and with shameless audacity they shout that they have grown rich, while those who strive to please the one who deems the All-King to be the shepherd of the flock do not slaughter nor prevent those which the sheep logically entrusted, so that they might unjustly grow rich from greed and shameful gains. … In order that such a thing might not happen through the inattention of the overseers of the Church, the proclaimer of the apostles, Peter, cries out, thus writing: 'I exhort the elders among you to shepherd the flock that is among you, not by compulsion but willingly, not exercising dominion over the appointed ones, so that, when the Chief Shepherd, Christ Jesus, is revealed, you may receive the unfading crown of glory' (1 Pet 5:2-4); meaning those who exercise dominion, namely the sheep of Christ, while the negligent shepherds are acting, selling for shameful gains the divine flocks so that they shout, 'We have grown rich,' devouring those whom they lift up through scandals. … Thus, having harmed and done evil to the peoples, the sheep allegorically called, their false shepherds suffered nothing from them, not sympathizing with the flock according to the one saying: 'Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is stumbled, and I am not burned?' (2 Corinthians 11:29).
